business-management/07-raw-materials/07-.title: 07-1 What Raw Materials Really Are
business-management/07-raw-materials/07-.description:
Part of 07 Raw MaterialsYou already use the phrase without thinking about it. "We need to order raw materials." "The raw materials got more expensive." It sounds obvious — the stuff you make things out of. But the word raw is doing something sneaky, and pulling it apart is worth ten minutes, because raw materials sit at the very bottom of your cost sheet, at the very start of your supply chain, and usually at the root of whatever is quietly eating your margin.A raw material is a basic physical input that a business buys and then transforms into the thing it sells.Three words in that sentence are doing the work: Buys — it came from outside. You didn't make it; somebody else did, and you paid for it. That makes it a Suppliers relationship, not an internal one. Physical — you can weigh it, spill it, store it, and lose it. This is what separates materials from services, information, or labour. Transforms — it doesn't sit next to your product. It becomes part of it. Flour doesn't accompany a loaf; flour is the loaf, rearranged. That third word is the one people get wrong, and it's the one that decides everything else.Here's the idea that unlocks the whole chapter: nothing is a raw material on its own. It's a raw material to somebody.The same bag of flour is a finished product to the mill that bagged it and a raw material to the bakery that bakes with it. Same bag. Same flour. Two completely different roles, depending on where you're standing.Two useful consequences follow. First, when someone says "we're a raw materials business," they mean they sell to other businesses that will transform what they produce — they're one step up from the ground. Second, and more practically, the same firm can be both things at once. A steel mill buys iron ore (raw material) and sells sheet steel (finished product), and it will describe itself either way depending on who it's talking to.So always ask the locating question: whose product is this an input to?Once you accept that "raw material" is a role rather than a category, the pile of things you buy sorts itself into distinct types. Each one behaves differently on your accounts and in your warehouse.The distinction matters because it decides where a cost shows up, and therefore what you can do about it. Raw materials and components move with your output — make twice as many loaves, buy twice as much flour. That's a variable, direct cost, and it's covered properly in the Costs chapter. The gas bill and the machine oil barely twitch when output doubles; they're overhead, and they behave nothing like materials.If you'd rather have it as a decision, here's the test in one picture:
Run your finger backwards along the chain and raw materials are always the furthest thing from you. You buy from a Tier 1 supplier. That supplier bought from a Tier 2. Somewhere at the far end, a farmer, a mine or a well produced the actual substance — and you will probably never meet them, never negotiate with them, and never see their name on a document.
Photo by Pixabay on PexelsThat distance has three real consequences.You don't control the price. Steel, wheat, oil, cotton, cocoa and copper are traded on world markets. Their prices move with weather, harvests, energy costs, shipping rates and geopolitics — none of which you vote on. This is the Market chapter's supply curve, applied to your own shopping list: a bad harvest isn't a small event, it's a supply-side shift that lands on your cost base whether you like it or not. The Economy chapter is where these ripples get explained properly.You don't fully control the quality, either. Raw materials arrive with natural variation. Wheat from one harvest behaves differently from the next; timber has knots; cocoa beans vary by origin. This sets a quality ceiling on your product, which is why the Product chapter and this one shake hands constantly. You can add skill, technology and care — but you cannot make a great loaf out of poor flour.You carry the risk of them running out. A shortage upstream stops production downstream, and the further away the cause, the later you find out.Aurelia makes chocolate bars and sells them for £2.50 each. Her raw materials are cocoa beans, sugar, milk powder, cocoa butter and vanilla. Notice that the sugar is a raw material to her and a finished product to the refinery down the road. Notice too that her cocoa arrives via a trader, who bought it from an exporter, who bought it from farmers she'll never visit.Say her figures look like this:A cocoa price that moves 20% — entirely normal in that market — has just taken more than half her profit. She did nothing wrong. She changed no recipe, lost no customer, hired nobody. A weather event four thousand miles away reached into her till.This is why raw materials matter so much more than their share of the invoice suggests. Every penny saved or lost on materials goes straight to profit. Shave 5p off the cost of a bar and her profit goes up by nearly half; win 5p more on price and she has to fight a competitor for it. Cost reduction on materials is the cheapest profit in business.She has three honest responses, and they map neatly onto decisions from other chapters: Charge more. Possible — but only if her customers aren't easily tempted by the bar next to hers on the shelf. That's the elasticity question from the Market chapter, and it's decided by how differentiated her bar really is. Reformulate. Swap some cocoa butter for a cheaper alternative, or change the recipe. That's a Product decision with a quality consequence — and a Customer Service consequence if anyone notices. Absorb it. Accept the thinner margin, or hedge by buying cocoa forward at a fixed price. Either way, the Financials chapter is where the damage eventually shows. A good strategist usually does a bit of all three — and, crucially, decides before the invoice arrives rather than after.Go back to the four jobs from the opening of this book and see how neatly they fit around a warehouse full of flour. Planning means forecasting what you'll need — your sales forecast, plus expected waste, plus a buffer for the weeks when supply is unreliable. Organizing means setting up the sourcing, the contracts, the delivery schedule and the storage. Leading shows up in the buyer–supplier relationship; suppliers bend over backwards for people they like and trust, as the Suppliers chapter argues. Controlling is the one businesses skip, and it's the one that finds money. Measure material usage per unit of output — kilos of flour per hundred loaves, grams of cocoa per bar. When that number creeps up, someone is wasting, spilling, over-portioning or stealing, and you'll know within a week instead of at year-end. Know your material base. Usually two or three inputs carry most of the cost. Those are the ones worth your attention; the rest are noise. Watch the market, not just the invoice. Your supplier's price is a result. The cause lives in a commodity market, a harvest, a shipping route or a currency — and it moves before the invoice does. Remember the quality ceiling. Materials set the upper bound on what you can sell; process and skill only decide how close to the ceiling you get. Treat materials as cash in a different form. Stock sitting in a warehouse is money you've spent and can't use. That's a Financials and Stores problem, and it deserves the same attention as the price you paid. Look for substitutes before you're forced to. The best time to find an alternative material is while the current one is still cheap. A raw material is a basic physical input a business buys and transforms into what it sells — bought in, physical, and turned into the product rather than merely used alongside it. It is a role, not a substance. The same item is a raw material to one firm and a finished product to another, so always ask whose input it is. Materials sort into raw materials, components, consumables, goods for resale and capital goods — and each lands in a different place on the cost sheet. Raw materials come from the far end of the supply chain, which means you rarely control their price, their quality or their availability. They are direct, variable costs, so savings and losses hit profit one-for-one — which is why materials are usually the most rewarding place to look for margin. Managing them is the management loop applied to the warehouse: plan the forecast, organise the sourcing, control the usage per unit. Next, we'll sort raw materials into their main types — and see why a cocoa bean, a barrel of crude oil and a sheet of steel behave nothing alike.
Photo by Bamidele Sodiq on Pexels

business-management/07-raw-materials/07-.title: 07-2 Types of Raw Materials
business-management/07-raw-materials/07-.description:
Part of 07 Raw MaterialsHere's the thing about raw materials: the word "raw" makes them sound uniform, like a single sack of stuff sitting at the back of the warehouse. In reality, a business's raw materials might be iron ore, live cattle, fresh basil, sand, crude oil, and recycled cardboard — all at once. Grouping them isn't academic box-ticking. Each type behaves differently, and that behaviour ripples straight through your costs, your suppliers, your factories, and your bottom line.Think of it like sorting a crowd of people. You can sort by age, by job, by hometown, or by how early they wake up. None of those is the right answer — each one tells you something different, and which lens you reach for depends on the question you're asking. The same is true here. Let's walk through the most useful lenses.This is the most intuitive way to carve things up, and it's a good starting point.Plant and agricultural materials. Cotton, timber, wheat, cocoa, rubber, sugar beet, palm oil. They're grown, and growth depends on weather, seasons, and soil. That means supply wobbles — a drought in one region moves prices worldwide. (Your Market chapter explained how supply and demand set price; agricultural raw materials are the clearest, most brutal example of that mechanism in action.)Animal materials. Hides and leather, wool, dairy, tallow. Niche but important for fashion, furniture, food, and some cosmetics.Mined and mineral materials. Iron ore, bauxite, copper, lithium, cobalt, potash, gravel. You can't grow more of these on a useful timescale, and they tend to sit in specific countries — which is exactly why so many Regulations and trade disputes revolve around them. Note the weight consideration here too: nobody ships gravel across an ocean to save a few pennies, because the Distribution cost dwarfs the material cost.Fossil and energy-derived materials. Crude oil, natural gas, and coal aren't just fuels — they're the starting point for plastics, fertilisers, synthetic fibres, and a huge range of chemicals. Buy a plastic bottle and you've indirectly bought petrochemicals.Water and industrial gases. Easy to forget, but breweries, soft-drink makers, and food processors treat water as a primary raw material, and they care enormously about its quality and consistency. Welders and hospitals buy oxygen and nitrogen by the tank.
Photo by Kefentse Molotsane on PexelsA second lens, and one that now carries real commercial weight: Renewable — timber, crops, wool. Replaceable within a human lifetime, if managed well. Non-renewable — metals, minerals, fossil feedstocks. Use it and it's gone. Secondary (recycled) — scrap steel, recovered paper, recycled plastic, reclaimed glass. That third category is the fastest-growing one in many industries, and it's a beautiful illustration of how chapters interlock. A recycled input can cut raw material Costs, reduce exposure to commodity price spikes, and satisfy tightening environmental Regulations and packaging rules. It can also become a marketing asset that lifts Revenue — customers will pay more for a product whose story they like. Skipping this category isn't just old-fashioned; it's ignoring a lever.Ask a simple question: does this material end up inside the thing we sell?Direct materials do. Flour in bread, steel in a bicycle frame, cotton in a T-shirt, glass in a bottle.Indirect materials don't, but production grinds to a halt without them — machine lubricants, cleaning chemicals, welding gases, safety gloves, replacement drill bits.Why care? Because this split maps almost perfectly onto the direct and indirect Costs you met earlier, and it shapes how you track inventory in your Financials. Direct materials scale with output: make twice as much, buy twice as much. Indirect materials often behave more like fixed overhead — a factory uses roughly the same drum of lubricant whether it runs at 70% or 100% capacity. Get that distinction wrong in your costing and you'll misjudge which products are actually profitable."Raw" is a matter of where you stand on the supply chain. The same substance is raw material to one business and finished input to another.
A bakery typically buys at the "commodity" or "intermediate" rung — flour and sugar are already refined. A carmaker buys at the "component" rung — stamped panels, wiring looms, tyres. A mining company sells at the very first rung.Where you choose to buy isn't a detail. It decides which Suppliers you deal with, how much of the Manufacturing work you take on yourself, and what your cost structure looks like. Buying lower down the ladder is usually cheaper per unit but demands more capability; buying higher up costs more but is faster and simpler. That's a genuine strategic choice, and it's one Competitors are making at the same time — often in the opposite direction.Finally, sort by how the material forces you to handle it. This is where raw materials meet your Stores and Distribution chapters.Perishable. Fresh milk, cut flowers, berries, live yeast. They have a shelf life measured in hours or days, which forces fast production, cold chain logistics, and ruthless stock rotation — first in, first out. Waste here is pure lost margin.Bulky or heavy. Sand, cement, gravel, coal. Low value per kilogram, so transport distance is the enemy. Plants that use them tend to sit right next to the source.Hazardous. Acids, solvents, flammable liquids. Extra storage rules, extra insurance, extra regulation, extra cost — but unavoidable in many chemical and metalworking businesses.Standardised vs critical. A standardised commodity like copper wire trades on global exchanges; you can buy it from almost anyone and hedge the price. A critical material — a rare-earth element, a specialised alloy, a single-origin botanical — might come from two suppliers on one continent. There, your supplier relationship is your risk management.
Photo by Willians Huerta on PexelsA small bakery. Direct materials: flour, butter, sugar, eggs, yeast, salt. Indirect materials: oven cleaner, pan grease, parchment paper, gloves. Classification by origin: mostly agricultural, highly perishable, water is a key input. By stage: buying at the intermediate rung. What should the owner worry about? Flour price volatility (a Market issue), spoilage (Stores and Distribution), and butter costs, which swing with dairy markets. Cheap, fast, simple — but not risk-free.A phone assembler. Direct materials: aluminium, glass, copper, gold traces, lithium. Indirect: solder flux, cleaning solvents, isopropyl alcohol. Classification by origin: mineral-heavy. By renewability: almost entirely non-renewable, with a growing recycled stream. By criticality: cobalt and rare earths sourced from a handful of regions, exposed to geopolitics, tariffs, and conflict-mineral Regulations. Same word — "raw materials" — but the second business lives in a totally different world of risk.
Photo by Marcelo Solis on PexelsRaw materials come in types, and the type tells you where you're exposed: By origin — plant, animal, mineral, fossil-derived, water and gases. By renewability — renewable, non-renewable, or secondary/recycled, with growing regulatory and reputational weight. By role in the product — direct materials become the product; indirect materials keep the machines running. By stage of processing — the ladder from extracted commodity to finished part, and the strategic choice of where you buy. By behaviour — perishable, bulky, hazardous, or critical, each demanding different storage, transport, and supplier tactics. Here's the payoff. Every one of those labels points to a lever you can pull: price risk points to contracts and hedging; perishability points to logistics and stock rotation; criticality points to supplier relationships; renewability points to regulation, cost savings, and brand. You don't need to memorise the categories — you need to look at your own material list and ask, honestly, which types am I actually dependent on? That question is where good business strategy starts, and it's the thread we'll pull on next, when we look at raw materials as a factor across the whole business.

business-management/07-raw-materials/07-.title: 07-3 Raw Materials as a Factor Across the Whole Business
business-management/07-raw-materials/07-.description:
Part of 07 Raw MaterialsRaw materials sit at the far end of the business — furthest from the customer, least visible on the shop floor, and easiest to treat as somebody else's problem. That's exactly why they deserve their own lens. You can run a beautiful operation and still watch your profit evaporate because the price of flour moved, because a harvest failed, or because a batch arrived a shade too damp. Nobody outside your business ever sees your raw materials. Everybody inside it feels them.This subsection zooms out. Rather than looking at raw materials as a purchasing task, we'll follow the threads that run from them into every other part of the business — cost, product, operations, risk, people, rules — and see how each thread changes what a good strategist should do.Start with the blunt truth: you cannot make a better product than your inputs allow. No amount of skill in the bakery makes a poor flour into good bread. No amount of polish on the shop floor makes up for a component that fails after six months.This puts raw materials directly underneath the Product chapter. Remember the three levels of a product — core benefit, actual product, augmented product? Raw materials decide the quality and consistency of the actual product, and that in turn decides whether the promises wrapped around it hold up. A brand is a promise; the product is the keeping of it. A raw material that varies batch to batch quietly breaks that promise, and the customer experiences it as a complaint — which lands in Customer Service, not in the purchasing ledger where it started.Two consequences follow: Consistency beats brilliance. A predictable material lets you promise a predictable product. That's why the boring supplier with reliable spec control often beats the exciting one with better samples. New materials create new products. Tastes and markets don't only pull products into existence; materials push them too. Cheaper solar cells, lighter alloys, better batteries — each one opened a market that couldn't have existed before. Watching materials is one way to spot a product opportunity before your rivals do. For most product businesses, raw materials are the largest single line inside cost of goods sold. That's the costs that rise with every unit you sell, as opposed to the fixed ones — rent, salaried staff, insurance — that you pay whether you sell anything or not.Costs come off profit pound for pound, which means a small change in material cost has an outsized effect at the bottom of the page. Watch what happens to a bakery with £1,000 of daily sales:*Assuming flour is roughly a fifth of the ingredient bill.A 6% rise in total costs wiped out the entire profit. That's the leverage: material costs are paid by the business, but only the profit line suffers. This is why purchasing is a profit centre, not an admin chore — and why the Costs and Financials chapters keep circling back to it.There's a cash dimension too. Materials you've bought but not yet sold are money sitting in a warehouse doing nothing — stock, which is cash you can't spend on anything else. Raw materials are unusually demanding here: they tie up cash, they may need paying for before you've sold the finished goods, and if you don't use them, they rot, rust or go out of fashion. A material price rise you can usually survive. A material price rise during a cash squeeze is how businesses die.Here's the pattern in one picture. Raw materials don't have one consequence; they have four, and all of them land on profit.
Note that last arrow. Profit funds the next round of buying — better materials, bigger volumes, keener terms — so advantages and disadvantages compound, exactly as the management loop in the opening chapter described.Manufacturing. The material dictates the process. Flour needs ovens and proving time; steel needs furnaces and presses; chemicals need tanks and precise temperatures. The whole vocabulary of the Manufacturing chapter — job, batch, mass, continuous production — grows out of what you're working with. Change your raw material and you may have to rebuild your factory.Stores. Materials carry their own storage rules. Grain keeps for months; milk keeps for days. Bulk materials need space, dangerous ones need containment, valuable ones need security. Every gram that spoils or walks out the door is a material cost with no revenue attached — pure loss, invisible in the accounts unless somebody is counting.Distribution. Weight and volume are paid for twice. A cheap heavy material can cost more to move than to buy, which is why businesses that make weight-losing products historically located near their source — mills by rivers, breweries by water. Add long lead times from overseas and your Distribution planning gets longer, and the stock you must hold gets bigger.Labour. Materials decide who you need, what you must train them to do, and how safe the work is. Hazardous inputs mean protective equipment, procedures, insurance and Regulations compliance. Fine tolerances mean skilled hands. This is the Labour thread running straight out of the material you chose.Raw materials are where the wider world reaches directly into your cash flow. Almost every big swing has an external cause: Harvests, weather and geology. A bad season lifts prices for everyone, including your rivals — but not equally, because the well-supplied firm has stock and contracts while the other one is buying at the spot price. Commodity markets. Materials traded in bulk get a going price set by supply and demand, exactly as the Market chapter described. You're a price taker. Currency. Buy in a foreign currency and an exchange rate move can change your material cost without a single supplier lifting a finger. Tariffs, duties and taxes. Goods crossing borders pick up charges, dealt with in the Tax chapter. Regulation. Restrictions on hazardous substances, sourcing rules, sustainability requirements and labelling all sit on materials rather than on finished products. If regulators ban an input, your production line stops until you reformulate. Interruption. Strikes, port closures, a fire at a supplier you've never met. This is the Suppliers chapter's tier problem: your Tier 2's disaster is delivered to you as your Tier 1's apology. And the quiet one: a rival who locks up supply. Control a scarce input — the best site, the only licensed processor, an exclusive contract — and you've built a barrier your competitors can't cross. In the language of the Competitors chapter, that's a structural advantage, and a durable one.Priya's bakery, from earlier in the book, sells 100 loaves a day at £4. Ingredients cost £1.20 a loaf; everything else — wages, rent, energy — comes to £230 a day.A 3% rise in costs cut her profit by a quarter. Now watch her think. Raising the price to £4.10 would recover £10 a day if the same 100 customers stayed — but as the Market chapter showed, her bread has close substitutes and her demand is elastic, so some of them walk to the café next door. So instead of one blunt move, a strategist plays several small ones: Cut waste. She counts what she throws away, finds 4% of her flour going in the bin, and gets it under 1%. Worth a few pounds a day, permanently. Reformulate. One of her six lines moves to a cheaper blend of the same quality grade. The customers don't notice; the margin does. Negotiate. She asks the mill for a small discount on a committed weekly volume — and gets it, because she's now a predictable customer. Adjust selectively. She puts 5p on the sourdough, where she has the most loyal buyers, and leaves the everyday white loaf alone. No single lever saves the day. Together they more than cover the £12. That's what raw materials as a factor across the business looks like in practice: not one heroic decision, but four ordinary ones in different corners of the company.You can apply this to any material, in any business, in about ten minutes: How much of my cost is it? A material that's 2% of your costs can be ignored; one that's 30% is a board-level topic. Know which is which. Could I substitute it? Flexibility — a second material, a second grade, a second specification — is insurance you buy before you need it. How easily could it be cut off, and by whom? One supplier, one country, one mine? Then you're managing risk, not price. How much do I lose? Waste, spoilage, shrinkage, over-ordering, expired stock. This is the cheapest saving available, because it needs no negotiation and no customer. Could it be an advantage rather than a cost? Better material, or exclusive access to it, can be the thing customers pay a premium for. That's a Product decision financed by a purchasing one. Raw materials set the quality ceiling on your product and the consistency your brand depends on — no amount of downstream skill fixes bad inputs. They are usually the biggest part of cost of goods sold, and because costs come off profit pound for pound, a small material price change swings profit hard. They tie up cash in stock, which links them directly to the Financials chapter and to survival during a squeeze. Materials shape your manufacturing process, storage needs, transport costs and labour requirements — they're an operations decision disguised as a purchase. The biggest shocks are external: weather, commodity markets, currency, tariffs, regulation and interrupted supply chains. Most of them are predictable, which means most of them are planable. The strategist's toolkit is a set of small moves — reduce waste, substitute, negotiate, design around the material, adjust prices selectively, hold buffer stock — rather than one heroic fix. Finally, ask whether a material is a cost to be minimised or a capability to protect. Sometimes control of supply is the advantage your rivals can't copy.

business-management/08-distribution/08-1.title: 08-1 What Distribution Means
business-management/08-distribution/08-1.description:
Part of 08 DistributionHand someone a perfect loaf of bread and ask what it's worth. In a locked cupboard, nothing. On a counter with a customer standing in front of it, four pounds. Same loaf, same recipe, same baker. The only thing that changed is where it was and who could get to it.That gap — between a product being made and a product being bought — is what distribution exists to close.Distribution is everything that happens to a product between it leaving production and a customer using it: the moving, storing, splitting, sorting, informing and handing over that puts the right goods in the right place at the right time.Three things are worth pulling out of that sentence.It's an activity, not a place. A shop is a place. Distribution is the work — the van route, the warehouse, the wholesaler breaking a pallet into singles, the website that takes the order, the app that tracks the parcel.It starts when the product is finished and ends when the customer has it. Everything before that is covered elsewhere in this book — raw materials, manufacturing, suppliers. Everything after is customer service, repeat purchase, and revenue. Distribution is the middle act.It's deliberately broad. Most people hear "distribution" and picture a delivery van, the same way they hear "market" and picture a fruit stall. Both pictures are true and both are about a tenth of the story.If you've met the classic four Ps of marketing — product, price, place, promotion — distribution is place. It's the one people forget, and often the one that decides whether the other three make any money.Here's why distribution has to exist at all. Making and buying don't naturally line up. They're mismatched in four ways, and each one is a job somebody has to do. Place. Production happens in one spot, or a handful of spots. Consumption happens in thousands of streets, kitchens and offices. Time. Your oven runs at 4am; your customers want bread at 8am. A farmer harvests in August; people eat in February. Quantity. A mill wants to sell flour by the tonne. A customer wants one loaf. Somebody has to split the difference. Assortment. Nobody wants everything from a single maker. A shopper wants bread from one baker, milk from a dairy and coffee from a roaster — and wants all three in one trip and one payment.
Every distribution system ever built — a Roman road, a corner shop, a courier network, a vending machine — exists to shrink one or more of those four gaps. This is the same idea you met in the Market chapter, where buyers and sellers are separated by space, time, quantity and trust, and a market is the arrangement that bridges them. Distribution is that bridging, viewed from the seller's side.Strip away the specific businesses and the same handful of functions show up in every distribution system: Moving — physically getting goods from one place to another. Storing — holding them until someone wants them, which is how you beat the time gap. Breaking bulk — turning a pallet into a case, a case into a loaf, a loaf into a slice. Sorting and combining — gathering many producers' goods into one place so a buyer can shop once. Informing — letting buyers know what's available, and letting producers know what's selling. Transferring ownership and taking payment — the boring, essential plumbing that makes a sale a sale. This links straight to the Financials chapter. Supporting after the sale — delivery, returns, installation, replacement. Now the part that trips people up. You can outsource these functions, but you cannot delete them. If you don't store your own stock, someone stores it for you. If you don't deliver, the customer travels instead. If you don't sort an assortment, the buyer makes four trips to four shops and pays for it in time.That's the honest version of the "middleman" question from the Market chapter. A wholesaler, a distributor, a delivery app or a retailer charges you money — but only earns it when the function they perform costs you less than doing it yourself. Remove them and the work doesn't vanish. It just moves, often onto your customer, who is less willing to do it than you'd hope.It isn't just transport. Driving goods about is one function out of seven. A business that moves things brilliantly but stores them badly, prices them badly or runs out of them constantly has a transport business, not a distribution system.It isn't just shops. A shop is one route to a customer. So is a website, a market stall, a wholesaler, a vending machine, a courier, a locker, a phone call and a van in a lay-by. Which route you pick is the subject of the next section; here, just note that a shop is a type of channel, not a definition.It isn't the same as inbound logistics. Bringing materials in from suppliers is upstream work — covered in the Suppliers and Raw Materials chapters. "Distribution" is usually used for the outbound half: getting your finished product out to buyers. The two halves are mirror images, and the same four mismatches apply to both.And it applies to services, not just goods. A plumber's van, a salon's location, a barber's booking system and a consultant's video call are all distribution decisions. Services can't be stored, so the time gap has to be closed by appointment systems and capacity planning instead of inventory. That's the Product and Customer Service chapters knocking on the door.placeholder
Photo by Pavel Danilyuk on PexelsTake Priya's sourdough and follow it from the oven to somebody eating it.Priya's loaf costs her £1.20 in ingredients. She sells it to the café at £2.60. The café sells the equivalent onward at around £4.00 once it's on a plate with coffee. So the loaf nearly doubles in price between the oven and the customer — and Priya keeps almost none of that increase.It's tempting to see that as someone taking a cut. Look again at the table. The café moved it across town, stored it, broke a baker's batch into single servings, combined it with everything else the customer wanted, took the risk that it might not sell, and handled the payment. That work is distribution, and the price gap is what the market pays for it. Remember the loop you've seen throughout this book — every function a business performs has to be paid for by somebody, out of the price the customer agrees to.Now try a second example, because it makes the point even harder to ignore. A bottle of water. Extracting, treating and bottling it costs a few pence. The bulk of the price you pay is packaging, transport, shelf space and someone's willingness to keep it cold and handy. For gravel, cement, bottled soft drinks and bread, distribution often costs more than production. That's why industries built on cheap, heavy, bulky things — brewing, quarrying, soft drinks — tend to cluster their plants near their customers rather than their ingredients. Raw materials set the quality ceiling; distribution sets the reach.placeholder
Photo by Tom Fisk on PexelsMost business decisions can be reversed next quarter. Distribution decisions are different. Sign a shop lease, buy a van, appoint an exclusive distributor, list on a platform that takes 25% of every sale, or commit to a cold chain — and you've made a decision for years, not weeks.And it doesn't just decide your costs. It quietly decides five more things: How much of the customer's price you keep — the more hands between your oven and the customer, the more mouths sharing the money. Who your competitors are. This is the point from the Competitors chapter worth repeating: the same product sold wholesale competes with industrial bakers on price and reliability; sold over a counter it competes with the café next door on atmosphere. Different channel, different fight. How much you know about your buyers. Sell direct and every conversation teaches you something. Sell through three layers and you're managing a relationship with a distributor, not a customer. How fast you can grow. Every channel has a ceiling — a counter serves a street, a website serves a country. How much cash is tied up. Stock sitting in a warehouse or in transit is money you've already spent and can't use yet, which is exactly the working-capital squeeze the Financials chapter warns about. One more thing, and it's the cheerful version: distribution doesn't only serve demand, it can create it. Deliver to villages that never had a shop, open a website that serves a country, put a coffee machine where no café would survive — and you've made a market that didn't exist before. Distribution is one of the few functions that can genuinely enlarge the pie rather than just slice it differently.placeholder
Photo by Frans van Heerden on Pexels Availability is part of the product. Remember the three levels of a product: the augmented layer — delivery, returns, convenience — is where most competition actually happens. Distribution builds that layer, so it isn't an afterthought, it's the offer. Run the four mismatches as a checklist. Place, time, quantity, assortment. For each one, decide: do we close this ourselves, or pay somebody else to close it? Write down the cost of both. That single exercise usually reveals where your margin is leaking. Don't try to delete a function. If you stop storing, splitting or informing, somebody still does it — your supplier at a price, or your customer at the cost of a lost sale. Back-of-envelope it before you commit. Every channel has a cost per unit sold. Compare them like-for-like, including commissions, delivery, packaging and the cost of holding stock. Then check it against what customers will actually pay — the same discipline you'd apply to any other price decision. Manage it like the loop from the opening of this book. Plan the route and the volumes, organise the vans, warehouses and people, and then control it with two or three numbers: cost per delivery, on-time rate, and stock-turn. Distribution is the easiest part of a business to run blind, and the most expensive when you do. Treat the channel as strategy, not plumbing. It's the single biggest lever on your margin, your reach, and who you're up against. Distribution is everything that happens between production and the customer using the product — moving, storing, breaking bulk, sorting, informing, transferring ownership and supporting after the sale. It exists because making and buying are mismatched in place, time, quantity and assortment. Every distribution system ever built closes one or more of those gaps. It is not just transport and not just shops. Transport and retail are single functions and single routes within a much wider activity — and services need distributing too. Functions can be outsourced but never deleted. A middleman is worth paying only when they close a gap more cheaply than you could. Distribution often costs more than making the product, especially for cheap, heavy or bulky goods — which is why plants cluster near customers, not ingredients. Channel decisions are sticky and structural: they set your margins, your cash, your reach, your knowledge of customers, and who your competitors are. Distribution can also create demand, not merely satisfy it, by putting goods where no market existed before. The strategist's habit: ask how your product gets from where it's made to where it's wanted, what that costs, and what would happen if it stopped.

business-management/08-distribution/08-2.title: 08-2 Types of Distribution Channels
business-management/08-distribution/08-2.description:
Part of 08 DistributionA loaf of bread, a dining table, a software licence — each one can reach its buyer in more than one way. You can hand it over yourself. You can sell it to a shop that sells it on. You can sell it to a wholesaler who supplies the shop. You can hand it to an agent who finds the buyer for a commission. Or you can push it through an online marketplace and let a platform take its cut.Each of those routes is a distribution channel: the path a product takes from the producer to the final buyer, including everyone who handles it along the way. And the type of channel you choose decides things that never appear on your price list — who finds the customer, who holds the stock, who carries the risk, who gets paid when, and who owns the relationship once the sale is done.Here's the reassuring part before we go any further: you don't have to pick one. Most healthy businesses run several channels at once, because different customers, products and regions need different doors. That mix is sometimes called an omnichannel or multi-channel approach, and choosing it well is one of the most profitable decisions a manager makes.Direct channels — economists call them zero-level — put you face to face with the final buyer. Your own shop counter, a market stall, your own website, a subscription box, a factory outlet, your own sales team knocking on doors.Indirect channels put somebody else in between. A retailer, a wholesaler, an agent, a platform.Neither column is "better". They're a trade: direct buys you margin and control at the price of reach and investment; indirect buys you reach at the price of margin and control. Everything else in this subsection is a variation on that trade.The simplest way to sort channel types is by length — the number of intermediaries between you and the buyer. A short channel has one or none; a long channel has three or four.
The longer the chain, the further the producer sits from the person who actually eats, uses or rides the product. Longer channels reach more buyers and smaller ones — a village shop can't buy a pallet of bread, but it can buy four loaves from a wholesaler. The price is that each link takes its own cut, and each link is another place where information, quality and speed can get lost.The names blur across industries, but the roles are stable. The most important distinction — and the one beginners miss — is between merchants and agents.Merchants buy the goods. They take ownership, pay you, and carry the risk that the stock doesn't sell. Wholesalers, retailers, industrial distributors and importers are all merchants. Once they've bought, the unsold loaf is their problem, not yours.Agents never own the goods. They introduce, negotiate or close a sale and earn a commission or fee for it. Sales agents, brokers, commission-based interior designers, travel agents, and most online marketplaces work this way. The stock stays on your shelf and the risk stays on your books.That single distinction decides who you invoice, who you chase for payment, and who is left holding the problem when the product doesn't move. Beyond it: Retailers sell to final consumers (your Stores chapter lives here). Wholesalers buy in bulk, break it down, and supply retailers. Distributors do the same job in business markets, usually with more services attached — installation, servicing, credit. Aggregators and platforms match buyers and sellers and take a fee: delivery apps, comparison sites, online marketplaces. Franchisees sell under your brand using your system, as a licensed operator rather than a buyer. “/assets/0596599aeb074814b9a63ec7c0f59bae/direct_channel_placeholder.jpg” could not be found. Photo by ready made on Pexels
Photo by Helena Jankovičová Kováčová on PexelsOnline selling gets talked about as if it invented something new. It didn't. It lowered the cost of closing the same gaps you met in the Market chapter — space, time, information, trust, quantity and risk.An online store closes the space gap without a building. A marketplace closes the information and trust gap with reviews and payment protection. Subscriptions close the quantity gap by delivering a small order every week. A delivery app closes the time gap at 9pm on a Tuesday.Two patterns are worth naming because they recur: Disintermediation — cutting out a link. Sell direct from your website and the retailer is gone. Re-intermediation — a new link appearing. Those delivery apps, payment providers and marketplaces are intermediaries too; they just arrived later and take their cut in software rather than warehousing. The gap rarely disappears. It just gets filled by somebody new — which is why every producer ends up choosing between who handles the gap, not whether anyone does.Channel type isn't only about length. It's also about how many outlets you use, and that choice follows almost mechanically from what kind of product you're selling.You've met this logic already in the Product chapter: convenience goods are bought fast and compared on availability, so they need to be everywhere; specialty goods are sought out and rarely substituted, so rarity is part of the value. Put a £40 artisan loaf in a discount supermarket and you haven't expanded your market — you've muddled what your product is for.
Photo by Eduardo Soares on PexelsWhen the buyer is another business, the channel types change shape. You'll see: A direct sales force, visiting buyers, quoting and negotiating (common for capital goods and big contracts). Industrial distributors, holding stock of parts and consumables so customers can order in small amounts quickly. Agents and manufacturer's representatives carrying several complementary product lines into the same buyers. Original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) — your product becomes a component inside theirs, which is the Raw Materials and Suppliers chapters viewed from the other side. Tenders and framework contracts, where the buyer chooses from an approved list rather than browsing. Business buyers are fewer but larger, so a single channel relationship can carry a much bigger share of your revenue — and, correspondingly, much bigger risk if it ends.Rowan and Ash, the furniture workshop from the Suppliers chapter, build dining tables. Each table costs them around £500 in materials and direct labour. They currently sell through four different types of channel, and the numbers explain why they keep all four.Look at what the table really says. The gallery gives the worst margin per table by far — £150 against £700 direct. But it takes ten tables a month, pays in batches, and doesn't consume a single hour of the owners' selling time. The designer brings the least volume but the most price-insensitive customers. The marketplace reaches buyers they'd never meet.And the showroom produces the best margin per table but also the highest cost per sale, because every direct sale spends the owners' afternoon.The honest lesson: no channel wins on every measure, and the right question isn't "which channel is best?" but "what does each channel earn me, after its cut, per hour and per table?" Notice too that the four channels together fill their production capacity of roughly twenty tables a month. Channel choice is a capacity decision as much as a marketing one.Once a channel is chosen, it reaches into nearly every other part of the business: Costs and revenue. The channel's cut is a cost, and it changes what price is realistic. That's the Costs and Revenue chapters meeting your distribution decision head-on. Cash and risk. Merchants buy stock from you — which converts your inventory into cash fast, at the price of a thin margin. Agents leave the stock on your books. That's a Financials question wearing a distribution costume. Your competitors. Sell wholesale and you're suddenly bidding against industrial bakers on price and reliability, not against the café two doors down on atmosphere. The Competitors chapter made this exact point: channel changes the competitive set. Customer experience. Whoever hands over the product owns the moment of truth — delivery speed, returns, a friendly hello. That's Customer Service, whether or not it's your staff doing it. Labour. A direct channel needs sales staff, drivers and shop workers; an indirect one needs account managers. The Labour chapter follows from the channel you chose. Rules and taxes. Cross-border channels bring duties, labelling rules and import paperwork — the Tax and Regulations chapters, arriving by van. A short checklist covers most channel decisions: Who is the buyer, and where do they already shop? Follow the customer, not the fashion. What does the product need? Fresh, bulky, fragile, regulated and high-value products each rule channels out. Can you afford it? Direct channels cost money up front; indirect ones cost margin. What do you get after the cut? Contribution per unit — not revenue. Who owns the relationship? If the answer is "not you", make sure the reach is worth it. Then close the management loop. Set a contribution target per channel, measure it monthly, and be willing to close a door that isn't earning its keep. Good strategists don't drift into a channel because everyone else uses it — they choose it deliberately, price it honestly, and check that it's paying.
Photo by RDNE Stock project on Pexels A distribution channel is the path a product takes from producer to final buyer, including everyone who handles it. The first split is direct (zero-level) versus indirect: direct buys margin, control and data; indirect buys reach and someone else's infrastructure. Channels are also sorted by length — zero, one, two, three levels — and longer channels add reach at the cost of margin, speed and connection to the customer. Intermediaries are either merchants (who buy the goods, take ownership and carry the risk) or agents (who earn a commission without ever owning the stock). That distinction decides who holds the risk and who you invoice. Digital channels closed the same old gaps more cheaply; they didn't abolish intermediaries, they produced new ones. Intensive, selective and exclusive coverage follows from product type — convenience goods go everywhere, specialty goods go almost nowhere. Business-to-business channels run through sales forces, distributors, agents, OEMs and tenders. The right question is never "which channel is best?" but "what does each channel earn me, after its cut, per unit and per hour?" — and whether you're measuring it. Next, we'll pull back and look at distribution as a factor across the whole business: how channel choices shape your costs, your cash, your customers and your competitive position all at once.

business-management/08-distribution/08-3.title: 08-3 Distribution as a Factor Across the Whole Business
business-management/08-distribution/08-3.description:
Part of 08 DistributionDistribution is easy to file away as "the delivery bit" — something that happens after the product is made and before the money arrives. That framing is a trap. In reality, distribution is a decision that reaches backwards into how you design products, forwards into what customers you can even reach, and sideways into your cash flow, your tax bill and your staffing. Change one distribution choice and you usually change five other things about the business.This subsection is about that ripple effect. We've already looked at what distribution is and the channels available; now let's treat it as a factor that runs through the whole business, the same way we treated raw materials, labour and manufacturing.Picture the business as a single physical thread running from your suppliers' loading docks to your customer's front door. Every function you've studied sits along that thread.
The important word in that diagram is thread. Cut it anywhere and the whole line goes slack. A manufacturing plant that can produce 10,000 units a week is useless if outbound logistics can only move 4,000. A brilliant product that takes three weeks to arrive loses to a mediocre one that arrives tomorrow. Distribution sets the ceiling on what the rest of the business is allowed to achieve.Distribution starts before you make anything. That's inbound logistics — getting materials from suppliers to your operation.Three factors from earlier chapters collide here: Distance. A supplier two hours away can be reordered weekly. A supplier two oceans away needs a six-week buffer of stock sitting in a warehouse, which is cash you can't spend elsewhere. Bulk and weight. Raw materials that are heavy, bulky or perishable — sand, milk, fresh produce — are expensive to move relative to their value. That pushes production towards the source. This is exactly why cement plants sit next to limestone quarries. Reliability. The less reliable the inbound flow, the more safety stock you must hold. Distribution risk quietly becomes an inventory cost. So your choice of supplier isn't just a purchasing decision. It's a distribution decision wearing a different hat.Manufacturing and distribution are two halves of one system. Where you put the factory determines your outbound logistics cost forever after; a plant far from customers is a permanent tax on every unit sold.Distribution also feeds back into product design. A product that's awkward to ship — fragile, oddly shaped, requiring refrigeration — costs more to distribute than to make. Designers who ignore this create products that are technically excellent and commercially hopeless. The classic fix is designing for cube efficiency: how much product fits into a standard pallet or container. Squeeze 20% more units into the same space and you've cut your freight cost per unit by roughly a fifth without touching the factory.Tie this to the product life cycle too. In the launch phase, small volumes and premium prices tolerate slow, expensive distribution. In the mature phase, volumes are huge and margins are thin, so distribution must become ruthlessly efficient. Distribution strategy has to move as the product ages.Outbound distribution decides where you are allowed to sell. Staying with direct delivery to your own town limits you to one market. Adding a national courier opens a country. Adding a third-party fulfilment network opens continents — with the trade-off that you lose some control of the experience.This is where distribution and sales become the same conversation. A salesperson promising a two-day delivery is making a distribution commitment. A distributor's margin is a sale you never see.And customer service is now largely a distribution story. "Where's my order?" is the most common support question in retail. Fast, accurate, trackable delivery is service; late or damaged delivery is a complaint. Returns — reverse distribution — are the same thread running backwards, and they're often the most expensive leg of all.
You can have two of those three at full strength. Pick fast and cheap and you stay local. Pick fast and wide-reaching and it costs a fortune. Pick cheap and wide and customers wait. Good strategists choose deliberately rather than drifting into a default.Distribution shows up on both sides of the income statement.On revenue: distribution is what turns a local product into a national one. Widening distribution widens the addressable market — the same product, the same brand, many more buyers. It's one of the few growth levers that doesn't require inventing anything new.On costs: distribution typically accounts for a meaningful slice of the sale price, and the useful metric is cost-to-serve — the total cost of getting one order to one customer, including picking, packing, freight and returns. Two customers paying the same price can be wildly different in cost-to-serve. A customer ordering one small item to a remote address might lose you money; a customer ordering in pallet quantities might be your most profitable account. Rational distribution pricing starts here.On cash: goods in transit are goods you've paid for but can't sell yet. Slow shipping lanes and long lead times lock up working capital. Speeding up distribution is often a cheaper way to free up cash than borrowing more.Notice how this links straight back to the Financials and Costs chapters: distribution isn't a line item you manage in isolation, it's a set of levers that move revenue, cost and cash at the same time.Distribution is labour-intensive in a specific way: warehouses, drivers, pickers, planners, customs clerks. That ties it directly to the Labour chapter — is that workforce permanent, agency, or automated? Automation of a warehouse is a heavy upfront cost that trades labour cost for fixed cost, which only pays off above a certain volume.It also creates a management problem, because distribution cuts across departments. Manufacturing wants long production runs; sales wants urgent exceptions; finance wants lower inventory; the customer wants it tomorrow. Someone has to own the trade-offs. Companies that treat distribution as a shared responsibility often find nobody is actually accountable for it — and that's when costs creep and service slips.Distribution is unusually exposed to external factors, because it involves moving things across distances and borders. Economy: fuel prices, freight rates and interest rates all hit distribution hard. When shipping costs spike, every business relying on long-distance distribution feels it immediately — and businesses with local supply chains become temporarily more competitive. Tax: where your goods are held and where your customers are can create tax obligations, from customs duties and import tariffs to sales tax or VAT registration in new regions. Expanding your distribution footprint can therefore expand your tax footprint. This is a genuine reason small firms grow through distributors rather than direct sales. Regulations: transport safety rules, driver hours, food and pharmaceutical handling standards, packaging and recycling rules, emissions zones. Each one raises the bar to entry — which protects established players and punishes newcomers. Competitors: distribution is one of the most visible competitive battlegrounds there is. Once a rival offers free next-day delivery, that becomes the market's expectation, and everyone else must match it or explain why not. Distribution promises tend to ratchet upwards and never come back down.
Photo by Tiger Lily on PexelsImagine a small coffee roastery, Beans & Co. It starts by delivering to twelve local cafés in its own van. Distribution is cheap, personal and fast — and completely capped. It cannot grow beyond a day's drive.Stage two: it adds a national courier. Sales triple, but freight cost per bag is high, delivery takes three days, and customers complain about stale coffee. The founder realises the product (bag size, packaging, roast date labelling) needs redesigning to suit the new distribution.Stage three: it moves to a third-party fulfilment centre that stores stock in three regions. Delivery drops to next day, freight cost per unit falls because the centre ships in bulk, and the business can now sell nationwide. But now inventory is spread across three sites, cash is tied up in stock, the business has tax registrations in new regions, and it depends on a partner it doesn't control.Every step widened revenue. Every step also added cost, complexity and risk somewhere else in the business. That's the nature of distribution as a factor: you never make one decision, you rebalance the whole system.Great businesses often win on distribution rather than on product. A slightly worse product that's everywhere beats a brilliant product nobody can get. So ask yourself a few questions as a strategist: Does my distribution reach the customers my strategy needs, or does it quietly cap my ambition? Is my cost-to-serve understood per customer and per channel, or averaged into a comfortable blur? Can my distribution survive a fuel spike, a new regulation or a competitor's new promise? Who in the business actually owns the trade-offs between speed, cost and reach? Distribution is not one activity at the end of the chain — it's the physical thread connecting suppliers, manufacturing, stores, sales and the customer. Upstream, it shapes supplier choice and inventory levels; downstream, it decides which markets you can reach and what service you can promise. It moves revenue (wider reach), costs (cost-to-serve) and cash (inventory in transit) simultaneously, linking straight back to your financials. It depends heavily on labour and requires clear management ownership, because it forces trade-offs between departments. It's exposed to the economy, tax and regulation, and it's one of the most visible fronts in competition. The core strategic trade-off is speed versus cost versus reach — choose two, and choose them on purpose.

business-management/08-distribution/08-4.title: 08-4 Distribution vs. The Other Factors
business-management/08-distribution/08-4.description:
Part of 08 DistributionDistribution is the factor that touches almost every other one. It is the physical, financial and informational bridge between the things you buy and make and the people who pay you. That makes it unusual: most factors are either inputs (suppliers, raw materials, labour), outputs (revenue, customer service) or constraints (tax, regulations, economy). Distribution is the pipe that runs through all three. Pull on distribution and something else moves — a cost, a promise, a tax bill, a competitor's opening.Here is the loop you should keep in your head for the whole section:
Everything below is a version of that picture, viewed from a different angle.The company is the container; distribution is the shape of the container. A small company often is its distribution: the founder's van, a laptop and a courier account. As the company grows, distribution turns into fixed assets — leases, warehouses, trucks, software — and those decisions alter what kind of company you now are. Recall the earlier chapter on company types: a consultancy barely distributes anything, a brewery distributes constantly, and a retailer is essentially a distribution business with a shopfront bolted on. Every channel decision is also a structural decision about the company, because channel commitments are hard to reverse. Signing a five-year warehouse lease to win a customer today is how a flexible company becomes a brittle one.Channel is one of the last honest moats. Anyone can copy your product description in a week; it takes years to build shelf space, exclusive distributor relationships or a delivery network that reliably hits a two-hour window. When you size up rivals in the competitors chapter, look at how they reach buyers, not just what they sell: direct, wholesale, marketplace, franchised, or a hybrid. Ask whether the channel is crowded or open. If every competitor fights for the same supermarket aisle, the shelf is the battleground and the retailer captures the profit. If you can build a route they can't copy — a route density, a cold chain, a local depot — you have leverage. The flip side: shared distributors and common carriers mean your competitor's promotion can quietly eat your stock allocation, and price wars are often fought in the channel before they reach the customer.Market is buyers, sellers and the space between them — and distribution is that space made physical. A market you cannot reach is not a market you serve. This is why distribution defines your real addressable market size, not the total number of people who might conceivably want your product. It also drives segmentation: convenience buyers need you nearby; bulk buyers will wait a week for a pallet. In marketing language, distribution is the "place" in the four Ps, and it is the P most people under-invest in because it is invisible until it fails. Strategically, the question is: what is the cheapest route that makes me genuinely present in the market I have chosen?Product characteristics largely dictate distribution design. Weight, volume, fragility, perishability and value density — value per kilogram — decide almost everything. Diamonds fly; sand is quarried locally. Fresh milk needs a cold chain measured in hours; canned milk needs a warehouse. Where a product sits in its life cycle matters too: a new product usually launches through selective, high-touch channels, then broadens as it matures and margins compress. Packaging is a distribution decision wearing a marketing costume — the pallet configuration and case size often save more money than the artwork. And don't forget returns and after-sales: if a product is likely to come back, design the inbound route before you design the outbound one.Suppliers sit upstream, and their location and reliability set your inbound logistics. A supplier who delivers to your door has taken on distribution cost — which is reflected in their price, so compare total landed cost rather than unit price. Techniques like drop-shipping (the supplier ships straight to your customer) and vendor-managed inventory (the supplier keeps your shelf stocked) move the distribution job without eliminating it; it is still your promise to the customer that gets broken when the shipment is late. A single-source supplier three continents away is a distribution risk before it is a price opportunity.Raw materials are usually the worst distribution problem in the business: heavy, bulky, low value density, sometimes perishable or hazardous. That is why processing plants tend to sit next to where the raw material comes from — sugar beet refineries near fields, sawmills near forests — while finished goods travel further because they are worth more per kilogram. The rule of thumb: move the material that loses value in transit as little as possible, and move the finished good as far as the customer demands. Your raw material choice therefore locks in part of your distribution network before you have made a single sale.Distribution is one of the most labour-hungry factors: drivers, pickers, packers, loaders, planners. Labour availability and wage rates shape where you put a depot more than land prices do. In tight labour markets, distribution costs rise and automation becomes attractive; in slack ones, handballing is often cheaper than capital. The gig economy blurred this line by turning a fixed labour cost into a variable per-delivery cost — brilliant for flexibility, risky for service consistency. When you model a channel, model the labour market underneath it, not just the fuel and the boxes.This is the tightest pairing in the book. Plant location is a distribution decision: one big efficient plant with long hauls, or several smaller plants with short ones. Batch size and lead time determine how much finished stock you must hold, and where. Flexibility in manufacturing lets you postpone — assemble, label or package late, close to the customer, so you ship generic components instead of finished variants. Choose your manufacturing strategy and you have chosen most of your distribution cost; choose your distribution strategy first and you constrain your manufacturing options just as firmly. Whichever you pick, decide them together.A store is a distribution channel that happens to have a door. Physical stores give reach, trust and instant availability, but they duplicate the inventory you also hold online. Modern practice merges the two: click-and-collect, ship-from-store, stores as micro-fulfilment hubs, returns accepted anywhere. That flexibility is powerful and dangerous — the moment your website undercuts your own store, you have channel conflict inside your own company, and your retail partners notice too. Store count is also coverage: more stores means denser distribution and shorter last-mile legs, usually at higher fixed cost.Sales sells the promise; distribution keeps it. A sales team incentivised purely on signed orders will happily sell into channels that are expensive to serve or impossible to fulfil, and the fallout lands on customer service and the returns budget. Align incentives with the true cost to serve. On the upside, sales is your best demand signal: territory data and order history feed the forecasts that decide stock positioning, route frequency and depot size. Sales territories and distribution routes are two views of the same map and should be drawn by the same people.Delivery speed, reliability and communication are customer service for most physical businesses. The whole discipline can be summarised as a trade-off frontier: you can have cheap, fast or reliable — stretch for all three and something breaks. Set a service level you can afford (for example, 95% of orders delivered next day), then design the network backwards from it. Returns logistics is the part everyone underestimates: a generous returns policy is a service feature and a distribution cost, and it should be costed as one. Great distribution is invisible; bad distribution is the only thing the customer remembers.Labour is the work; staff are the people you employ to do it. In distribution the distinction decides your business model. Own the fleet and warehouse and you carry recruitment, training, safety and retention obligations — plus control. Outsourcing to a third-party logistics provider converts those into a contract and a variable rate, at the cost of control and transparency. Either way, the capability you need is real: planners who can model routes, supervisors who can run a safe shift, and someone accountable for the number.Channel design is a management decision, and it exercises every core job from the opening chapter. Planning: which channels, which geographies, which service levels. Organising: which parts you own and which you contract. Leading: getting performance out of partners and drivers you don't employ — influence without authority is the hardest skill in distribution. Controlling: measuring cost per order, on-time delivery and stock accuracy. Managers who treat distribution as a logistics chore rather than a strategic lever leave margin on the table every single day.Distribution is where accounting meets reality. Stock in transit is working capital tied up and invisible on a warehouse count. Owned warehouses and vehicles are capital expenditure with depreciation and maintenance; a 3PL contract is operating expenditure that keeps the balance sheet light. Either choice changes your return on capital, your break-even point and your cash conversion cycle — the number of days between paying suppliers and being paid by customers. Cutting inventory to free up cash without touching service levels is one of the most reliable ways to improve a business's finances without selling a single extra unit.Revenue is units sold times price. Distribution determines how many units you can sell (availability) and, often, what price you get (a premium department store and a discount marketplace are different prices for the same product). So distribution is a revenue factor disguised as a cost factor, which is why it keeps getting underfunded by people reading only the cost line. Small operational choices compound here: a delivery slot that suits the customer, a subscription that ships on a schedule, a stock position that never runs dry. Revenue is also unforgiving — a stockout doesn't just lose today's sale, it teaches the customer to buy elsewhere. Recall the revenue chapter: the same product through a different channel is effectively a different revenue stream with a different margin.Distribution typically eats somewhere between 5% and 20% of revenue, and the last mile — the final leg to the customer — is usually the single most expensive part. So route density, drop size and minimum order values matter enormously: delivery cost per item falls as you deliver more items to the same place. That is the whole logic behind free-shipping thresholds and clustered delivery days. Separate fixed network costs (depots, systems) from variable costs (fuel, per-drop labour), because they behave differently when volumes rise or fall. And remember the service trade-off: every promise of speed you add pushes cost up faster than it pushes revenue.Distribution is unusually exposed to the wider economy. Fuel prices move delivery costs directly; interest rates change the cost of holding inventory and of financing vehicles; wages set driver and warehouse pay; exchange rates and trade flows decide whether importing is sensible. In a downturn, customers trade down to cheaper channels and slower delivery options, so your channel mix shifts without you changing a thing. Economic geography — where people and production actually are — quietly sets your network's optimal shape. Build slack into distribution plans, because this is the factor that punishes just-in-time thinking hardest when a shock arrives.Movement creates tax events. Cross a border and there may be customs duty, import VAT and clearance paperwork; the duty rate can decide whether you source locally or import. Hold stock in a state or country and you may create a tax presence — nexus — that obliges you to register and collect sales tax or VAT, which is why some businesses deliberately distribute from fewer locations. Transfer pricing between your own entities, excise duties on fuel and alcohol, and marketplace rules that make the platform collect tax on your behalf all sit on top of the physical network. Design the channel, then check the tax consequence — not the other way round.Regulation shapes what distribution is legally allowed to look like: transport licences and driver hours, vehicle weight and emissions rules, cold-chain and food-safety requirements, dangerous-goods handling, packaging and recycling obligations, distance-selling and returns rights, and cross-border documentation. Two strategic points follow. First, compliance is a fixed cost, so heavy regulation tends to favour large incumbents with compliance teams and squeeze small entrants — unless the regulation creates a new market (reusable packaging, reverse logistics, EV fleets). Second, regulation changes the economics of geography: a low-emission zone can make one depot viable and another obsolete overnight.Distribution rarely wins or loses a business on its own. It multiplies whatever else you have. Great product plus weak distribution equals a well-kept secret. Great distribution plus a mediocre product equals a fast-growing churn problem. The strategist's job is to notice that distribution is the factor where product, manufacturing, stores, sales, service, costs, tax and regulation all meet — and to make one coherent set of choices there rather than nineteen separate compromises. Distribution is the connecting tissue of the business: inputs flow in, promises flow out, money flows back. With the company, it decides structure and flexibility; channel commitments are hard to unwind. With competitors and market, it is both a moat and the definition of your reachable market. With product, raw materials and manufacturing, it is a joint decision — value density, shelf life and plant location set most of the cost. With suppliers and labour, it is about who carries the work: inbound terms, wage rates, insourcing versus outsourcing. With stores and sales, it is about channel mix, conflict and incentives — sell what you can serve. With customer service, staff and management, it is about hitting a service level someone is accountable for. With financials, revenue and costs, it converts working capital and last-mile economics into profit or its opposite. With economy, tax and regulations, it operates inside rules and shocks you don't control — so build slack, check the tax, and treat compliance as both a barrier and an opening. The strategic takeaway: get distribution broadly right and its cost becomes a moat; get it wrong and it quietly taxes every other factor in the business.
