what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.title: 3-2 Falsifiability & what makes claims meaningful
what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.description: Part of 3 Act II — The Structure of Knowledge (knowing)Most of what people assert about the world comes with no specified failure condition. "Everything happens for a reason," "the market is driven by sentiment," "this hire just gets it" — each is phrased so that no possible observation could contradict it. Falsifiability is the habit of asking, before the evidence arrives, what would count against a claim. It is less a law of science than a sorting tool: it separates the claims that experience can settle from the ones it cannot, and it tells you which kind of conversation you are actually in.Verification and refutation are not symmetrical, and this asymmetry is the engine of the whole idea. No finite number of confirming observations can establish a universal statement: however many white swans you count, the next one might be black. But a single counterexample destroys it. Karl Popper built his account of science on this point in The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1934): theories are bold conjectures, and what makes a theory scientific is not that evidence supports it but that we can specify in advance the kind of event that would refute it.The logic is modus tollens. If the hypothesis is true, then this observation should occur. The observation did not occur. Therefore the hypothesis is in trouble.The corollary is that confirmations are cheap and mostly worthless. A prediction you could not have failed is not evidence of anything. "It will rain somewhere on Earth tomorrow" is nearly certain and nearly empty; "it will rain in Lisbon between noon and 2 p.m. tomorrow" is risky — and therefore informative when it holds. Popper's word for this is severity: a test is severe to the extent that it was likely to catch the claim out. This is why confirmation bias is not merely a moral failing — it is a structural one. If you go looking for support, you will find it, because support is abundant for almost any claim worth arguing about.Worked example. Two commentators forecast the same tax cut. The first says it will boost growth "unless monetary conditions offset it, which they currently do." The second says corporate investment will rise at least 2% within eighteen months. Both sound like predictions. Only the second has a settlement date and a threshold, which means only the second can teach its author anything. The first will be "right" regardless of what happens, which is precisely why it is useless.Here is where the story gets harder. Pierre Duhem (1906) and later W. V. O. Quine pointed out that hypotheses are never tested alone. What meets the data is always a bundle: the hypothesis, plus assumptions that the instrument works, that the sample is representative, that no confounding variable moved, that the background theories are roughly right. When a prediction fails, logic does not tell you which element of the bundle to blame. Any of them can absorb the damage.Blaming an auxiliary is sometimes exactly right. When Uranus's orbit refused to match Newtonian predictions, Urbain Le Verrier did not discard gravity — he proposed an unseen planet and predicted where to look. Neptune was there. That is a rescue of the highest quality: the patch was specific, risky, and independently checkable.The failure mode is the rescue that only absorbs the anomaly. "The polls were accurate; voters lied to pollsters." "The trial failed because the participants weren't motivated." "The strategy worked — the market just moved against us." Imre Lakatos framed this as the difference between progressive and degenerating research programmes: a programme is healthy when its patches generate new, testable predictions, and degenerating when patches do nothing but save the theory from the last result.The plainest test for an ad hoc rescue is directional: would you have accepted this same excuse if the evidence had gone the other way? If the answer is no, the excuse is not part of your model — it is damage control.Conspiracy theories are this failure mode taken to its limit. "The absence of evidence is evidence of the cover-up" makes every observation compatible with the claim. A structure that cannot lose is not a strong position; it is a claim that has quietly left the empirical game.Popper's criterion was a demarcation between empirical science and non-science — not a test of meaning. It is worth being precise, because the distinction is routinely collapsed.The logical positivists tried the stronger move: only statements verifiable by observation are meaningful. That programme collapsed partly on its own terms, since the verification principle cannot itself be verified. Meanwhile, entire categories of meaningful claims are unfalsifiable by nature. Mathematical theorems are proved, not tested. Moral claims — "you ought to keep your promise" — cannot be refuted by any observation, because no observation entails an ought. Singular historical claims, legal judgments, and aesthetic ones are likewise not the kind of thing a counterexample overturns.So "is this falsifiable?" is not the question "is this true?" or "does this matter?" It is the question "which kind of conversation are we having?" Much apparent disagreement about facts is really disagreement about values or identity, dressed in the grammar of empirical dispute. Detecting that shift is a large part of what the is/ought gap is for.It also matters that unfalsifiable frameworks can be genuinely productive as heuristics — "supply and demand," "the unconscious," "selection pressure" generate testable hypotheses by the dozen. The error is not using the lens; it is presenting the lens as a finding.Operationalize before you look. State the claim, the observation that would sink it, the threshold, and the deadline — and write it down while the prediction is still live, for the same reason you should write down decisions rather than trust your recall of them. A practical template: Claim: the new onboarding flow is better. Prediction: users exposed to flow B convert at least 1 percentage point higher than flow A. Window: 30 days, 10,000 users. Settlement: if the lift is under 1 point, we revert. Contrast that with "our product is more delightful," which cannot lose, cannot be measured, and therefore cannot improve anything.Statistical claims need a caveat. A probabilistic hypothesis is never cleanly refuted by one result; an unexpected outcome makes it less likely rather than dead. That is where the Bayesian machinery does the work, and where pre-registration and replication discipline come in — deciding the analysis before seeing the data is falsifiability's statistical form.Two matching errors to avoid. The first is demanding falsifiability of claims that were never empirical, then declaring victory — a cheap rhetorical move, and a category mistake. The second is the quiet one: holding a belief as though it were an empirical finding while refusing to name anything that would change your mind. If nothing could, you are not holding a belief. You are holding an identity. Falsifiability — the property of a claim such that some possible observation would count against it; Popper's criterion for demarcating empirical science from non-science. Demarcation problem — the question of what distinguishes science from pseudo-science, as opposed to what distinguishes sense from nonsense. Modus tollens — the valid inference form: if H then O; not O; therefore not H. The logical backbone of refutation. Severity (of a test) — how likely a test was to expose the claim as false; a test you could not have failed provides no evidence. Risky prediction — a specific, improbable-in-advance forecast whose success genuinely supports the theory that generated it. Duhem–Quine problem — the underdetermination of theory by evidence: hypotheses are tested in bundles with auxiliary assumptions, so a failed prediction does not identify the culprit. Auxiliary hypothesis — a background assumption bundled with the main claim during testing; revising one can legitimately save a theory, or illegitimately insulate it. Ad hoc rescue (immunizing stratagem) — a patch that absorbs a disconfirming result without generating any new testable prediction. Progressive vs. degenerating programme (Lakatos) — a research programme is progressive when its modifications yield novel predictions and degenerating when they merely protect the core. Underdetermination — the situation in which the same evidence is compatible with more than one theory; the reason evidence alone rarely forces a unique conclusion.

what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.title: 3-3 Bayesian reasoning
what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.description: Part of 3 Act II — The Structure of Knowledge (knowing)Bayes' theorem is a two-line piece of algebra that most people can derive and almost nobody applies. That gap is the point of this section. The formula tells you how to combine what you already believed with what you just observed; the difficulty is not the arithmetic but the discipline of admitting that you had a prior at all, that it was probably wrong, and that new evidence rarely moves it as far as it feels like it should.Your new belief should be your old belief, reweighted by how much more likely the evidence you just saw would be if you were right than if you were wrong.Everything else is bookkeeping. Written out, the odds form of Bayes' rule is: prior odds × likelihood ratio = posterior odds The prior odds express what you thought before. The likelihood ratio (LR) is the strength of the evidence — specifically, P(evidence | hypothesis) ÷ P(evidence | alternative). The posterior odds are what you should think now. Odds convert to probability with p = o / (1 + o), and back with o = p / (1 − p). Working in odds rather than probabilities is not a stylistic choice: it makes the update a multiplication, which is why the whole thing can be done in your head.The prior is not optional. A common misunderstanding is that Bayesian reasoning means approaching questions with an open mind. It does not. It means being explicit about the belief you already hold, because if you don't state a prior you still have one — it is just hidden, and the hidden default is usually either 50/50 (I have no idea) or 100% (I am certain). Both are strong claims, and neither survives contact with evidence particularly well.The likelihood ratio is where the work happens. The useful question about any piece of evidence is not "how consistent is this with my view?" — almost everything is consistent with almost everything — but "how much more likely is this under my view than under the alternative?" Evidence that is equally likely either way has an LR of 1 and tells you nothing, no matter how vivid or personally satisfying it is. This one question eliminates a startling amount of bad reasoning.A disease affects 1 in 100 people. A test for it is 90% sensitive (it catches 90% of true cases) and has a 5% false positive rate (it flags 5% of healthy people). You test positive. What is the probability you have the disease?The intuitive answer is "about 90%" — the number the test advertises. The correct answer is about 15%.Run it in natural frequencies, imagining 1,000 people:Of the ~59 positive tests, only 9 come from genuinely sick people. Nine out of fifty-nine is roughly 15%.In odds form, the same calculation: Prior odds = 1 : 99 Likelihood ratio = 0.90 / 0.05 = 18 Posterior odds = 18 : 99 ≈ 1 : 5.5, so p ≈ 1/6.5 ≈ 15% Notice what the LR of 18 did: a genuinely strong test pushed a rare hypothesis from 1% to 15% — a fifteen-fold increase in odds, and still far from a diagnosis. This is the arithmetic behind a claim you will hear in clinics, in courts, and in risk departments constantly: a positive result on a good test for a rare condition usually means you probably don't have it. The test is fine. The rarity is doing the work.A colleague reports that a new hire "solved a bug that had stumped the team for a week, in ten minutes." Does this mean she's exceptional?Set the prior. In a typical hiring pipeline, maybe 10% of hires are genuinely exceptional (odds 1 : 9). Now the LR: how much more likely is a ten-minute fix under "exceptional" than under "competent and happened to have seen this exact bug class before"? Perhaps 3 : 1 — she is more likely to do it, but a lucky pattern match is a live possibility, and one anecdote is a single draw. Posterior odds = 3 : 9 = 1 : 3, or a 25% chance.That is a real update — from 10% to 25% — and it is also nowhere near a conclusion. The lesson is not to discount the observation, but to see how many such observations would be needed. At an LR of 3 per anecdote, four independent anecdotes get you to roughly 3⁴ : 9 = 81 : 9 = 90%. One anecdote is a hint. Four are an argument. Priors are moved by accumulation, and the mind's error is to treat the first vivid data point as if it carried the weight of all four.Base rate neglect. The screening example is the canonical case: the prior (1%) gets ignored and the test characteristic (90%) is treated as the answer. This is common enough to have its own section later in this act — the outside view is just Bayes done with a properly sourced prior.The transposed conditional. P(positive | disease) is not P(disease | positive). The prosecutor's fallacy — "there's a 1-in-a-million chance of this DNA match occurring at random, therefore the chance of innocence is 1 in a million" — is exactly this error, and it has convicted people. Whenever you hear a conditional probability quoted, check which way round it points.Assuming a 50/50 prior. "I'll start with no assumptions" sounds neutral and is actually a strong, arbitrary claim. If you are estimating whether a given startup will succeed, the base rate for startups is not 50%.Multiplying evidence that isn't independent. LRs combine by multiplication only when the pieces of evidence are independent given the hypothesis. Three colleagues saying the new hire is brilliant, after discussing it with each other, are closer to one piece of evidence than three. Correlated evidence is the most common way confident people end up wrong.Priors that can't move. An LR of 18 applied to prior odds of 1 : 10,000 still leaves you at 1 : 555. Strong priors are not a bug — they are what protects you from every plausible-sounding crank — but they mean that evidence has to be very strong to change your mind, and that a mind which treats every disconfirming observation as a coincidence has effectively set its prior to infinity. Naming in advance what evidence would move you is the only audit that catches this. Ask the LR question out loud. "How much more likely is this if I'm right than if I'm wrong?" You will often discover the answer is "about equally," which is the most useful verdict available. Use natural frequencies. "Out of 1,000 people…" is far easier to compute correctly than percentages, and it makes the base rate impossible to skip. Update in small steps rather than jumping to certainty. A 3 : 1 update applied five times is a huge change; applied once, it's a nudge. Most real inference is a sequence of nudges. Notice silence. An absent observation is evidence when the observation would have occurred under the alternative. A detector that would certainly have fired if the hypothesis were true, and didn't, has a large LR against it. This is where Bayesian reasoning meets falsifiability: a claim that predicts nothing is a claim no evidence can move. Keep score. Stated probabilities can be scored; hedged ones cannot. Updating is only a skill if you find out whether your updates were the right size, which is where calibrated confidence comes in. One caveat keeps this honest: Bayesian reasoning is a normative standard — how a perfectly coherent reasoner would update — not a description of what brains do. People are demonstrably bad at it in the laboratory. But the predictive-processing account from Act I suggests the machinery is at least in the same family: perception itself behaves like a prior being corrected by prediction error, which is why the failure modes are so persistent. You are not learning a foreign language here. You are learning to do deliberately, with numbers, what your perceptual system does automatically and silently. Prior — the probability assigned to a hypothesis before new evidence is considered; expressed as odds when updating. Likelihood — the probability of observing the evidence given a hypothesis; not the same as the probability of the hypothesis. Likelihood ratio (LR) — P(evidence | hypothesis) ÷ P(evidence | alternative); the strength of the evidence, and the only quantity that does any updating work. Posterior — the updated probability after combining prior and likelihood ratio; tomorrow's prior. Odds form of Bayes' rule — prior odds × likelihood ratio = posterior odds; converts to probability via p = o / (1 + o). Base rate — the prevalence of a hypothesis in a reference class; the usual source of a prior, and the thing most often ignored. Base rate neglect — treating a test's accuracy as if it were the posterior probability, ignoring how rare the condition is. Transposed conditional — confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A); the engine of the prosecutor's fallacy. Prosecutor's fallacy — arguing that a small random-match probability equals a small probability of innocence. Natural frequencies — restating probabilities as counts out of a concrete population (e.g. 9 of 59), which makes correct updating far easier. Conditional independence — the assumption that pieces of evidence are unrelated given the hypothesis; required for multiplying likelihood ratios, and routinely violated. Weight of evidence — the cumulative effect of many updates, conveniently measured by adding the logarithms of the likelihood ratios rather than multiplying them.

what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.title: 3-4 Base rates & the outside view
what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.description: Part of 3 Act II — The Structure of Knowledge (knowing)Two people can look at the same decision and reach opposite conclusions without disagreeing about a single fact — because they started in different places. One reasons forward from the details of the case in front of them; the other starts from how often this kind of thing happens in general. The first is the inside view, the second the outside view, and the gap between them is one of the most reliable sources of error in ordinary judgment.Suppose someone asks: how likely is this? There is no way to answer without a reference class — a set of comparable cases whose frequency you can count. "How likely is this startup to succeed?" is unanswerable in the abstract; "what fraction of startups at this stage, in this sector, with this much funding, succeed?" is answerable. Probability is always probability relative to a class, and much of the skill lies in noticing that the class exists and choosing it well.Base rate neglect is what happens when we skip that step. Instead of counting comparable cases, we reason causally from the vivid specifics: this founder is impressive, this plan is detailed, this project is different. Each claim may be true. The error is using that information instead of the base rate rather than in addition to it.The classic demonstration comes from medical testing. A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A screening test catches it 90% of the time when present (sensitivity), and gives a false positive 9% of the time when absent. Your test comes back positive. What is the chance you have the disease?Most people — including, in Gigerenzer's studies, a large share of physicians — answer around 80–90%. The correct answer is about 9%.The base rate is doing almost all the work, and it is invisible in the way the question is phrased. Lay it out for 1,000 people:Of 98 positive tests, 9 are true. The vast majority of positives are false alarms, because the disease is rare and even a good test generates a lot of noise across a large healthy population. Nothing about the test changed; the prevalence did. Run the same test in a clinic where 20% of patients have the disease and a positive result means something entirely different.That last step is the odds form of Bayes' rule: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. The base rate supplies the prior; the evidence supplies the multiplier. Because a likelihood ratio is finite, evidence can only shift a base rate, never erase it — a point developed at length in the chapter on Bayesian reasoning.The practical trick is to convert probabilities into natural frequencies — "9 out of 98" rather than "9% given a positive test" — and to draw the 1,000-person table. Conditional probabilities invite the transposed error: confusing P(positive | disease) with P(disease | positive). That swap has a name, the prosecutor's fallacy, and it has convicted people: a "1 in a million" DNA match means something very different when the pool of potential matches contains millions.Kahneman tells a story against himself. Running a workshop on judgment, he asked each member of his team to estimate how long their textbook project would take. Everyone gave roughly two years. He then asked a colleague with experience of such projects how long similar efforts had taken — and learned that around 40% of them were never finished at all, and those that were took seven to ten years. The team had detailed, sincere, internally coherent reasons for saying two years. The base rate said otherwise, and the base rate was right.This is the planning fallacy: the systematic tendency to underestimate time, cost, and risk because we plan by imagining the specific sequence of steps going well, rather than by asking how often this kind of project finishes on schedule. It is not optimism about our abilities so much as a failure to consult the class. Flyvbjerg's studies of large infrastructure found average cost overruns on the order of 45% for rail projects, 34% for bridges and tunnels, and 20% for roads — a distribution so stable across countries and decades that it functions as a base rate you can plan against before you know anything about the specific project.The discipline that follows is reference class forecasting: before estimating anything, find the distribution of outcomes for the class your case belongs to, and use that as your starting point. The class is usually available — cost overruns on construction, survival rates for restaurants, publication lag for journal articles, tenure rates for academic job searches, relapse rates for a treatment. What makes the outside view uncomfortable is precisely what makes it valuable: it tells you almost nothing about your case, which is the information you already have too much of.The outside view has an obvious soft spot. There is always more than one class you could belong to — this is the reference class problem, and it has no fully general solution. "Most novels sell fewer than 500 copies" and "most novels by authors with this agent and this advance sell more" are both true, and they disagree.Three habits keep the choice honest: Start broad, then narrow only for reasons you could defend to a stranger. Narrow the class when you have a measurable, causally relevant difference — same sector, same stage, same regulatory regime — not because your case feels special. Everyone's case feels special; that feeling is the thing base rates exist to correct. Distrust classes built from survivors. "Most companies that made it did X" is not a base rate about X; it is a sample selected on the outcome. The class that matters includes the failures, and they are the ones that rarely leave data behind — which is the subject of the chapter on survivorship bias. Do not narrate the class away with one anecdote. A single vivid counterexample is evidence, but it is one data point; the base rate is thousands. The correct move is to ask how much better your case would have to be to beat the distribution, and whether you have any grounds for believing that. The outside view is not a rule that says "always predict the average." It is a prior, and priors get updated. Three legitimate reasons to depart from a base rate: You have information that is genuinely diagnostic. A particular hospital's infection rate, a named track record, a specific engineering assessment. Diagnostic means it would change the prediction for this case, not just feel reassuring. The class has structurally changed. Base rates from an era before a technology, a regulation, or a market shift may simply not apply — the terrain of the black swan and fat-tailed chapter. You are selecting on it. Deliberately filtering for the top of a distribution — picking only projects in the best decile — is a strategy, not base rate neglect. Just be honest about how you know you are in that decile. A related and quietly powerful application is regression to the mean. Extreme outcomes are usually a mixture of skill and luck, and luck does not persist. The best predictor of next year's performance, absent other information, is not this year's — it is the class average. The outside view, in this sense, is simply the formal version of a rule most experienced people carry without naming: when something looks remarkable, ask what the unremarkable expectation was. Forecasting and planning — schedules, budgets, and deadlines set from the inside view, systematically short. Medicine — screening in low-prevalence populations, where most positives are noise. Law and forensics — the prosecutor's fallacy; also why eyewitness confidence is a weak signal about accuracy. Hiring and admissions — a strong interview is vivid, the base rate of job performance is dull, and the dull number predicts better. Diagnosis of systems — "this team underperformed last quarter" may be regression to the mean rather than a problem to be fixed. Your own beliefs — the outside view applied to a claim is simply asking what usually happens to claims of this type, which is a habit that overlaps heavily with calibration. The discomfort is structural. The inside view is constructed, specific, and yours; the outside view is borrowed, coarse, and impersonal. That asymmetry is why the base rate is so often skipped, and why the person who reaches for it first so often turns out to be right.Base rate — The underlying frequency of an event or condition in a population, independent of the evidence at hand; the prior in a Bayesian update.Reference class — The set of comparable cases used to establish a base rate; the choice of class largely determines the answer.Outside view — Estimating by locating the case within a reference class and using that class's distribution of outcomes.Inside view — Estimating by reasoning forward from the specific details of the case, ignoring the class.Base rate neglect — The error of judging probability from case-specific evidence while ignoring the underlying frequency.Transposed conditional / prosecutor's fallacy — Confusing P(evidence | hypothesis) with P(hypothesis | evidence), usually in legal or forensic reasoning.Natural frequencies — Presenting probabilities as counts out of a concrete population ("9 in 98") rather than conditional percentages; markedly improves reasoning accuracy.Likelihood ratio — The ratio of the probability of the evidence under one hypothesis versus another; the multiplier applied to prior odds in Bayes' rule.Planning fallacy — The systematic underestimation of timelines, costs, and risks that results from planning from the inside view.Reference class forecasting — A formal method that anchors an estimate in the outcome distribution of comparable projects before adjusting for specifics.Reference class problem — The unresolved difficulty that any case belongs to many possible classes, which may yield conflicting base rates.Regression to the mean — The statistical tendency for extreme outcomes to be followed by more average ones, absent a genuine change; the outside view applied across time.

what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.title: 3-5 The replication crisis & how science self-corrects
what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.description: Part of 3 Act II — The Structure of Knowledge (knowing)Replication is science's error-correction routine: you run a study, someone else runs it again, and if the result holds up it becomes knowledge. The replication crisis is the discovery — made mostly in the 2010s, mostly in psychology, medicine, and economics — that this routine had quietly stopped running. When researchers finally went back and checked, a large fraction of published findings turned out not to hold. The interesting part isn't that scientists get things wrong; it's how the error accumulated, and how the same institutions that produced it are now repairing it.A "replication" means repeating a study and asking whether you reach the same conclusion. Starting around 2011, researchers began doing this at scale, and the results were consistent and uncomfortable: Psychology (2015). A coordinated effort repeated 100 published studies from three top journals. About 36% produced a statistically significant result in the same direction; the average effect size was roughly half the originally reported one. Cancer biology (2012). Of 53 landmark preclinical studies, 6 could be confirmed. Economics (2016). Of 18 experimental studies from two leading journals, 11 replicated (61%). Social science (2018). Of 21 papers published in Nature and Science, 13 replicated (62%). Note the spread. Economics and high-profile social science fared much better than psychology, and preclinical cancer biology worst of all. Replication rates are not a single number describing "science"; they describe particular fields at a particular time, with particular habits.Two definitions keep the discussion honest, because they are routinely conflated: Reproducibility — same data, same code, same analysis, same answer. This is about whether anyone can check your arithmetic. Replicability — new data, same protocol, same conclusion. This is about whether the finding is real. A study can be perfectly reproducible (the analysis code runs cleanly) and completely unreplicable (the effect was noise).The seductive explanation is fraud. It is mostly wrong. Outright fabrication exists, and paper mills have made it worse — more than 10,000 papers were retracted in a single year recently — but the bulk of the crisis is ordinary people responding rationally to ordinary incentives while using methods that permit too much freedom.The loop looks like this:Five mechanisms drive it:Analysis flexibility. Given one dataset, there are dozens of defensible choices — which outliers to drop, which covariates to include, whether to stop collecting now. If you try enough combinations, something will reach p < .05. The result isn't fabricated; it's the product of a garden of forking paths, and the researcher usually cannot tell you afterwards which fork they took.Publication bias. Null results are hard to publish, so they go in a file drawer. The literature you read is the surviving half of the distribution — a survivorship problem applied to knowledge itself.Low statistical power. Most psychology studies had enough subjects to detect a real effect maybe a third of the time. Underpowered studies don't merely fail to find real effects; they systematically overestimate the effects they do find, because only unusually large flukes clear the significance bar. The most dramatic result in a noisy field is usually the most exaggerated one.Incentives. Careers, grants, and journals reward novelty and certainty, not careful understatement. A survey of more than 2,000 psychologists found that a majority admitted to at least one questionable practice — failing to report every measure collected, or deciding to collect more data after peeking at the results.Base rates. Even a well-run study produces misleading evidence more often than intuition suggests, because of what Ioannidis pointed out in 2005: in a field where most hypotheses tested are false and the tests are weak, a "significant" result is more likely to be a false positive than a true one.This is Goodhart's Law wearing a lab coat: once p < .05 became the target by which papers, jobs, and journals were measured, it stopped being a good measure of anything.It is worth being precise about what has been discovered. The replication crisis was found by scientists, using scientific methods, and published in scientific journals. Meta-science — the study of how science itself performs — is now a field. The failure mode being exposed is not "the method doesn't work" but "the method was being run with weak statistics and perverse incentives, and it took institutional self-examination to find that out."That is exactly what a self-correcting system is supposed to look like — late, expensive, and against the interests of the people who have to do the correcting.The repairs now underway are structural, not moral. They change what is rewarded and what is checkable. Pre-registration and registered reports. Researchers post their hypothesis, sample size, and analysis plan before collecting data; some journals then accept or reject the paper on the plan, before results exist. This removes the flexibility that p-hacking requires, and it removes the publication penalty for a null result. Multi-lab replication. Consortia run the same study simultaneously in dozens of laboratories, which separates a real effect from one lab's quirks and produces samples large enough to measure modest effects honestly. Adversarial collaboration. Researchers who disagree design a study together, agreeing in advance what each outcome would mean. It's a genuinely clever move: it converts an argument into an experiment. Open data, materials, and code. If anyone can re-run your analysis and see your raw measures, errors surface in months rather than never. Meta-analysis and p-curve techniques. Pooling many studies, or examining the distribution of reported p-values, can reveal whether a literature looks like the byproduct of selective reporting. Post-publication review. PubPeer and Retraction Watch have made it possible to challenge a paper publicly and permanently, independent of the journal that published it. Statistical reform. Journals increasingly ask for effect sizes and confidence intervals rather than a binary significant/not-significant verdict, which discourages the illusion that a threshold settles a question. The crucial bottleneck is the arrow from "effect shrinks" back into the literature. Correcting a published claim requires someone to fund, conduct, and publish a replication — activities that earn little credit. Failed replications are easier to publish than they were, but they are still nobody's path to tenure.In 2011, a distinguished social psychologist published a paper in a top journal reporting nine experiments showing that people's responses were influenced by events that had not happened yet. The effects were small but statistically significant, and the paper was methodologically conventional — nothing about it was obviously fraudulent.Within a year, independent researchers ran the procedure with larger samples and found nothing. Statisticians reanalysed the original data and showed that the pattern was consistent with selective reporting rather than precognition. The finding is now treated as noise.Look at what the cycle required: someone willing to run an unglamorous replication, a journal willing to publish a null result, and a field willing to accept that a well-published paper was wrong. It also required years, and the original paper still gets cited. That is the machinery working at realistic speed.Four honest limitations:Correction lags citation. Retracted papers continue to be cited for years, and many practitioners never learn of the retraction. The literature has no automatic memory update — this is path dependence applied to knowledge."Failure to replicate" is itself ambiguous. A replication that fails may indicate a false original, a real effect that is smaller than reported, a real effect that only holds under boundary conditions (a different population, dose, or context), or simply an underpowered replication. The correct response to one failed replication is usually "this is now uncertain," not "this is false."Fields vary enormously. Physics and chemistry have hard measurement standards, precise theory, and effects that are either there or not. Fields studying humans, with flexible measures and noisy outcomes, are where the crisis lives. Beware of anyone porting the finding from one to the other.The fixes must be paid for. Pre-registration is cheap; multi-lab replication and long-term data sharing are not. And structural reform is slow because the people who would have to change are the people currently winning under the old rules.The practical rules are simple and mostly about not over-reading single results: Trust distributions, not papers. One study is an anecdote with a methods section. A systematic review or meta-analysis is where a field's knowledge actually lives. Prefer registered studies — especially anything labelled a registered report or a pre-registered replication. The plan existed before the result did, which rules out most of the ways a finding can be manufactured. Look for the failed attempts. Search for the phenomenon name plus "failed replication." What you're looking for is whether anyone tried and what happened. Watch the effect size, not the adjective. "Significant" means "unlikely under a null hypothesis," nothing more. A real but tiny effect and a large but fragile one both get printed as "linked to." Expect shrinkage. In fields with flexible analysis, a finding's true magnitude is usually smaller than the headline. The bigger the claim, the more shrinkage to expect. Ask what would change your mind, and then ask whether anyone has done it. The broader lesson reaches past science. Any institution that produces knowledge — journalism, medicine, intelligence, your own memory — has some version of this problem: the outputs are shaped by what gets rewarded and published, not only by what is true. The unusual thing about science is that it contains a mechanism designed to catch itself. That mechanism is slow, expensive, and occasionally humiliating, which is precisely why it deserves more trust than any method that never has to apologize.Replication — Repeating a study to see whether its conclusion holds; the core test of whether a finding is real rather than a fluke.Reproducibility — Obtaining the same result from the same data and analysis; distinct from replication, which requires new data.Replication crisis — The large-scale discovery, from around 2011 onward, that many published findings in psychology, medicine, and related fields do not replicate.p-hacking / selective reporting — Using analytic flexibility — dropping outliers, adding covariates, trying measures — until a desired significance threshold is crossed.Garden of forking paths — Gelman's term for the many defensible analytic choices that produce spurious findings even when no deliberate p-hacking occurs.HARKing — Hypothesizing After the Results are Known: presenting a post-hoc explanation as though it had been predicted.Publication bias / file-drawer problem — The tendency for positive results to be published and null results to disappear, distorting the visible literature.Statistical power — The probability a study will detect an effect that is actually there; low power both misses real effects and inflates the ones it finds.Winner's curse — The tendency for the most extreme reported effects in a noisy field to be the least likely to hold up, because they cleared a significance threshold by luck.Pre-registration — Publicly recording hypotheses, sample size, and analysis plan before data collection.Registered report — A paper accepted or rejected on the basis of its pre-registered plan, with results published regardless of outcome; the strongest structural fix for publication bias.Multi-lab replication — The same study run simultaneously by many laboratories to separate real effects from local quirks and to achieve adequate sample size.Adversarial collaboration — A study designed jointly by researchers holding opposing views, with agreement in advance on what each possible result would mean.Meta-analysis — Statistically pooling many studies to estimate an overall effect and expose patterns of selective reporting.Retraction — A journal's formal withdrawal of a published paper; typically slow, and rarely accompanied by an update to everyone who has cited it.Credibility revolution — The name for the reform movement — open data, pre-registration, replication, statistical reform — that emerged in response to the replication crisis.

what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.title: 3-6 Is-ought gap
what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.description: Part of 3 Act II — The Structure of Knowledge (knowing)Every argument for what we should do contains something that was not in any argument about what is. That observation, made in passing by David Hume in 1739, turns out to be one of the most practically useful distinctions in this book — not because it forbids reasoning about ethics, but because it tells you exactly where reasoning about ethics must be checked. The is/ought gap is less a wall between facts and values than a demand for bookkeeping: if a conclusion tells you to act, at least one of your premises must already have told you what was worth wanting.Hume's remark is worth quoting, because it is more careful than the slogan it became: In every system of morality, which I have hitherto met with, I have always remark'd, that the author proceeds for some time in the ordinary way of reasoning, and establishes the being of a God, or makes observations concerning human affairs; when of a sudden I am surpriz'd to find, that instead of the usual copulations of propositions, is, and is not, I meet with no proposition that is not connected with an ought, or an ought not... (Treatise of Human Nature, 3.1.1) His complaint is about a silent transition. The argument runs along on descriptive premises — how the world is — and then, without announcement, delivers a prescriptive conclusion. Hume's point is that this move needs a licence, and the licence was never shown.Stated as logic rather than as complaint: from premises containing only descriptive terms, no conclusion containing an evaluative "ought" follows validly. You can derive oughts from oughts, and is-statements from is-statements; you cannot get from one to the other for free. Nothing here says moral claims are irrational, arbitrary, or merely emotional — Hume himself thought moral sentiment was a natural and motivating part of human psychology. The claim is narrow and formal: check the premises, because the conclusion contains something the premises did not.The bridge premise is where all the interesting disagreement lives, and it is almost always the premise left silent. That silence is not usually dishonesty. It is that the speaker's values feel like facts to them — self-evident, universal, not worth stating.Three misreadings are common enough to be worth disarming.It is not "values are irrational." Logical entailment is one relation among many. Values can be argued for by appeal to consistency, to consequences, to coherence with other values, to what you'd accept behind a veil of ignorance, or to their track record in producing lives people endorse. None of that is entailment from description, and none of it is nothing.It is not "facts and values never mix." Philippa Foot, Elizabeth Anscombe, and Alasdair MacIntyre all pointed out that many concepts are thick: "cruel," "cowardly," "brave," "honest," "generous" simultaneously describe and evaluate. To identify an act as cruel is already, in part, to appraise it. Anthropologists, evaluators, and doctors cannot do their jobs with only thin, purely descriptive terms. So the gap is not a clean boundary between two territories; it is a boundary that is easy to cross, hard to notice crossing, and worth noticing. A functional concept — "a knife," "a heart," "a farmer" — carries built-in standards, which is why the gap looks narrower in Aristotle's framework than in Hume's.It is not the naturalistic fallacy. G. E. Moore's target was different: the claim that "good" can be defined as some natural property (pleasure, evolutionary fitness, what we desire to desire). His open-question argument — for any proposed definition, it remains an open question whether that property is actually good — is a claim about definition, not about inference. The two are routinely conflated. Keep them apart: Hume's gap is about derivation, Moore's is about meaning.The traffic runs both ways, and the reverse direction is just as common and more seductive. Moralistic fallacy: inferring what is from what ought to be. If the world should be fair, we begin to perceive it as fairer than it is; if a policy should work, its failures get reinterpreted as implementation problems rather than disconfirmation. Every ideology does this, and so does every well-run team protecting a favoured project.The practical damage is that it corrupts the empirical side of the argument, which is the side you can actually settle. The is/ought gap tells you the value premise needs defending; the moralistic fallacy is what happens when, rather than defending it, you quietly rewrite the evidence to agree with it.The gap is a diagnostic tool with two main uses.The premise audit. When someone (including you) says "the evidence says we should…", stop and locate the bridge. Not to refute the argument — usually to complete it, so that the actual disagreement becomes visible. Group disagreements that look like fights about data are often fights about values wearing a lab coat; conversely, loud value fights sometimes dissolve into a shared value plus an unresolvable empirical question. Separating the two tells you whether to go get more evidence or to go negotiate.The honesty check. Naming your own bridge premise in advance is a strange kind of freedom. "I think we should fund this because I weight the next fifty years heavily" is a defensible position that can be argued with. "The data leave no choice" is not a position at all; it is a claim of exemption from reasoning.A hospital committee is deciding whether to keep a costly treatment available to a small number of very sick patients. Is-claims: the treatment costs $2.1M per year, extends median survival by 11 months in a specific subgroup, and would need to be cut to fund a new emergency-department triage system projected to save an estimated 6 lives annually. Bridge premises, unstated: that scarce resources should go where they save the most lives; that saved lives are comparable units; that 11 months of life is worth less than an expected full life; that aggregate lives saved should outrank identifiable patients; that the committee has the authority to make this trade. Notice how many bridges there are, how plausible each is individually, and how contested each becomes when stated. The committee is not choosing between evidence and no evidence. It is choosing between value frameworks, using evidence to inform each. Making that explicit doesn't produce agreement — but it moves the argument from a dispute about facts, which cannot be won, to one about priorities, which at least can be conducted.This connects directly to the veil-of-ignorance construction and to moral luck: much of what feels like a difference in moral perception is a difference in which premises you find obvious. It also connects to falsifiability. Value claims cannot be tested against the world the way a mechanism can, but they can be tested for consistency across cases, for the costs they impose, and for whether you would accept them applied to you. That is not science, but it is not arbitrary either — and it is the only terrain on which the normative half of any decision can honestly be argued.Is/ought gap (Hume's guillotine) — the thesis that no valid inference can move from premises containing only descriptive statements to a conclusion containing an evaluative "ought," unless a normative premise is smuggled in.Descriptive statement — a claim about what is the case, in principle checkable against the world.Normative statement — a claim about what should be the case, or about what is good, right, or worth doing.Bridge premise — the unstated normative premise that licenses the move from facts to a prescription; the real locus of disagreement.Validity (logical) — the property of an argument whose conclusion follows from its premises regardless of whether those premises are true. The gap is a claim about validity, not about truth.Naturalistic fallacy — Moore's charge that "good" cannot be defined in terms of any natural property; distinct from, and often confused with, the is/ought gap.Open-question argument — Moore's test for such definitions: for any proposed natural property, it remains an open question whether that property is good.Thick and thin ethical concepts — thick concepts (cruel, brave, honest) describe and evaluate at once; thin ones (good, right) evaluate without describing. The existence of thick concepts blurs but does not erase the fact/value boundary.Moralistic fallacy — inferring what is from what ought to be; the reverse smuggling, which corrupts evidence in favour of a preferred value.Premise audit — the practice of identifying every bridge premise in an argument before evaluating the argument, so empirical and normative disputes can be separated and addressed on their own terms.

what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.title: 3-7 Epistemology of disagreement (when to defer)
what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.description: Part of 3 Act II — The Structure of Knowledge (knowing)Most treatments of disagreement frame it as a contest: someone is wrong, and the job is to work out who. But once you accept that your beliefs are fallible and that you cannot audit them alone, disagreement changes role — it becomes an instrument, one of the few error-correction mechanisms a single mind has access to. The interesting question is no longer "who is right?" but "what does this disagreement license me to do with my confidence?" Answer that, and you can be wrong in public without being destabilised, and right in private without becoming a crank.Sorting matters, because the correct response differs sharply by type: Disagreement from below. The other person has less evidence or less competence than you. No revision is owed on the object level — though they are often right about a local detail you've abstracted away, which is worth harvesting. Disagreement from above. They have more evidence, better tools, or a track record you don't. The default is to defer — but deference has an identification problem (below). Peer disagreement. Someone with the same evidence, the same competence, and the same honesty reaches the opposite conclusion. This is the hard case, and the one the philosophical literature is actually about. The definition of an epistemic peer is deliberately strict: same evidence, same reasoning ability, same intellectual honesty, no distorting incentives. Most people you argue with fail one of those conditions, which is why "peer disagreement" is rarer than ordinary disagreement and why the intuition that you should always split the difference is wrong so much of the time.Two positions define the debate.Conciliationism (Elga, Christensen, Feldman) says that the bare fact of a peer's disagreement is higher-order evidence about your own reliability. I might be unable to find my error — that is exactly what an error looks like from the inside — but the fact that someone equally well placed reached a different answer is evidence that I've mis-stepped somewhere. On this view, you should move toward their position, often roughly to the midpoint.Steadfastness (Kelly's "right reasons" view) replies that what matters is the first-order evidence. If I have correctly evaluated it, the disagreement is fully explained by their error, and the disagreement itself gives me no new reason to move. Concentrating on who did the evidence better is the only rational response.Both capture something real. Conciliationism explains why persistent disagreement between competent people is humbling; the right-reasons view explains why a physicist should not halve their confidence in Newtonian mechanics because a neighbour disagrees. The practical resolution is that the tie is broken by asymmetry: not total symmetry, but asymmetry you can actually see.Actual peerhood is rare, so the operative skill is detecting the asymmetry. The recurring asymmetries:Evidence access. If they have seen something you haven't, the disagreement is a pointer to evidence, not a verdict. Ask what they've seen.Track record, not confidence. Deference is owed to demonstrated calibration, not to conviction. Someone whose 80% forecasts come true 80% of the time has earned weight; someone who is merely certain has not. Note that confidence and calibration come apart in the wrong direction — the loudest disputant is frequently the least scored. This is the payoff of keeping score at all.Predictability of error. Experts fail in patterned ways, and patterns are usable. You do not need to master a field to notice that its practitioners are systematically optimistic about timelines, or systematically captured by whoever funds them.Legibility. Can they state what evidence would change their mind? Someone who answers that question concretely is offering you a testable position; someone who cannot is offering you an identity.Meta-expertise and its limits. You often cannot evaluate the content of an expert claim without already being an expert, so you fall back on proxies: credentials, the endorsement of other experts, track record, and incentives. This is rational but fragile — every proxy is a measure, and measures under pressure get gamed (which is why credentialism decays, and why "consensus" is worth less when careers depend on it). The workaround is to use several proxies and to weight the ones that are hard to fake: resolved predictions, records of admitting error, and being willing to lose arguments in public.A crucial asymmetry runs the other way: apparent crowds are often one witness wearing many hats. The Condorcet jury theorem says a majority of independent voters, each better than chance, converges on the truth — but its independence assumption does the work, and real agreement is usually correlated. Five colleagues agreeing often means four of them read the fifth.The diversity prediction theorem makes the same point arithmetically: crowd error equals average individual error minus diversity of the group. Correlated agreement adds nothing to the first term and subtracts from the second. This is why deference has a hidden cost — if everyone defers to the same apparent authority, the aggregate signal gets worse, and the disagreeing person who holds an independent line is performing a public service even when wrong.Holding firm is legitimate in specific, nameable situations — and illegitimate as a general mood. The dispute is downstream of values. Expertise bears on what will happen, not on what you want. Defer on the forecast, keep the decision. (Facts and preferences are different kinds of claim; treating a technical answer as a value answer smuggles in an ought.) Your evidence is genuinely private and unshareable. You were there; they weren't. The corollary is uncomfortable: you may be misremembering, which is why contemporaneous notes outrank retrospective certainty. Their position cannot be falsified by anything. A claim that survives every possible observation is not a strong belief but a non-empirical one — you owe it no evidential deference. Incentives predict the conclusion. Not always, but often enough to weight. The failure mode here is motivated reasoning wearing the mask of principle. The test is the one you've already met: name what would change your mind. If nothing would, you're not defending a belief, you're defending a self.You estimate a project will take three months. A colleague with the same specifications estimates nine. Neither of you has privileged information.Running the protocol: you are, on the formal definition, peers. You ask whether the disagreement is one claim or several — and it turns out to be several: you differ on how much rework testing will trigger, and on whether a dependency will slip. Localising it converts an argument about a number into two answerable questions. You then check track records and the reference class: how long do projects of this type usually take, and how accurate have your past estimates been? If the answer to the second is "I say three months, it takes five," your estimate is not a peer of theirs; it is a biased instrument, and you should move most of the way toward the better-calibrated estimator — not to the midpoint, and not to nine months either. If both of you are equally well calibrated, the honest number is somewhere in between, and the way to shrink the range is to go find evidence about rework and the dependency, not to argue about the number. Classify it: below, above, or genuine peer. Locate the crux — the smallest sub-claim on which your disagreement turns. Test for independence: is your evidence a second source or the same source twice? Compare calibration, not confidence. State what evidence would move you, and ask them to do the same. Defer on the object level if they're better placed; keep the meta-level judgement that they might be wrong. The discomfort of this protocol is that it is sometimes an argument for submission: occasionally the right answer is that you should simply believe the person who knows more, and stop adjudicating. That is not intellectual weakness. It is what epistemic humility looks like when it has a target. Epistemic peer — someone with the same evidence, comparable competence, and comparable honesty on the question at hand. Peer disagreement — a conflict of opinion between epistemic peers; the case where the rational response is genuinely contested. Higher-order evidence — evidence about the reliability of your own reasoning, such as the fact that a competent person disagrees, rather than evidence about the subject itself. Conciliationism — the view that peer disagreement provides higher-order evidence and should move you toward the other position. Steadfastness / right-reasons view — the view that if you evaluated the first-order evidence correctly, the mere fact of disagreement gives you no reason to revise. Asymmetry — a detectable difference between disputants in evidence access, calibration, or vulnerability to error; the practical tie-breaker over full symmetry. Crux — the smallest specific sub-claim on which a disagreement turns; localising it converts an intractable dispute into answerable questions. Independence of evidence — the property of two sources being error-correlated or not; only independent sources multiply the weight of agreement. Diversity prediction theorem — crowd error equals average individual error minus group diversity; correlated agreement destroys the crowd's advantage. Meta-expertise — knowledge about which experts to trust, used when you cannot evaluate the substance of a claim directly.

what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.title: 3-8 Tying it all together
what-nobody-taught-you/3-act-ii-—-the-st.description: Part of 3 Act II — The Structure of Knowledge (knowing)Seven sections, one act, and at first glance they do not look like members of the same family: a theory of maps, a rule about refutation, a piece of probability algebra, a statistical scandal, a point of moral philosophy, and a protocol for disagreeing with people. Presented one at a time they read like a toolbox assembled from six different trades.They are not. That is the claim of this closing section, and it is worth stating plainly because it changes how you use everything in the act: the ideas in Act II are not a list of good practices. They are five stages of a single instrument, and each stage exists because the previous one has a specific, predictable way of failing. Learn them apart and you get slogans — "correlation isn't causation," "check the base rate," "the map is not the territory." Learn them as a pipeline and you get something rarer: a way of knowing where in your own reasoning a mistake has probably just occurred.The act's tools answer five questions, in order. Each answer feeds the next, and each one is a repair for a failure mode you met in Act I.The ordering is not arbitrary. Compressing comes first because you cannot reason about a territory directly — the map is not an unfortunate concession, it is the precondition of thought. Committing comes second because a claim with no failure condition cannot be combined, tested, or contested; it is not yet in the empirical game. Combining comes third because that is where evidence actually gets weighed. Contesting comes fourth because it is slow — replication and genuine peer disagreement take months or years, which is exactly why they are the backstop rather than the first move. And converting comes last because it is the only stage that produces action, and action is the only stage that changes the territory and starts the loop over.Notice what the loop does that no single section did. A map can be excellent and the claim built on it still fail at Commit. A claim can be sharp and beautifully falsifiable while the evidence is applied with the wrong prior. Bayes can be run flawlessly on a base rate borrowed from a class selected on survivors. And an entirely correct empirical conclusion can be converted into an action that serves a value nobody stated. Every stage can be executed well while the whole thing is wrong — which is why the act resists being summarised as a set of tips.Here is the pattern that runs through the act and is easy to miss when you read the sections separately.Falsifiability works only if you specify the failure condition before you see the result. Base rates work only if the prior is sourced before the vivid specifics arrive. Pre-registration works by fixing the analysis before the data. The disagreement protocol works by naming what would change your mind before the argument starts. In every case the tool is a contract you signed while still ignorant, and its entire value derives from having been signed early.The reason is Act I. Your confidence is manufactured after the fact — memory reconstructs, hindsight feels like foresight, and the moment you have a conclusion, the reasons for it become available and satisfying. An instrument like that cannot audit itself in real time; it can only be constrained in advance. So the tools of this act are not virtues you cultivate. They are commitments you make while you are still able to make them honestly.This is the same trick as writing down a decision before you make it, and the same reason pre-registration outperforms good intentions. It is also why the tools feel unnatural: they require you to do administrative work at the moment you feel most certain, and to accept the result at the moment you feel least inclined to.A second synthesis point, and a quantitative one. Reliability across the pipeline is multiplicative, not additive. If each stage is roughly 90% likely to be done well, the end-to-end result is about 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 ≈ 0.59. Add one genuinely shaky stage — a poorly chosen reference class, a value premise nobody examined — and the compound collapses.Treat that table as an illustration rather than a probability model — the stages are not strictly independent, and "done well" is not really a Bernoulli trial. The structural lesson survives the loose arithmetic: the weakest stage dominates the output. This is why "I did the Bayesian part correctly" is not a defence. Rigorous arithmetic on a map that discarded the thing that mattered is not a partial success; it is a confident failure, and often a worse one than a cheerful guess, because the arithmetic launders the error.It also explains a pattern you will meet constantly in real institutions: sophisticated methods deployed on an unexamined question. Elaborate forecasting models fed by a metric that no longer tracks the thing it was built to track. Cost-benefit analyses whose "cost" quietly excludes the people who bear it. The sophistication is real, and it is doing nothing, because the ceiling was set two stages earlier.A headline lands on your desk: hybrid work raises productivity by 13% — and the question is whether your organisation should mandate it. Watch the five moves, and notice that each one is cheap at the point where it is applied and expensive later.Compress. What is "productivity" here? Output per hour in what kind of work, measured how — shipped units, self-reported focus, manager ratings? The study's map of productivity is one projection; your organisation's is another, and the gap between them is not a detail. The first question is not whether the 13% is real, but what it is 13% of. If the study measured a task with a clear output and your work is mostly coordination, the finding may be perfectly true and simply inapplicable — omission failure wearing the costume of evidence.Commit. Turn the choice into something that can lose. "If we adopt a two-day-per-week hybrid pilot for two quarters in the engineering group, cycle time improves by at least 5% over baseline; if it does not, we revert." That sentence has a threshold, a window, and a settlement rule, and it exists before the pilot starts, which is the only time it could have been written honestly.Combine. How much should one study move you? The prior comes from the reference class, not from the study's abstract: what is the distribution of measured effects for organisational interventions on output? It is wide, centred near zero, and the published effects are subject to the winner's curse, so a headline of 13% is more likely to be near the top of the distribution than to be typical of it. Assign a likelihood ratio in the range of 2 to 3 — real, upward, and nowhere near decisive. The posterior is "this is now somewhat more likely than before," which is a very different input to a decision than "a study proves."Contest. Two of your colleagues disagree, one for and one against. Before weighing them, check independence: if both read the same single study, they are one witness in two bodies, and their disagreement tells you about their prior dispositions rather than about hybrid work. Then localise the crux — here, almost always whether the metric that improved generalises to work whose output is hard to measure. That is an answerable question, and it converts an argument about a policy into a question about a measurement.Convert. Nothing so far entails "mandate." That step requires a bridge: we should privilege measured throughput over the unmeasured benefits of co-location, mentorship, and serendipity. That premise may be right — it may even be obviously right to you — but it is a value claim, and it is the actual thing your organisation is arguing about. Stating it is not pedantry. It moves the disagreement from a dispute about facts, which will not resolve, to a dispute about priorities, which at least can be conducted.Then you act — and the act changes the territory, generates second-order effects, and hands the problem to a different set of tools entirely. That hand-off is the subject of the next act.Because the stages differ by orders of magnitude in cost, the pipeline works best as triage rather than as a checklist you run in full every time. Naming a failure condition takes seconds. Asking what a map discarded takes minutes. Locating a base rate takes an afternoon. Replication and genuine peer disagreement take months and, usually, other people's cooperation. The ascending cost is the reason to run them in order and stop as soon as a stage fails.Most bad reasoning in the wild fails at one of the two gates on the left. A claim that cannot lose is not a belief. A prior drawn from nothing is a guess wearing a number's clothing. Catching either costs almost nothing, and no amount of downstream sophistication recovers from missing it.One framing deserves to survive the act, because it prevents a common and specific disappointment. None of these tools makes you neutral. Each is a deliberate tilt against a specific default error. Falsifiability is a tilt against confirmation, which is abundant and cheap. The outside view is a tilt against the vivid particulars in front of you, which are always more persuasive than the distribution. The disagreement protocol is a tilt against the feeling that your own evaluation was careful. Bayesian updating is a tilt against your sense that the latest thing you heard is the most important thing you know.This is a consequence of Act I rather than a concession to it. If the biases are features — cheap heuristics that work often enough in the environments that built them — then the tool for correcting them is not an inner state of impartiality, which nobody sustains. It is an external commitment that costs you something in the moment you would rather not pay it. The direction of the tilt is chosen in advance for exactly that reason.Two closing applications, both recursive.Apply the disagreement protocol to your past self. The person who set your priors last year had less information and the same confidence you have now. Treating your own earlier beliefs as an epistemic peer with a worse track record is a strange manoeuvre that resolves cleanly: where you can identify a specific mistake, correct it; where you cannot, the fact that a similarly-placed version of you reached the opposite conclusion is genuine higher-order evidence, and it should move you.Apply falsifiability to the toolkit. What would show you that the outside view is being misused — that your reference class is selected on survivors? What would show that your disagreement protocol has become a ritual for deferring to the loudest person in the room? If nothing would, the tools have stopped being instruments and become a personality. This is the failure mode that arrives last, because it arrives precisely for people who have learned the material well enough to use it fluently.What the act leaves you with is not a body of knowledge but a set of standing instructions — things to have decided in advance, so that the decision is not available to you when it matters. Write the claim, the threshold, and the date before you look. Whether it is a forecast, a hire, or a decision, the pre-commitment is the whole mechanism. For any metric you rely on, name two things it cannot see. If you cannot, you have not finished understanding it. Ask the likelihood-ratio question out loud: how much more likely is this if I am right than if I am wrong? "About the same" is the most common and most useful answer. Start from the class, then adjust for the case. Broaden before you narrow, and mistrust any class assembled from things that survived. Trust distributions, not single findings, and expect published effects to shrink. Separate the empirical question from the value question before arguing, and state your own bridge premise where others can see it. Count sources, not people, and treat an independent dissenter as a public good rather than an obstacle. Name what would change your mind — about the claim, and periodically about the toolkit. Every one of these is the same move in different clothing: give up a little freedom now, while you are still able to, in exchange for the ability to be corrected later. That is what knowing looks like when the knower is a fallible instrument. And it is why the answer to "how do I know?" is never a state you reach. It is a loop you keep running.
