what-nobody-taught-you/5-act-iv-—-the-co.title: 5-7 Moloch - multipolar traps
what-nobody-taught-you/5-act-iv-—-the-co.description: Part of 5 Act IV — The Coordination Problem (us)A multipolar trap is a situation in which everyone involved would prefer a different outcome, everyone involved is doing something entirely reasonable, and the outcome is bad anyway. Its defining feature is the absence of a villain. Nobody has to be greedy, shortsighted, or malicious for the trap to close; the participants can describe the structure perfectly and still be unable to leave it. Once you can see this shape, you find it everywhere — in antibiotic resistance, exam prep, advertising, fisheries, litigation, arms races, and the thirty seconds before every meeting where somebody proposes a new metric.Start with the smallest version, the prisoner's dilemma. Two players each choose to cooperate or defect; the payoffs are:Whatever B does, A does better by defecting — defect against a cooperator and you get 5 instead of 3; defect against a defector and you get 1 instead of 0. The move is dominant. The same reasoning runs for B, so both defect, and the pair lands on (1, 1). Yet both would clearly have preferred (3, 3). The outcome is a Nash equilibrium — nobody can improve by changing strategy alone — and it is simultaneously Pareto-dominated, meaning everyone could be better off at a different outcome.That gap between "no one can move" and "everyone would prefer to move" is the whole phenomenon. Three ingredients produce it: A competitive margin. Something is being contested — a resource, a rank, a market, a mate, a vote — and effort placed on that margin buys an advantage. An uninternalized externality. The cost of your move lands somewhere other than on you: on other users of a shared resource, on your rivals' customers, on strangers, or on the future. If the cost did land on you, the market would handle it. No ability to contract your way out. The parties either cannot agree, cannot trust each other's promises, or cannot verify compliance. That last point is where Ronald Coase's insight bites: externalities are fundamentally a bargaining failure. When the affected parties are few, well defined, and able to write and enforce an agreement, they will usually fix the problem themselves — the polluter and the downstream fishermen can strike a deal. When the parties are numerous, anonymous, and unable to check whether anyone is cheating, they cannot, and the trap holds. Every escape route in this chapter works by attacking one of the three ingredients.The label multipolar comes from Nick Bostrom's work on the strategic risks of advanced artificial intelligence, where he used it for competitive scenarios in which each agent is driven toward a course of action it would rather avoid, because any agent that unilaterally restrained itself would simply be outcompeted. The AI context is exotic; the structure is ancient.What the many-player version adds is a ratchet. With two players choosing cooperate or defect, the trap is a one-step collapse. With many players and a continuous variable — how much to spend, how many fish to take, how hard to compete — the level climbs and never comes back down, because at every point along the climb the locally best move is to add a little more.Two features make the ratchet worse than the collapse. First, it is invisible: each individual step is small, defensible, and looks like a normal decision. Second, it is sticky: when pressure eases, nobody steps back down, because stepping down first is exactly the move that was punished on the way up. This is why arms races, ad budgets, and regulatory standards so rarely return to earlier levels even in peacetime, and it is the reason traps are a close relative of path dependence — the level you are at is a residue of history rather than a response to current conditions.Almost every trap you meet is a variation on one of these. The differences matter, because they determine which escape is available.The last one deserves a note, because it is the most common and the least recognized. A positional good is one you value only by comparison — a place at the top school, a house in the good catchment area, a title. Competition for positional goods is a pure ratchet: the total stock of status never increases, so the escalation burns resources without producing anything anyone actually wanted. This is the mechanism behind the education arms race, credential inflation, and the peculiar sensation of running very fast to stay in place. (The best-known trap of all, the depletion of a shared resource, is the commons; it earns its own treatment next.)The cleanest demonstration available is Martin Shubik's 1971 dollar auction, and it fits in a paragraph.An auctioneer offers a $1 bill. Bidding starts at 5 cents and rises in 5-cent increments. The twist: both the highest and the second-highest bidders pay, but only the highest receives the dollar.The trap springs at around 55 cents. The two leading bidders now face a choice that is locally rational and globally absurd: withdraw and lose 50 cents outright, or bid 60 and pay 60 cents for a dollar — which is still, at that instant, a good deal. Both bid. The escalation continues until bids exceed $1, at which point every further bid increases a certain loss in order to avert a larger one. Pairs of rational adults have bid many dollars for a single dollar bill in classrooms, repeatedly, while fully understanding the structure.Three features are worth extracting: The sunk cost is genuine, not imagined. Past bids are unrecoverable, but they change the payoff of quitting now, because quitting converts them from "spent in pursuit of a prize" into "lost." The trap uses a real accounting change, not a psychological error alone. Asymmetry of loss, not hope of gain. Past a certain point, both players are choosing between a small loss and a larger one. Nobody is being greedy; both are minimizing damage. There is no unilateral exit. Either bidder could have declined at the start. Neither can stop the other's escalation, and stopping alone guarantees the loss. Real instances share the anatomy: litigation that both sides would settle if they could coordinate, price wars that destroy an industry's margins, bidding wars for acquisitions, campaign spending, R&D races. In each case, the participants are not confused. They are stuck.The most consequential contemporary example runs on a slow clock, which is why it has been allowed to get this far.Antibiotic resistance is a commons problem with a delay. The resource — the continued effectiveness of a class of drugs — is shared by everyone on the planet and belongs to no one. The move is to use antibiotics generously: prescribe them when a patient pressures you, use them prophylactically in livestock, use broad-spectrum ones because a culture takes two days.Trace the incentives: The benefit is concentrated and immediate. The patient recovers and stops calling. The farm's animals grow cheaper. The prescriber avoids a difficult conversation and a bad review score. The cost is diffuse and delayed. Every unnecessary prescription contributes a tiny increment to resistance, which lands on strangers, decades in the future, through a mechanism no individual can see. Unilateral restraint is actively punished. A doctor who withholds antibiotics today pays the full cost — patient dissatisfaction, and the occasional missed infection — while the benefit to the global commons is imperceptible. The structure pays for overuse and fines restraint. Run the unilateral-restraint test on this and you get a clear verdict: materially punished, with no compensating reward. That is a structural trap, and it is why individual virtue alone has never been a sufficient fix. The available escapes work on each ingredient in turn — stewardship programs and prescribing audits make behaviour visible (reducing transaction costs), a regulatory ban on growth-promotion use supplies an enforcer, rapid diagnostics that distinguish bacterial from viral infection change the arena, professional norms change the payoffs, and "subscription" payment models that decouple drug company revenue from volume attack the incentive at its source.The name most often attached to this family of outcomes comes from outside economics. Moloch was a Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice, mentioned in Leviticus and given a memorable role by Milton in Paradise Lost as the fiercest of the fallen angels. Allen Ginsberg's Howl (1956) turned the name into a one-word indictment of industrial civilisation — "Moloch whose mind is pure machinery!" In 2014, Scott Alexander's essay "Meditations on Moloch" stitched the older literary image to the game-theoretic structure, and the name stuck in a certain corner of the internet.The name earns its place for one reason: it names an outcome without naming a perpetrator. Ordinary causal language is built for agents — someone did this, someone is to blame — and traps break that language. "Who is responsible for credential inflation?" has no answer, and the search for one produces conspiracy theories and scapegoats. "Moloch" is a shorthand that stops that search and points at the structure instead.But the metaphor carries a real hazard, and it is worth stating plainly: Moloch is not an agent. There is no entity with preferences pursuing child sacrifice. The moment the word is used as though it were a force, an explanation, or an excuse, it stops being analysis and becomes a way of saying "the system made me do it." The structure is always just a payoff matrix, an externality, and a set of agents. If you cannot point to those three things, you have not identified a trap; you have invoked a mood.This is also the sharpest demonstration of a point made earlier in this act: emergent order is not salvation. A multipolar trap is a spontaneous order — nobody designed it, nobody wants it, and it is stable. Emergence is a claim about where a pattern came from, never about whether it is good.The concept has a characteristic failure mode in each direction, and they are worth separating because they are often confused.The first is blame-the-villain thinking. Human causal cognition reaches for an agent, so we look for the bad actor behind a structural outcome — the greedy executive, the lazy regulator, the feckless consumer. Sometimes there is one. Usually the villain is a role someone occupies and would be replaced in within a month.The second is subtler and, in practice, more dangerous: Moloch laundering. Because structural coercion is a real and respected phenomenon, claiming it is a cheap way to justify what you intended to do anyway. "We have to cut quality, or competitors will." "We can't be the only ones paying a living wage." "There is no alternative." Some of these claims are true. Many are not, and the tell is always the same.The test is not rhetorical. Ask: name the competitor who would take your customers, the mechanism by which you'd lose, and roughly how much. If that answer exists, you have a trap and should be designing an escape. If it dissolves into vagueness under questioning, you have a preference dressed as a constraint — which is the same move as smuggling a value premise in as a fact.A genuine trap, moreover, is falsifiable in the ordinary way. It predicts that players who restrain while others continue will lose ground measurably. Look for cases where someone actually did restrain unilaterally and check what happened. That is the difference between a structural claim and an alibi.No — and the distinction matters, because a blanket suspicion of competition is its own error. The same mechanism that produces Moloch produces most of the world's progress, and the difference lies entirely in the payoff structure. Productive competition escalates toward something whose benefits spill over: cheaper solar panels, better vaccines, faster chips, more accurate forecasts. The race is real, the losers lose, and the output is a shared gain. This is the "invisible hand" case — Adam Smith's mechanism producing a public benefit — and it is the same mechanism as a multipolar trap. Nothing about the market changed; the topology of who gains and who pays did. Positional competition escalates toward nothing. The resource is fixed, so effort is consumed without raising the total. This is the pure trap, and the diagnostic is simple: ask whether the escalation raises the aggregate or only the relative position. Evolution supplies the same spectrum: the peacock's tail and the Red Queen arms race between predator and prey are genuine traps in the individual-cost sense, and they are also where much of biological complexity came from. Some arms races build the world; some just burn it. The question is never "is this competitive?" but "who captures the benefit, and who absorbs the cost?"Every available exit attacks one of the three ingredients: it lowers the cost of contracting, it adds an enforcer, it changes the payoffs, or it changes the arena so the contested margin stops mattering.Reduce transaction costs. Traps require parties who cannot agree or cannot verify. Fewer players, well-defined rights, repeat interaction, and visibility all attack that. Repeat play is the single strongest lever: when the game is repeated and behaviour is observable, reputation does work that contracts cannot, which is the finding behind Robert Axelrod's tournaments on the iterated prisoner's dilemma — reciprocity succeeds, but only when the "shadow of the future" is long enough and defection is detectable. Making behaviour visible to the group is often all that is needed.Add an enforcer. Hobbes's answer, and the right one when parties are too numerous to bargain and detection is cheap: an authority that changes the payoffs by fiat. Treaties like the 1987 Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances, bans on growth-promotion antibiotics in livestock, and standardised charging ports are all examples of a third party internalising an externality that the market could not. The failure modes are equally instructive — the enforcer can be captured by those it regulates, can be too weak to detect violations, or can itself be caught in a race to the bottom with other jurisdictions.Change the payoffs. The cheapest escape and the hardest to build: norms, taboos, and internalised standards that make the defecting move costly to the person doing it, independent of enforcement. Professional ethics, queue discipline, and the refusal to bargain over certain things all work this way. This is also where religion and culture have historically done their heaviest lifting — not by explaining the trap, but by making one branch of it simply unavailable.Change the arena. Sometimes the contested margin can be removed rather than managed. Vertical integration internalises the externality by merging the players. A technological substitution can make the contested resource irrelevant — a new pricing mechanism, a substitute input, a design that removes the need for the scarce thing. Exit to a different game is a real strategy, and it is usually the one people forget to consider.Three cautions about the menu. First, escapes are themselves coordination problems: a cartel is an escape from a price war that must solve monitoring and sanctioning, which are the same problems it was trying to escape. Second, every fix creates new margins, and those margins will be found — the second-order effects chapter applies in full. Third, the level is not the goal. The question is not "how do we reduce advertising spending?" but "what is the structure we want, and who pays for it?" A trap broken by a rule that no one can renegotiate has traded one form of stuckness for another.Run this on any situation that feels like everyone is losing and no one is at fault: Name the agents and their moves. Who is choosing what, on what margin? Run the unilateral test. What exactly happens to one player who restrains while the others continue? If you cannot answer specifically, you have not found a trap. Find the externality. Whose cost is missing from whose payoff? That gap is the engine. Check the ratchet. Is the level rising over time, or is it static? A static bad equilibrium is a different problem — an unpleasant settlement rather than an escalation. Ask why contracting fails. Too many parties? Unverifiable behaviour? No trust? No enforcement? The answer names the escape. Ask whether it should be escaped. Does escalation buy a shared good, or only a relative position? Name the settlement. In the style of everything else in this book: state what you expect to change, by when, and what you would see if the trap has actually been broken rather than merely relabelled. The uncomfortable implication, and the reason this topic sits in the act on coordination, is that most of what looks like moral failure at scale is structural. People are not secretly worse than they appear; the incentives reach into ordinary decency and pull out the outcome nobody chose. That is bad news for anyone hoping to fix the world by exhortation. It is good news for anyone willing to work on the rules — because rules are the one thing in the picture that a small number of people can actually change.Multipolar trap — A situation in which multiple agents each have an incentive to take an action that is individually advantageous and collectively self-defeating, with no agent able to improve the outcome unilaterally.Moloch — Shorthand for the structure, rather than the perpetrator, behind traps; a metaphor drawn from Ginsberg's Howl and popularised by Scott Alexander. Names an outcome with no author, and is a mood rather than an explanation when invoked without a payoff structure.Prisoner's dilemma — The minimal two-player trap: a dominant move leading both players to a Pareto-dominated outcome they would both prefer to avoid.Dominant strategy — A move that yields a better payoff than the alternatives regardless of what others do.Nash equilibrium — An outcome in which no player can improve by changing strategy alone; it can be collectively terrible.Pareto-dominated / Pareto-superior — An outcome is Pareto-dominated when some alternative makes at least one party better off and none worse off; the alternative is Pareto-superior.Rivalrous and excludable — Two properties of a good: whether one person's use reduces what is available to others, and whether non-payers can be kept out. Traps live where a good is rivalrous but not excludable.Common-pool resource — A rivalrous, non-excludable resource — a fishery, aquifer, grazing range, or the atmosphere — where each user's extraction subtracts from every other user's supply.Externality — A cost or benefit of an action that falls on someone who did not choose it and is not party to any transaction with the actor. The missing term in the trap's payoff.Transaction costs — The costs of reaching, monitoring, and enforcing an agreement. High transaction costs among numerous parties are the reason traps cannot be bargained away.Escalation ratchet — The tendency of a trap's contested level to rise and stay risen, because the first party to step back down loses ground.Arms race — A trap in which competing parties escalate a capability whose value is largely relative, leaving all of them worse off in absolute terms.Race to the bottom — A trap in which jurisdictions or firms compete by lowering standards, each step justified by the competitive threat of the others.War of attrition / dollar auction — A trap of continued escalation over a single all-or-nothing prize, in which the rational calculation shifts from winning a gain to minimising a certain loss. Shubik's dollar auction is the canonical demonstration.Sunk cost — An unrecoverable prior expenditure; in a trap it changes the relative cost of quitting, which is a real accounting effect and not only a psychological error.Positional good — A good valued for one's rank relative to others; competition for it consumes resources without raising the total, producing escalation with no aggregate gain.Shadow of the future — Axelrod's term for the prospect of continued interaction; when it is long and behaviour is observable, reciprocity can sustain cooperation that a one-shot game destroys.Productive vs. positional competition — The distinction between escalation whose output everyone can use and escalation that only rearranges rank; the same competitive mechanism with opposite aggregate verdicts.Unilateral-restraint test — The practical diagnostic for distinguishing a structural trap from a rhetorical one: identify specifically what a player would lose by restraining alone. No specific loss, no trap.Moloch laundering — Invoking structural compulsion to justify a preference that would otherwise need defending; the failure mode of the concept in the hands of someone who already knows what they want to do.Enforcer (Leviathan) solution — Escaping a trap by introducing a third party with the power to change payoffs through regulation, mandate, or treaty; effective when parties are numerous and detection is cheap, vulnerable to capture and to its own competitive races.Capture — The condition in which the enforcing body comes to serve the interests of those it regulates, converting a solution into a new form of the problem.

what-nobody-taught-you/5-act-iv-—-the-co.title: 5-8 Moral luck + veil of ignorance
what-nobody-taught-you/5-act-iv-—-the-co.description: Part of 5 Act IV — The Coordination Problem (us)Two ideas from very different literatures turn out to be a diagnosis and a prescription. Moral luck is the discovery — by Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, in a 1976 volume of essays — that a great deal of what we praise and blame people for depends on factors they did not control. The veil of ignorance is John Rawls's design response: if position is so often an accident, then rules should be chosen by people who do not yet know which position they will occupy. Read together, they give you one of the few genuinely portable tools in this book: a test for whether a rule you are about to impose is one you would accept from underneath.The control principle is the moral intuition almost everyone holds and almost nobody can consistently apply: you are morally assessable only for what is within your control. It underwrites "ought implies can," the excuse of accident, and the difference between a mistake and a crime. Kant built it into the foundations of ethics, and ordinary moral practice assumes it continuously.Nagel's argument is that almost nothing survives it. He distinguishes four places luck gets in, and they form a chain from who you are to what you did: Constitutive luck — your temperament, talents, capacity for courage or sympathy. Nobody chose to be born patient or quick-tempered. Circumstantial luck — the situations you happen to face. The same person born in Nuremberg in 1920 and in Buenos Aires in 1920 lived under different moral demands. One had the opportunity to be a hero or a collaborator; the other mostly had the opportunity to be unremarkable. Causal luck — how your actions were caused, which is where this runs into the free-will problem. Nagel sets it aside as the deepest case; it is not needed for the argument to bite. Resultant luck — how things turned out. This is the one that disturbs moral practice most, because it is visible every day. Worked example. Two drivers leave the same pub over the legal limit. Both are equally reckless, equally impaired, equally fortunate in their cars and reflexes. One gets home. The other, at exactly the same speed and reaction time, meets a child who steps into the road half a second earlier. The first driver has a story; the second has a manslaughter conviction, a lifetime of guilt, and a permanent place in the moral record. Nothing that distinguishes them is something either one controlled. We can feel the unfairness and we still — courtrooms, newspapers, and the drivers themselves — treat them as different people.Williams's contribution is a second, subtler case. His example is a lorry driver who, through no fault whatever, kills a child who runs out in front of him. He is not morally guilty. But Williams argues he nonetheless owes a special kind of response — agent-regret — precisely because it was his lorry and his hands on the wheel. It is not ordinary regret (which anyone might feel) and not guilt (which would presume fault). It is the first-person residue of having been the vehicle of a catastrophe, and telling the driver "you did nothing wrong" does not dissolve it. Moral luck therefore contaminates not only how others judge you but how you must judge yourself.The result is what Nagel called an antinomy: two things we cannot give up, which cannot both be true. We cannot abandon the control principle without turning morality into a lottery. We cannot abandon our practices of praise, blame, and punishment without abandoning moral life altogether. Nagel's honest conclusion is that this is not a puzzle with a clever solution; it is a structural feature of morality that we mostly paper over.You cannot dissolve moral luck, but you can act on the knowledge that it exists, and the payoff is mostly institutional.Separate blame from liability. Blame is retrospective: it asks what you deserve, and it is contaminated by luck. Liability is forward-looking: it asks who should bear a cost, and it is a design question. A hospital can require a surgeon whose patient died to undergo review — because review reduces future deaths — while declining to assert that she is a worse person than a colleague whose identical patient survived. Consequence and condemnation are separate judgements that habit fuses.Assess process where you can, outcome where you must. Outcome-based judgement is the source of resultant luck and of survivorship bias; purely process-based judgement loses the discipline that makes care matter, and invites the failure mode where the metric replaces the goal. Most good systems mix: judge the process contemporaneously, judge the outcome only across many cases where the noise averages out.Expect the just-world reflex. People have a strong tendency to infer desert from outcome — the successful must have deserved it, the unlucky must have done something. This is a comfort mechanism that makes the world feel ordered, and it is wrong in exactly the way survivorship bias is wrong. It is also the main reason the veil of ignorance feels counterintuitive to people who are well placed: if your position is earned, there is no reason to choose rules without knowing it.Rawls's original position is a thought experiment about how to choose the basic rules of a society. Parties in it are rational, mutually disinterested, and choosing principles to govern their shared institutions — but they choose behind a veil of ignorance. They do not know their class, their natural talents, their family, their conception of the good, or which generation they belong to. They know general facts about economics and psychology; they do not know who they are.It is worth being precise about what this device is. It is not a state of nature, not a bargaining session, and not a claim about how societies began. It is a device of representation: a way of modelling the requirement that a rule not be tailored to advantage whoever happens to be writing it. Rawls's phrase for what it screens out is that the distribution of benefits should not be settled by factors "arbitrary from a moral point of view."The mechanism is straightforward. If you do not know whether you will be the landlord or the tenant, the healthy or the ill, the majority or the minority, then self-interest no longer tells you to write a rule for the strong. Rawls argued that parties so situated would choose two principles: equal basic liberties for all, and social and economic inequalities permitted only when they also improve the position of the worst off — the difference principle.That conclusion is contested, and one objection is worth knowing because it defines the tool's sensitivity. John Harsanyi argued that if the parties are genuinely ignorant, they should assign equal probability to each position and maximize average utility — a straightforward expected-value calculation. Rawls's parties instead reason as if the worst outcome is the one that matters, which is maximin. The two produce different societies. Which is right depends on what you assume about the choosers' attitude to risk — which means the veil does not generate answers by itself. It relocates disagreement from "what should we do?" to "what would reasonable people behind the veil agree to?" — a better question, but still a question.Most people will never settle the Harsanyi–Rawls dispute, and do not need to. The practical value of the veil is that it is a fast consistency check on any rule you are about to impose, and it can be run in a few minutes.Step three is the one people skip and the one that does the work. You cannot run the test without naming the affected population and identifying the worst position in it — which is why the veil is a useful complement to baselines and base rates: it forces you to look at the tail rather than the typical case.Worked example: a firm's layoff rule. A company needs to cut 10% of costs. Option A: lay off the 10% with the weakest performance reviews. Option B: a 10% pay cut across the board, no layoffs. Option C: reduce the dividend and the executive bonus pool first, then a smaller pay cut.Run the veil. Population: employees, shareholders, customers. Positions: top performer with a mortgage, middling performer with a sick parent, recent hire, long-tenured specialist whose role has been automated, shareholder, customer. Worst positions: the worker laid off in a weak local job market, and the worker whose pay falls below what the household needs. Behind the veil, not knowing which you are, Option A looks like a lottery over ruin; Option C concentrates the pain where it is most survivable. Notice that the tool has not told you that layoffs are wrong. It has told you that if you would not accept a rule knowing you might be the one it destroys, you owe an argument for why not — an actual argument, not the observation that it is efficient.Worked example: drought pricing. A water utility must cut consumption by 20%. Option A: a flat restriction on all households. Option B: steeply rising per-litre prices. Option C: a free allocation per person, with trading above it. Behind the veil, you do not know whether you are a large household, a small one, a landlord passing costs to tenants, or a business whose competitors are in the next jurisdiction. Option B's burden falls hardest on people for whom water is a large share of the budget; Option C preserves the signal while capping the damage; Option A ignores that the same litre means different things to different households. Again the tool produces a critique rather than a verdict — and the critique is where the useful argument starts.Three honest limits.You can smuggle yourself back in. Whoever specifies the parties — their risk aversion, their preferences, whether they care about future generations — determines much of the answer. A person who wants low taxes can populate the original position with parties who happen to dislike redistribution. The veil is a consistency check, not an oracle; it detects rules that advantaged their author, and it cannot manufacture agreement where values genuinely differ.The boundary problem is unresolved. Who gets a seat behind the veil? Rawls's own treatment of future generations is notoriously awkward, and non-human interests and outsiders who never get to negotiate fit poorly. Every real application involves drawing a line that some affected party does not get to help draw.It does not generate compliance. Knowing what a fair rule is does not make anyone follow it, which is why moral luck and the veil both sit inside an act about coordination rather than an act about knowledge. Fairness arguments operate on people who are already persuaded; the rest is institutions, incentives, and the multipolar traps covered elsewhere in this act.Moral luck is the empirical claim; the veil is the procedural response. If a large share of your position, your character, and your outcomes is not your doing, then a rule chosen by people who know they hold the good position will encode an accident as a desert.The link is not merely thematic. It explains why the veil is politically unstable: it asks people to reason as though their advantages were contingent, and the just-world reflex — reinforced by every survivorship-biased success story they have ever read — tells them the opposite. It also explains what the veil is for. It is not a machine for producing just institutions. It is a machine for catching the moment when you were about to write your own position into a rule and call it neutral. That is a smaller claim than Rawls's, and it is one you can use this afternoon. Severance and restructuring — choosing a layoff rule behind the veil rather than defending the one that protects you. Sentencing and liability — the drunk driver example, generalized: outcome-based penalties when outcomes are noisy. Insurance and credit — pricing that is actuarially accurate and veil-unacceptable, and the reverse. Algorithmic systems — the appeal procedure matters more than the model, because you do not know whether you will be the one who needs it. Disaster relief and pandemic policy — rules written before you know which neighbourhood you live in. Admissions, funding, and promotion — where the assessor's own path is the unexamined template. Family and team rules — the same test at small scale, where it is cheapest to run and most often skipped. State the rule as a rule, not as a decision. Name everyone affected, including people who cannot speak in the decision. List the positions and identify the worst one. Ask whether you would accept the rule without knowing which position is yours. If not, name what would have to change — a floor, a compensation, a different rule — and then ask what your actual objection was. Step five is where the honesty lives. Often the answer is that you would accept the rule, and you simply prefer your current position to be protected. That is a legitimate thing to want, but it is a value claim, not a fairness claim, and it belongs on the table as one.Moral luck — The phenomenon that a person's moral record depends substantially on factors beyond their control; Nagel's and Williams's term for the tension this creates with the control principle.Control principle — The intuition that agents are morally assessable only for what they could control; the assumption moral luck undermines.Constitutive luck — Luck in who one is: temperament, capacities, and dispositions that shape action without being chosen.Circumstantial luck — Luck in the situations and moral demands one happens to face; the reason the same person can have radically different moral records in different times and places.Causal luck — Luck in how one's actions were caused; the free-will dimension of the problem.Resultant luck — Luck in how an action turned out; the source of the drunk-driver asymmetry and of outcome-based blame generally.Agent-regret (Williams) — The special first-person response of someone who, though blameless, was the vehicle of a harm; not guilt, and not dissolved by being told one is blameless.Antinomy (of moral luck) — The unresolvable conflict between the control principle and ordinary moral practice; Nagel's claim is that it has no clean solution.Just-world tendency — The inclination to infer desert from outcome, so that the successful and the unlucky are assumed to have earned their positions; the main psychological obstacle to veil reasoning.Original position (Rawls) — The hypothetical choice situation in which parties select principles of justice for their society.Veil of ignorance — The restriction in the original position that parties do not know their own class, talents, family, or conception of the good; a device for preventing rules from being tailored to their author's position.Device of representation — Rawls's description of the original position: not a historical or psychological claim, but a way of modelling impartiality.Difference principle — Rawls's claim that inequalities are just only if they also improve the position of the worst-off group.Maximin — The decision rule of choosing the option whose worst outcome is least bad; Rawls's characterization of choice behind the veil.Harsanyi's objection — The argument that genuinely ignorant parties should assign equal probabilities across positions and maximize average utility, yielding a different (broadly utilitarian) conclusion than Rawls's maximin.Arbitrary from a moral point of view — Rawls's phrase for the natural and social contingencies — birth, talent, family — that should not determine distributive outcomes.Smuggling — The failure mode in which the person specifying the parties behind the veil encodes their own preferences into the parties' preferences, making the device yield the answer they already wanted.

what-nobody-taught-you/5-act-iv-—-the-co.title: 5-9 Survivorship bias
what-nobody-taught-you/5-act-iv-—-the-co.description: Part of 5 Act IV — The Coordination Problem (us)Every claim about what works is a claim about a sample — and samples are rarely drawn fairly. Survivorship bias is what happens when the cases you can see are only the ones that made it through some gate, while the ones that didn't left no record behind. Nothing in your data is false. The data are accurate, the numbers add up, and the sample is real. The inference is still wrong, because the population you are generalising from is not the population your claim is about.Ordinary sampling bias means your sample is unrepresentative but mixed: you got too many young people, too few rural households. If you know the proportions, you can reweight and repair it. Survivorship bias is worse behaved, because the missing cases are missing because of the outcome you are trying to explain. They are not underrepresented; they are absent, and their absence is systematic.The thing doing the filtering is called the sampling frame — the rule that determines who could have appeared in your data at all. The frame, not the measurement, is where the lie lives. This is why the bias survives so well in careful, numerate people: they audit the arithmetic and never audit the gate.The canonical case comes from the Statistical Research Group in New York during the Second World War. Aircraft were returning from missions with bullet holes, and the question was where to add armour. The obvious reading of the damage reports was: armour the places that get hit most.Abraham Wald's contribution was to notice what a returning plane is. It is a plane that took hits and still flew home. The holes on it are therefore a map of where a plane can be hit and survive. Planes hit in the places that show no holes — engine, cockpit, fuel lines — are not underrepresented in the data. They are the data that never arrived.The general lesson is portable and worth stating as a rule: the pattern of survivors tells you where the filter is survivable, not where the danger is. The same logic applies to a market's winners (the losers are gone from the index), a disease's diagnosed cases (the undiagnosed never entered the cohort), and a genre's classic albums (the bad ones stopped being played).One honest footnote, in the spirit of the rest of this book: the popular telling compresses Wald's actual 1943 memorandum, which developed a formal method for estimating vulnerability from damage observed on survivors rather than delivering a single clever quip. The logic is exactly as described; the anecdote is a tidy version of a technical paper. Use it as an illustration, and cite it carefully.Survivorship bias is a family, not a single error, and the variants require different corrections. Silent failure. The failed cases existed and vanished from the record — closed funds, defunct firms, abandoned drugs, discontinued product lines. The fix is to find an archive; the difficulty is that no one is obliged to keep one. Invisible success. Cases that passed the filter but never entered your sample because they were never visible in the first place — the successful small firms with no press coverage, the patients who recovered without ever seeing a doctor. This is non-participation rather than death, and it biases in the opposite direction from what you expect. Selection on the outcome. This is the most analytically damaging variant: choosing your sample by the thing you want to explain, then hunting for its causes. Study "great companies" and identify what they had in common, and you will find things they shared with companies that failed. The shared traits were not causes; they were the entry ticket. Selection on the observer. The advice you are given is, by construction, from someone for whom the advice worked — or someone lucky enough to think it did. The unsuccessful practitioner is not on the conference circuit. A database of 1,000 mutual funds reports the returns of the funds still reporting after twenty years. The surviving funds averaged, say, 8% a year — a figure that quietly becomes "the stock market returns 8%."But suppose roughly half of the original thousand closed or merged along the way, and those funds averaged closer to 4% in the years before they folded. An investor choosing at random in the first year did not get the database's 8%. They got a blend of the survivors' 8% and the dead funds' losses — plausibly closer to 5–6%, with a meaningful chance of having picked one of the funds that disappeared entirely.Two details make this worse than it looks. First, the missing funds are missing non-randomly: funds close when they perform badly, so the absence correlates precisely with the variable of interest. Second, the loss is not just in the average but in the tail. The distribution of outcomes you can observe is truncated exactly where the bad outcomes were, which is why survivorship bias is a close cousin of the fat-tail problems discussed later. This is why regulators in several jurisdictions require fund companies to disclose survivorship-adjusted figures: the correction has to be imposed institutionally, because no individual has an incentive to volunteer it.This is where survivorship bias stops being a cognitive quirk and becomes a coordination problem, which is why it belongs in this act.An archive of failures is a public good. It is non-rival (everyone can use it), largely non-excludable (you cannot stop competitors learning from it), and — critically — nobody is paid to build it. Meanwhile the incentives run the other way at every level: Failures have reasons to stay quiet. Reputation, legal exposure, commercial confidentiality, embarrassment. A closed fund's manager does not publish a post-mortem. Successes have every reason to publish. Case studies, memoirs, keynote speeches, and bestsellers are all survivorship-powered genres. They are also genuinely useful, which is what makes them so persuasive. The centre cannot see what leaves no trace. Failures are often illegible to any institution that could have recorded them: no filing, no headline, no attendance at the conference. The parties who know why something failed are the ones closest to it, and they disperse. The counterfactual never arrives. There is no committee whose job is to ask what would have happened to the other nine hundred. The result is a self-reinforcing loop, and it is worth following round:As the traits spread through the population, they stop discriminating between success and failure at all — but the record still shows only winners, so they look universal and causal forever. The practical consequence is the one worth carrying: the more confidently a piece of advice is asserted, the more likely it has been sampled from survivors. Confidence is not evidence of a graveyard having been consulted. Usually the opposite.Three tests, in increasing order of effort:Find the denominator. For any claim of the form "X leads to success," ask how many entities did X and failed. If you cannot construct that number, you have a numerator and no rate. This is the outside view applied to advice, and it is the same move as sourcing a prior from a reference class rather than from the vivid case in front of you.Look for matched pairs. The strongest version of the test is comparative: take survivors who did X and failures who also did X. If most failures did X too, X explains nothing. Clinical research calls this a control group; business writing rarely bothers.Ask what the failure of this claim would look like. If no observation could count against the advice — if the survivors' traits are unfalsifiable in the sense covered earlier in this book — then the claim has left the empirical game regardless of its provenance.Two related habits keep the distinction sharp. First, distinguish persistence from merit: a convention can survive because of lock-in rather than because it is good, and a practice can survive because it is adequate. The Lindy effect says survival is information about durability, not about quality; survivorship bias is what you get when you read durability as approval. Second, remember that under a Bayesian lens, absent evidence is evidence when that evidence would otherwise have been likely to appear. A graveyard you cannot see, in a domain where corpses are usually visible, is itself a signal. Name the filter before reading the data. Who had to pass something, and what happened to those who didn't? Go and count the dead deliberately. Bankruptcy filings, retraction notices, clinical trial registries, discontinued product lines, obituaries of firms. Someone has to do this, and it is usually a research project rather than a dashboard. Prefer registries to narratives. A registry — trial registration, pre-registration, mandatory fund disclosure — records entities at entry rather than at success. Pre-commitment is the institutional form of "I will count the failures too." Read survivor accounts as testimony, not as data. They are one trajectory, selected on being interesting. Invert the Wald question. Ask where the damage isn't, where the successful sample never ventures, and what that silence rules out. Business and investing. Fund databases, "great company" studies, hedge fund indices, startup advice, "what I learned from failing" content that only reaches you when the failure was followed by a success. Careers and education. The dropout-founder story, the graduate of an elite school, the person who moved cities and thrived. The base rate for each strategy is computed over a population whose failures are not giving talks. Health and safety. Cats brought to veterinary clinics after falls, where cats that died on impact were never brought in; treatments evaluated only on patients who survived long enough to be evaluated; screening programmes that count detected cases rather than all cases. Knowledge itself. Publication bias and the file-drawer problem are survivorship bias applied to findings: the literature contains the studies that reached significance, and the null results are the planes that did not come back. This is what pre-registration and registered reports are designed to fix. Culture and taste. "The music of the 1970s was better," "they built things to last" — the past you can still see has been filtered by decades of selection, and the dross is not on the radio. Survivorship bias — Drawing conclusions from a sample that has been selected on the very outcome being explained, because cases that failed to pass a filter left no record. Sampling frame — The rule determining which cases could appear in the data at all; the location of the bias. The filter (gate) — The selection process — survival, publication, profitability, admission — that admits some cases and discards others. Silent evidence — The absent cases whose absence is itself informative; a graveyard invisible from where you stand. Selection on the outcome — Building a sample from entities that share a result, then searching for the causes of that result; the analytically worst variant of the bias. Invisible survivor — A case that passed the filter but never entered the sample, because it was never visible or never reported. Matched-pair (survivor–failure) comparison — Testing a claimed cause by checking whether failures shared it too; a control group by another name. Denominator problem — Possessing a numerator (how many successes did X) without the base rate (how many did X and failed). Survivorship-adjusted return — A performance figure corrected to include funds or firms that disappeared; mandated in some jurisdictions precisely because no one volunteers it. File-drawer problem / publication bias — The same bias applied to research findings, where unpublished null results are the missing graveyard. Persistence versus merit — The distinction between surviving because something resists elimination and surviving because it is good; conflating them is the error Lindy is often misused to commit.

what-nobody-taught-you/6-act-v-—-living-.title: 6-1 Black swans & fat tails
what-nobody-taught-you/6-act-v-—-living-.description: Part of 6 Act V — Living With It (synthesis)The normal distribution is the most useful model in the history of applied statistics and the most dangerous default in ordinary reasoning. It is the reason insurance works, the reason quality control works, and the reason most people's intuition about "average" and "risk" is calibrated to a world where extreme events are small, bounded, and mostly ignorable. A great deal of what determines your life — market crashes, pandemics, wars, technological adoption, book sales, career outcomes, scientific discoveries — does not live in that world. It lives in the other one, where the largest thing that happens is not a slightly bigger version of the typical thing, but a different order of magnitude altogether, and where the word "average" quietly stops meaning anything about anybody.This subsection is about that second world: what a fat tail is, what a black swan is and is not, how to tell which world you are standing in, and — the only part that is actionable — what you can still do when you cannot see the event coming. It is synthesis material, because the answer draws on several things this book has already built: the arithmetic of multiplication over repetition, the difference between the ensemble and the trajectory, the limits of base rates as priors, and the discipline of naming in advance what would change your mind.The normal distribution earns its place honestly. When a quantity is the sum of many small, roughly independent influences, none of which dominates, the result converges on a bell curve. Human height, measurement error, the sum of many dice, the average of a large survey sample — all genuinely normal. The central limit theorem is not a myth; it is a description of a real regularity.The property that matters here is the tail. In a normal distribution the tail decays exponentially: probabilities fall off so fast that an event ten standard deviations out is not merely rare, it is arithmetically negligible on any human timescale. The largest observation in a million draws will be a modest multiple of the average. The mean is a reliable summary of the whole distribution. Variance is a real, computable, stable property. In this world, "how much does one more observation move the average?" has a reassuring answer: almost not at all.A fat-tailed (or heavy-tailed) distribution is one whose tail decays like a power rather than an exponential — roughly, the probability of something bigger than x falls in proportion to x raised to some negative power, the tail exponent. That single change of shape produces a set of properties that break almost every default statistic: The maximum dominates the sum. In a thin-tailed world, one observation is never more than a rounding error on the total. In a fat-tailed world, the largest single observation can be larger than everything else combined. The largest city, the largest war, the largest firm, the largest market move, the largest pandemic — each can be an outlier on a scale the rest of the distribution cannot reach. The mean is unstable and unrepresentative. The sample mean is dominated by the extremes, which means it converges slowly and never settles. Add one observation and your estimate can jump. Variance may not exist. For tail exponents below about 2, the theoretical variance is infinite and the sample variance never converges. Every statistic built on standard deviation — volatility, Sharpe ratios, "sigma events" — is then describing an artefact rather than a property. The typical case and the average case come apart. Median and mean diverge wildly. Most outcomes are below average, and the average is carried by a small number of enormous ones. The fastest way to see the difference is a two-line comparison. The median adult male is about 1.75 m tall; the tallest human recorded was roughly 2.7 m — about 1.5 times the median. Now take household wealth. The median household is worth on the order of a few hundred thousand dollars; the wealthiest individual is worth on the order of two hundred billion — roughly a million times the median. Height is capped by physiology and is an additive product of many small genetic and nutritional contributions. Wealth is compounding, winner-take-all, and multiplicative.That is the generative point, and it is worth stating plainly: fat tails are usually made by multiplication, not by exotic randomness. Processes that compound — capital, reputation, citations, network reach, word of mouth, city growth — generate lognormal or power-law outcomes even when every individual step is mild and well behaved. Processes that add — height, measurement error, the sum of many small independent contributions — generate thin tails. This is the same arithmetic that ran through the material on ergodicity, and the same self-reinforcing structure that produces lock-in: multiplication plus feedback is the engine.An event is a black swan when it has three properties at once: it is an outlier relative to regular expectations; it carries extreme impact; and afterwards, human beings construct an explanation that makes it look as though it had been predictable all along.The third property is the one people skip, and it is the one that does structural damage. Post-hoc explanation feels like learning. It rarely is: a story assembled after the fact has no settlement date, and therefore no way to be scored — which is exactly the diagnostic this book has used throughout. The test of whether you have learned anything from a surprise is whether the explanation you have produced would have generated a prediction beforehand, with a threshold and a date.Taleb's illustration for the first property is the turkey. A turkey is fed every day for a thousand days. Each day of feeding is evidence for the turkey's model that humans care for turkeys, and — this is the crucial detail — it is evidence of the strongest kind by the turkey's own standards, because it is repeated, consistent, and increasing. The turkey's confidence in its risk assessment is at its maximum on day 1,000. On day 1,001 comes Thanksgiving.Read that loop carefully, because it is the whole mechanism. A long run of quiet is not neutral information; it feeds a reinforcing loop that reduces your estimated risk, raises your confidence, and increases your exposure — so that the day the tail finally arrives, you are holding the largest position of your life. This is exactly the drift-loop failure: a risk estimate updated only by a record of calm, with nothing outside the loop allowed to speak. And it explains why the events that hurt most are so often ones that everyone had privately considered and then discounted, precisely because they had not happened recently.Two clarifications keep the term from dissolving into "any surprise," which is how it is usually used.Black swanness is partly a property of your map, not only of the event. An event that flattens one observer's model is a Tuesday for someone whose prior included it. If your model assigned probability zero, the event is a black swan for you; the world did not become unpredictable, your map was too narrow. This is the predictive-processing point arriving with consequences: surprise is prediction error, and prediction error is the signal that your model needs widening — not evidence that the world is perverse.Shape and instance are separable. "A pandemic will occur" was not a surprise; "this virus, this year, this transmissibility" was. That distinction is the practical heart of the section, because it is the difference between the thing you cannot forecast and the thing you can.You cannot audit a tail without first knowing whether you have one, and the diagnostic is cheap.Six questions do most of the work: Max-versus-median. Is the biggest thing you have seen in this domain within two or three times the typical thing, or a thousand times it? Add-one test. Does adding a single observation materially change your estimate of the average? If it does, the mean is not a stable summary. Is there a hard cap? Physiology, physics, and clock time cap outcomes. Attention, capital, networks, and credibility barely do. Additive or multiplicative? Percentages, compounding, and cascades generate fat tails; sums of small independent contributions do not. (This is the same arithmetic that made averages lie about your actual fate.) Does "unprecedented" recur? A domain with a history of once-in-a-century events every decade — financial crises, floods, supply shocks, wars — is fat-tailed by its own record. Is there a winner-take-all structure? Network effects, preferential attachment, and scale economies produce the kind of concentration that makes the top observation dominate. Two cautions. First, a fat-tailed distribution is not automatically your problem — if your exposure is capped (insurance, a fixed-fee contract, a small fixed position), a wild world can be a thin-tailed problem for you. Second, the outside view gets weaker here. The Bayesian machinery still applies, but in a domain with very few recorded instances of the tail, your reference class is thin and your prior is correspondingly weak. Use base rates where a class is well populated — "large drawdowns in leveraged structures" has plenty of members — and hold them loosely where it is not. Base rate neglect is still a real error; it is just no longer a cheap fix.Expected value is an ensemble concept. In a fat-tailed world it is dominated by outcomes so rare that no individual trajectory contains them, which is precisely the situation the ergodicity material described: the average across many parallel players and the experience of one player come apart.Worked example. A strategy returns +5% in 97% of years and −80% in 3% of years. The arithmetic expected return is positive: 0.97 × 5 − 0.03 × 80 = +2.45% per year. Every dashboard, pitch deck, and risk committee would approve. Now compute the geometric return, which is what compounds: exp(0.97 × ln 1.05 + 0.03 × ln 0.20) ≈ exp(−0.001) ≈ −0.1% per year. Slightly negative. Over thirty years, the chance of taking at least one −80% hit is 1 − 0.97³⁰ ≈ 60%, and recovering from a −80% loss requires a +400% gain. The ensemble average is real and it belongs to a pool of players none of whom you are. The time average is what happens to you.Three further breakages are worth naming, because they recur in every domain where tails matter: Sigma events. Once you quote a "25-sigma move," you have already assumed a thin tail, because in a genuinely fat-tailed world the variance is undefined and sigma has no meaning. A risk report whose worst case is expressed in standard deviations is a report about a distribution you do not have. Independence fails exactly when you need it. Diversification assumes that many separate bets do not all fail together — conditional independence, in the language used earlier. In the tail, correlation goes to one: everything falls at once, and the diversification that looked robust was thinnest precisely where it mattered. Regression to the mean is brutal. An extreme observation in a noisy, fat-tailed domain is mostly luck, so the next observation is likely to be far closer to the median. This is why survivorship-biased samples look so dominated by skill, and why "what made them great" studies find traits that are shared with the invisible failures. The black swan argument does not license fatalism. It relocates the work: away from forecasting the event, and toward three things that remain tractable even when the instance is not.Forecast the shape, not the instance. You frequently cannot date a tipping point, but you can often name the mechanism — leverage, a single supplier, a coupling between two networks, a self-reinforcing loop that has become self-sustaining — and specify the direction of your exposure. That is a claim you can write down with a settlement date, which is all the Adversary question ever asked for. A risk you cannot date is still a risk you can describe.Manage exposure rather than prediction. The decisive question is not "will it happen?" but "what is my worst case, and can I keep going?" That is the asymmetric shape from the ruin argument: the arithmetic of repeated multiplication means avoiding the absorbing barrier is worth more than any forecast you will ever make.Positions that are convex — capped downside, open upside — let you survive a fat-tailed world and occasionally be its beneficiary. Positions that are concave — steady small gains, unbounded loss — make you the counterparty to someone else's tail, and they feel safe right up until the day they do not. The barbell follows from this: keep the bulk of your exposure extremely safe, and confine the aggressive part to bets whose loss you can absorb in full.Buy robustness directly, without a forecast. Redundancy, slack, margins, reversible decisions, and cheap experiments all work regardless of which way the surprise comes. None requires you to be right about the future, which is what makes them the honest tools for a fat-tailed world. This is the robustness–efficiency trade-off in practice: an optimally lean system has nothing to absorb a shock, which converts a local failure into a cascade.Two supporting habits sit underneath all of this: Score your surprises, not just your predictions. Keep the calibration discipline — state a number, resolve it, compare — and then watch whether your misses cluster. A cluster is direct evidence that your prior is too narrow, which is more useful than any single post-mortem. Look for the positive tail deliberately. Fat tails cut both ways. Discoveries, viral reach, and compounded skill are the same shape on the other side. Cheap, capped-cost experiments are how you buy exposure to a tail you cannot predict, and the Lindy caveat applies: surviving things are evidence of durability, not of merit — so prefer the robust, but do not read survival as a verdict. Fatalism in structural clothing. "Black swans are unpredictable" is true about dating and false about exposure. It is often used to escape accountability for a foreseeable vulnerability, in the same shape as any structural excuse: no named mechanism, no stated exposure, no settlement date, and a conclusion that happens to match what the speaker wanted to do anyway. The audit is the unilateral-restraint test's cousin — name the mechanism, name the worst case, and say what you would have done differently if you had expected it.Over-fitted preparation. The opposite error is to build a better fat-tailed model and then treat it as complete. But models of tails have their own tails. The durable answer is not a superior forecast; it is margins, reversibility, and optionality — features that pay off without being right about which surprise is coming. Run the max-versus-median test. Which world are you in? Ask whether your exposure is capped. A wild world you have insured is not a wild problem for you. State your worst case in units of ruin, not standard deviations. Name the absorbing barrier and how far away it is. Name the mechanism, in advance, that would produce the bad tail — and the observation that would tell you it is starting. Check the direction of your position: convex or concave? Capped downside, or capped upside? Count your surprises by category. Clustering means the prior is too narrow, and that is a measurement, not a mood. Fat tail (heavy tail) — A distribution whose tail probabilities decay like a power rather than an exponential, so that extreme values are far more likely than a normal distribution would predict and the largest observation can dominate the total.Tail exponent — The parameter governing how fast a power-law tail decays; lower exponents mean heavier tails. Below roughly 2 the theoretical variance is undefined.Thin-tailed (normal) — A distribution whose tail decays fast enough that extremes are negligible; the regime in which means, variances, and standard deviations are stable and informative summaries.Black swan — An event that is an outlier relative to regular expectations, carries extreme impact, and is retrospectively explained as though it had been foreseeable.Narrative fallacy — The post-hoc construction of a story that makes an unforeseen event appear predictable; it mimics learning without producing a prediction that could have been scored.Turkey problem — The illustration of inductive risk: a record of calm feeding raises confidence and increases exposure, so that confidence peaks immediately before the tail arrives.Tail risk — The risk of an outcome in the extreme tail of a distribution; not a probability of any particular event, but a property of the shape.Sigma event — An outcome described in standard deviations from the mean; the description itself presupposes a thin tail and is therefore a tell when used in fat-tailed domains.Sample-mean instability — The tendency of the mean to be dominated by the largest observation in a fat-tailed sample, so that it converges slowly or not at all.Multiplicative process — A process in which each step multiplies the current quantity (compounding, word of mouth, network growth); the usual generator of fat-tailed outcomes.Regression to the mean — The tendency for extreme observations in a noisy domain to be followed by more typical ones, because the extreme was largely luck.Conditional independence failure — The breakdown of the assumption that separate bets do not fail together; in fat-tailed crises, correlations rise and diversification weakens exactly when it is needed.Convexity — An exposure with capped downside and open upside; a position that benefits from variance.Concavity — An exposure with bounded upside and potentially unbounded downside; a position that is damaged by variance, typically the seller of insurance against the tail.Barbell strategy — Holding predominantly extreme safety alongside small, aggressive, capped-loss positions, avoiding the fragile middle where moderate risk meets unlimited loss.Ruin (absorbing barrier) — An outcome from which there is no recovery and no continuation of the trajectory; the only consideration that overrides expected value in repeated decisions.Shape versus instance — The distinction between forecasting that and why a tail event can occur, which is often tractable, and forecasting the specific event and date, which usually is not.Positive tail — The upside counterpart of tail risk: rare, large beneficial outcomes reachable through cheap experiments, optionality, and wide search.
