what-nobody-taught-you/6-act-v-—-living-.title: 6-2 Discounting & the far future
what-nobody-taught-you/6-act-v-—-living-.description: Part of 6 Act V — Living With It (synthesis)Open almost any spreadsheet used to justify a long-lived project and you will find one number doing more work than all the others combined. Change the discount rate from 3% to 7% and a benefit due in a hundred years loses a factor of fifty in value — not because anything about the future changed, but because of a line in a cell. That single parameter decides whether a dam, a forest, a pension promise, a climate policy, or a species is worth protecting, and it is almost never argued for out loud. This subsection is about where that number comes from, why it is a value choice wearing the costume of an interest rate, and what to do when you are the one who has to pick it.Act III introduced exponential growth as the thing human intuition refuses to feel. Discounting is that same exponential with a minus sign on the rate.Compounding says: £1 now becomes about £1,000 in a century at 7%. Discounting says exactly the reverse: £1,000 in a century is worth about 98 pence today. The rule of 72 from the deep-time material applies unchanged — 7% halves the value every ten years, so a hundred years is ten halvings, and 2⁻¹⁰ ≈ 0.001.The present value of a future benefit is what you would have to invest today, at the assumed rate, to end up with that benefit. Formally, PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ. This is not a trick or a fudge; it is the correct answer to a well-posed question: if the alternative is putting the money in something that earns r, what is this promise worth?Everything interesting lies in which question you are actually asking.Question one: the firm's question. I can spend £1M on a machine that returns £1.6M in ten years, or put the £1M in an index fund earning 7%. The machine is worth £813,000 in present-value terms, so I should buy the fund. Here, r is an opportunity cost, and using the market rate is not a preference — it is arithmetic. Nothing ethical is happening.Question two: the generation's question. I can spend £1M on coastal defences that will spare people in 2126 a cost of £1.6M, or spend it on hospital beds now. Here, r is doing something entirely different: it is a statement about how much less a person's welfare counts for the sole reason that they will be born later. That is not arithmetic. It is a bridge premise in the sense Act II used the term — a normative assumption that has to be stated and defended, and which no amount of data can supply.The catastrophic habit is to let the answer to question one be smuggled into question two — to say "the discount rate is 7% because that's the market rate" when the actual claim being made is "the suffering of people a century from now counts for a thousandth of yours." That is the is/ought gap wearing a suit, and it is the single most consequential instance of it in public policy.Frank Ramsey's 1928 formulation separates the rate into the two things actually going on: δ (delta) — the pure rate of time preference. This is discounting for the sole reason that a benefit arrives later. Ramsey's own verdict on it has never really been improved: discounting later enjoyments merely because they are later is "a practice which is ethically indefensible and arises merely from the weakness of the imagination." η (eta) — the elasticity of marginal utility, or how fast an extra pound loses usefulness as you get richer. A pound to a rich person buys less welfare than a pound to a poor one. g — the growth rate of consumption per person. The decomposition does real work, because only the first dial is ethically loaded. The second is not discounting at all in the moral sense — it says that a marginal pound buys less welfare in a richer world, which is true for the same reason that pounds buy less welfare across income levels today. Even with δ = 0 — a flat refusal to privilege the present — the rate stays positive whenever growth is positive. Growth is what makes the future cheap in money, not a preference for the present.The practical payoff: when someone quotes "the" discount rate, you can ask which dial it came from. If the entire number is δ, you are being asked to accept that later people matter less. That may be defensible — most people do discount their own futures slightly, and institutions that don't discount at all behave strangely — but it needs saying.The most instructive dispute in the modern literature is the one between Nicholas Stern's 2006 Review on the Economics of Climate Change and William Nordhaus's response to it. They used the same framework and reached opposite policy conclusions.Watch how little separates them and how much follows. On the empirical side — how fast the economy grows, what damages look like — they largely agree. The entire disagreement is about δ: whether near-term consumption is worth pursuing for its own sake because it is near.At 1.4%, a 2% loss of global output in 2100 has a substantial present value. At 5%, the same loss shrinks toward irrelevance, and the model dutifully recommends that the cheapest course is to grow richer now and pay to adapt later. The model is not lying. It is faithfully reporting the ethical premise it was fed.That is the point to carry: a disagreement that presents itself as technical is often a value dispute in which the value is a parameter. Locating it — in one cell of a spreadsheet — is the premise audit from Act II applied to the most consequential number in economics.There is a genuinely surprising result that rescues you from having to settle the Stern–Nordhaus argument before you can plan. Martin Weitzman's gamma discounting (2001): if you are uncertain about the correct discount rate — it might be 1%, it might be 5% — then the certainty-equivalent rate you should use is not the average. It declines as the horizon extends, converging toward the lowest plausible rate.The mechanism is the compounding arithmetic from Act III, applied to uncertainty. Weight the two scenarios by their probabilities, and at long horizons the 1% branch contributes vastly more present value than the 5% branch, because it compounds the discount slower. So the effective rate you should apply is a declining sequence: perhaps 4% for a decade, 3% for fifty years, approaching 1% for a millennium.This is why several governments — including the United Kingdom, France, and Norway — now use declining discount rates in official project appraisal rather than one flat rate. It is one of the few places where a philosophical dispute has been partially defused by a probabilistic argument, and it fits the pattern this book keeps returning to: uncertainty does not require you to resolve the question, only to be honest about the distribution of answers.Two cautions. First, Weitzman's own later dismal theorem (2009) argued that with sufficiently heavy-tailed uncertainty about catastrophic outcomes, expected-value reasoning may fail altogether — the expectation can be dominated by events so extreme that no finite estimate is meaningful. Do not take a declining rate as a licence to relax; take it as evidence that this is fat-tailed territory. Second, a declining rate schedule is still a choice about the shape, and can be gamed by choosing a schedule that produces the answer you wanted.The same structure appears inside one skull, and it is worth naming because it is the most immediately actionable form.Human beings do not discount exponentially. Experiments consistently show hyperbolic discounting — very steep for the near term, much shallower for the far term — which produces preference reversal. Offered £100 today or £120 next month, most people take the £100. Offered £100 in twelve months or £120 in thirteen, most people wait. The same twelve-month delay, valued differently depending on where it sits. That is time inconsistency: your preferences today and your preferences-in-twelve-months are not the same preferences.The response is the commitment device — the Ulysses contract. Automatic pension enrolment, standing orders, a savings rule deducted before the money is visible, a deadline made public. These are institutions at the scale of one person, and they work for exactly the reasons institutional commitment devices work at scale: they change the payoffs facing a future self who would otherwise prefer to defect.This connects directly to the dual-process and institutions material. Present bias is not a character flaw; it is the default setting of hardware that evolved for immediate, personal risk. The fix is structural — the same conclusion the rest of the book keeps reaching. Climate policy — the discount rate has done more to shape policy conclusions than any physical estimate, which is why the Stern–Nordhaus dispute matters beyond its own field. Infrastructure — a bridge, rail line, or dam is justified or rejected by the terminal value assigned to benefits beyond the appraisal window, which is a number chosen by convention more often than by argument. Nuclear waste and long-lived hazards — the deep-time material is the mirror image: institutions planning markers for 10,000 years are operating outside any horizon an ordinary discount rate can represent, which is precisely why they require a mandated rather than a computed answer. Pensions and sovereign debt — promises across decades, discounted at rates that flatter whoever is currently in office. Healthcare prioritisation — where a QALY in fifty years is implicitly worth a fraction of one today, usually without anyone deciding that. Biodiversity and extinction — irreversible losses are structurally invisible to net-present-value analysis, because the loss is not a flow that can be discounted but a stock that has been eliminated. Your own career and health — the multi-decade compounding in both directions: the body you will have at seventy, and the skills that compound or decay. When you face a decision with a long tail, six moves do most of the work. Separate the dials. Write the rate as δ + ηg. Only the first needs ethical defence; the second is a factual claim about future wealth that you can test. Say your δ out loud. "I am using 3% pure time preference, which means I am asserting that a person born in 2100 counts for about a twentieth of a person alive today over that horizon." If the sentence is unbearable when spoken, the number is wrong. Run the sensitivity before the analysis. Compute the answer at 0%, 1.5%, 3%, and 7%. If the conclusion flips between two adjacent rates, the discount rate is the argument, and you should be arguing about it rather than presenting a result. Show the undiscounted quantity alongside. "£1.6M of damage in 2126, present value £2,000" keeps both the map and the territory visible in the same sentence — the cheapest possible inoculation against reification. Prefer a declining schedule and say why. It is the honest representation of your uncertainty and it is now standard practice in several governments. If you use a flat rate, note that you are asserting something a declining rate denies. Choose behind a veil. You do not know which generation you will be born into. Ask what rate you would accept if you did not know whether you were the beneficiary in 2026 or the payer in 2226. This is the veil of ignorance from the previous subsection, and it is the only test that reliably catches a rate chosen to flatter its author. Two further habits prevent the drill from becoming a way of doing nothing. Act on the robust moves regardless of the rate — anything that is worth doing at 1%, 3%, and 7% is worth doing without settling the argument, and reversibility is the property that makes a decision safe to take under deep uncertainty. And name the settlement date even when it is far off: a claim about the year 2126 cannot be checked, but a claim that "this policy will be extended after its first five-year review" can.The uncomfortable implication of this whole subsection is that the far future is not neglected because people are callous. It is neglected because our tools for thinking about it have a built-in parameter that erases it, and the parameter usually goes unexamined. Compounding and discounting are one curve; the direction you run it in is a choice, and it is the clearest case in this book of a technical-looking number that is really a statement about what matters.Discount rate — The rate r at which a future benefit is reduced to its present value; conventionally the consumption discount rate in social appraisals.Present value — The amount that would have to be invested today, at the assumed rate, to yield a given future amount; FV ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ.Pure time preference (δ) — The component of the discount rate that values a benefit less purely because it arrives later; the ethically contested dial.Elasticity of marginal utility (η) — The rate at which an additional unit of consumption loses welfare value as consumption rises; governs how much the growing wealth of future people reduces the weight on their welfare.Ramsey equation — r = δ + ηg; the decomposition of the discount rate into a pure time preference and a diminishing-returns term.Consumption discount rate — The rate applied to welfare-relevant consumption across time, as distinct from the market interest rate facing a particular investor.Opportunity cost rate — The return available on the best alternative use of funds; the appropriate rate for commercial appraisal, and not automatically appropriate for intergenerational welfare questions.Hyperbolic discounting — Discounting that is steep in the near term and shallow in the far term, unlike the constant proportional reduction of exponential discounting.Time inconsistency / preference reversal — The property that today's preference over two future options differs from the preference that will be held when the earlier option arrives.Commitment device (Ulysses contract) — An arrangement that removes a future option in order to make a present plan credible, whether at personal scale (automatic saving) or institutional scale (a mandate, an entrenched rule).Gamma discounting / declining discount rate (Weitzman) — The result that uncertainty about the true discount rate implies a certainty-equivalent rate that falls as the horizon extends, approaching the lowest plausible rate.Dismal theorem (Weitzman) — The argument that with sufficiently heavy-tailed uncertainty about catastrophic outcomes, expected-value analysis may be dominated by unmodellable extremes and cease to be informative.Certainty-equivalent rate — The single rate whose application yields the same value as the probability-weighted average of several possible rates over a given horizon.Terminal value — The value assigned to all benefits beyond the explicit appraisal period; frequently the largest and least examined number in a long-horizon cost-benefit analysis.Irreversibility — The property of a loss (extinction, aquifer depletion) that cannot be represented as a flow and therefore cannot be meaningfully discounted.Discounted at the market rate — The practice of applying an observed financial return to an intergenerational welfare question, converting an opportunity cost into an implicit claim that future people matter less.Sensitivity analysis — Recomputing a result across a range of discount rates and other contested parameters to identify which one the conclusion actually hangs on.Veil-of-ignorance test for the rate — Choosing a discount rate without knowing which generation one will inhabit; a consistency check on rates that advantage their author.

what-nobody-taught-you/6-act-v-—-living-.title: 6-3 The map of mental models (how to think about thinking)
what-nobody-taught-you/6-act-v-—-living-.description: Part of 6 Act V — Living With It (synthesis)A mental model is close to worthless in the form it is usually held: a name, a definition, and a memorable anecdote. That form survives exams and does nothing in a meeting. The gap is not knowledge — you can recite Goodhart's Law and still ship a target next quarter — it is that the model was never attached to anything that would make it fire. A map of mental models is not a catalogue of concepts. It is a retrieval index, a small set of distinctions for choosing between models, and a maintenance regime. And like every other map in this book, it compresses, and its failures live in what it discards.The catalogue failure. You accumulate thirty named concepts, can define each one, and reach for none. This is the illusion of explanatory depth wearing a syllabus: recognition is mistaken for capability. The test is the one from Act I — generation, not recognition. Try to run the model out loud on a live problem and see where the sentence stalls.The single-lens failure. A model applied to everything stops being a model and becomes an ideology. "It's all incentives." "Everything is a feedback loop." "That's just Moloch." The tell is that the lens has become unfalsifiable: no observation could make you put it down. A tool that explains every case has left the empirical game, exactly as an immunizing stratagem does.Both failures have the same root. In the first, the model never acquired a trigger. In the second, it never acquired a falsifier.There is a territory, there are maps of it, and there is a map of the maps. This subsection is an object at the third level, which means it inherits the third level's characteristic disease.Level 2 fails by reification — the model gets confused with the thing. Level 3 fails by collecting: the library grows, the confidence grows with it, and nothing in the system ever goes back outside. Notice what this map cannot show you: when to reach for which model, how a model feels when it is about to be misapplied, and whether the person holding the library is calibrated. Those live in practice, not in the diagram.The decisive design choice is what you index on. A library sorted by discipline, alphabet, or chapter is a reference work — useful for looking things up, useless under pressure, because you cannot look things up in the middle of a decision. Sort by presenting symptom instead, the way a clinician sorts a differential. The question is never "what do I know about systems?" but "what does this situation look and feel like?"Two habits make this table work. First, the right-hand column is a shortlist, not a verdict — its job is to get three candidates onto the table, not one. Second, whenever you add a model, add the symptom row with it, or you have added a fact rather than a tool.Not everything in the library behaves the same way, and confusing the kinds is a common source of nonsense.A lens cannot be falsified case by case and shouldn't be. A rule can be, and must be, and its domain matters — the rule of 72 is excellent arithmetic and useless for a population growing logistically. A drill is not a belief at all; it is a procedure, and its only failure mode is not happening.Beginners assume that holding several models means averaging them. It does not. Models rarely contradict each other — they usually partition a situation, each describing a different mechanism that may be operating simultaneously. The work is not to pick a winner but to find which mechanism is binding right now, and that requires an observation that can tell them apart.A short procedure: Check the kind. A lens and a rule cannot contradict each other; they answer different questions. Localise the crux. Convert the disagreement into the smallest sub-claim on which it turns. Name a discriminating observation. What would you see if mechanism A were binding rather than B? If nothing would tell them apart, you are not choosing between models — you are narrating. Ask about dominance. For most structural pairs (reinforcing vs. balancing loop, growth vs. constraint), the system's behaviour is a story about which one is currently winning. If it stays irreducible, weight by evidence and move — and state a settlement date, so the choice becomes scoreable. Monthly churn rose from 2.1% to 3.4% after you added an identity-verification step at signup. Here is the shortlist the trigger table produces, and what each one predicts: Second-order effects. Friction at signup filters out exactly the marginal-but-legitimate users. Predicts: the effect appears in cohorts created after the change, is not seasonal, and is larger for users acquired through paid channels. Goodhart. If activation is your North Star, support staff are pre-filling fields to keep it up. Predicts: activation holds steady while downstream retention falls, and the gap is concentrated in one team or region. Survivorship / denominator drift. Churn is a ratio, and the denominator may have been redefined alongside the flow. Predicts: the break is an artefact — recompute under both definitions and the discontinuity softens. Base rates. Churn rose in Q1 for the past three years. Predicts: this cohort looks like every other Q1; pull the reference class before doing anything. Legibility. Manual review carried judgment the scripted flow cannot encode; the residue reappears somewhere the funnel does not measure. Predicts: chargebacks or support escalations rise while churn alone looks stable. Ergodicity. 3.4% monthly compounds to roughly 34% annual attrition, and a small tail of accounts carries most of the revenue. Predicts: the mean churn is not the story; check the distribution and the top decile specifically. Moloch. A competitor's price cut set a floor. Predicts: the rise is uniform across cohorts and correlates with their announcement, not with your change. Note what the map did. It converted one alarming number into seven predictions with different signatures, and it named the observations that would separate them. That is the whole point: models earn their keep by generating discriminating observations, not by being true in general.Knowing a model's name and being able to run it under load are different states, and the transition is practice, not reading.Four specifics do most of the work. Name it out loud in the moment — "this looks like a fix that fails" — because labelling forces retrieval rather than recognition. Apply it to something with a settlement date, so the model's use, not just its content, can be scored. Run an after-action review with the model as the frame, asking which one would have caught what actually happened. And teach it, because generation is the only reliable test; the sentence that stalls is where your understanding stops.Keep the active set small — somewhere between ten and twenty-five, each with a trigger, a failure case, and a use from the last year. Everything else is a library, and libraries are for lookup, not for thinking.A tool collection needs the same discipline as a belief. Four questions, run annually, take twenty minutes. Which model did you apply in the last year and make things worse? If none, you have not been applying them under stakes. Which model can you not describe a failure case for? That one is a candidate for reification or for rhetoric. Which model do you reach for because it is flattering? Structural compulsion is real, and so is Moloch laundering — invoking the structure to justify what you wanted anyway. Which model do you have a rhetorical use for and no operational use? That is a slogan with a bibliography. The Lindy logic applies here as it does elsewhere, with the same caveat: old models have survived real selection pressure, which is evidence of durability rather than of quality. Keep them, and keep asking whether the terrain that selected them has moved.Three things, and naming them is the honest close of a subsection about metacognition.Timing and feel. Which model to reach for in the first thirty seconds of a conversation is tacit knowledge, learned by contact, not retrievable from any index. This is why the map is thin compared to the practice.Your blind families. Everyone has a cluster they never use. The useful diagnostic is the one from disagreement theory: look at where your predictions have repeatedly gone wrong, and see which family of models would have caught it. That is your gap, and it is invisible from the inside.Whether you are calibrated. The library can tell you to use base rates. It cannot tell you whether your priors are any good, whether your 80% is really 80%, or whether the class you chose was the flattering one. That requires scorekeeping, which is a practice rather than a page.The map of mental models is therefore less an achievement than a regime — something run rather than possessed. Its health is measured by one thing: whether something outside it can still change what you think.Map of mental models — A structured, indexed collection of models and drills held for use in live decisions; distinguished from a catalogue of concepts by the presence of triggers, failure cases, and a maintenance routine.Trigger (retrieval cue) — The symptom or situation pattern that causes a model to be recalled; the indexing key for a usable library.Catalogue failure — Holding many named models and applying none; recognition mistaken for capability, the collective form of the illusion of explanatory depth.Single-lens failure — Treating one model as universally applicable, so that it becomes unfalsifiable and ceases to be a model; Maslow's hammer in its epistemic form.Lens / rule / drill — The three kinds of entry in a library: perceptual habits that cannot be falsified case by case, checkable heuristics with domains, and procedures that must be scheduled and run.Discriminating observation — An observation whose outcome differs depending on which of two candidate models is binding; the mechanism by which multi-model reasoning is settled rather than averaged.Dominance question — Asking which of several simultaneously operating mechanisms is currently determining the system's behaviour, rather than treating them as competing explanations.Partition, not contradiction — The usual relationship between models: they describe different mechanisms operating at once, rather than incompatible accounts of the same one.Multi-model reasoning — Using several models on one problem to generate a shortlist, localise the crux, and produce a discriminating test; never the averaging of their answers.Installation (of a model) — The transition from recognising a model to running it under load, accomplished through live naming, application, scoring, and teaching rather than through reading.Retrieval under load — Recalling and applying a model in the moment of a real decision, when the pressure and the missing information are what make it hard; the condition under which a model is genuinely held.Blind family — The cluster of models a person systematically fails to reach for; detectable from a pattern of past prediction errors rather than from introspection.Moloch laundering — Invoking structural compulsion to justify a preference that would otherwise require defending; the failure mode of a powerful model in the hands of someone who already knows what they want to do.Library maintenance — The periodic audit of a model collection: which models were used, which made things worse, which have no failure case, and which are held for rhetoric rather than for use.Third-level error — Confusing the map of models with either the models or the territory; the characteristic failure of a section about thinking about thinking, and the reason this one ends by naming what it cannot show.

what-nobody-taught-you/6-act-v-—-living-.title: 6-4 Putting it together- a toolkit for thinking in a complex world
what-nobody-taught-you/6-act-v-—-living-.description: Part of 6 Act V — Living With It (synthesis)Every tool in this book arrived separately — feedback loops, base rates, ergodicity, commons design, the is/ought gap — and each earned its place by explaining something the others could not. But a toolkit is not defined by its contents. It is defined by its access pattern: which tool you reach for, in what order, how quickly you can tell you have reached for the wrong one, and how little time the whole thing takes. That access pattern has not been supplied yet. This subsection supplies it.It is deliberately short. A synthesis that takes an hour to run will be run once, admired, and abandoned. A synthesis that takes ten minutes can be run on a Tuesday.Three properties do the work, and all three are absences in an ordinary catalogue of concepts.Portable. The five moves below contain no domain content. They apply to a hospital policy, a hiring decision, a mortgage, a rumour, and a forecast with equal ease, because they interrogate the structure of a claim rather than its subject matter.Ordered. This matters more than it sounds. Asking whether a conclusion is falsifiable is meaningless before you know what the conclusion is about; sourcing a prior from a reference class is impossible before you have chosen the class. Order is what separates a toolkit from a heap.Self-checking. Every move terminates in something observable — an answer you can look up, a number you can score, a premise you either can or cannot state. A move that produces only a feeling of insight has failed, and you can tell.Those five scales are where the book's concepts live, and the three recurring threads — how we predict, how we handle uncertainty, how we coordinate — run vertically through all of them. The toolkit's job is to make sure a question posed at one scale gets checked at the others. Most expensive mistakes are not errors within a level; they are answers computed at one level and applied at another.Run in order. Each is one sentence, and each has a tell that you have actually done it rather than merely nodded at it.Zoom runs in two directions, and both count as the same operation: out to the class (how does this kind of thing usually go?) and in on the representation (what did the compression drop?). Refusing the level at which the question was posed is the whole move.Loop is where second-order effects, tipping points, and metric decay all get caught, because they are the same structural event: the system responding to your intervention and changing the payoffs you were reasoning from. The tell is being able to say whether the dominant loop is reinforcing or balancing right now — not in general.Position carries the book's hardest arithmetic. It asks whether you are an observer outside a system or an agent inside it; whether the relevant statistic is an ensemble average or one trajectory's fate; and who absorbs the costs your proposal generates. A model with excellent average performance and a fatal tail is unacceptable to anyone who is a trajectory rather than a pool, which is nearly everyone, nearly always.Settle is the corrective for every move above it. A settled claim is one where you named the failing observation in advance — the same discipline as pre-registering a trial or writing a decision down while it is still live. Without a settlement date, an update is a mood.Bridge is last because it is not an empirical move at all, and treating it as one is the error it exists to catch. The evidence can tell you what will happen; it cannot tell you what is worth wanting. Naming the premise converts an apparent disagreement about facts into a real one about priorities, which is progress even when nobody moves.And one standing question, not a move, running underneath all five: are my sources actually independent? Three colleagues who read the same report are one witness. A dashboard derived from the same dataset as the forecast it confirms is one estimate. Independence is the property that makes corroboration mean anything, and it is the first thing real agreement destroys.Readers of the earlier material will recognise that the four-question audit from the knowledge act — Map, Adversary, Prior, Should — is the subset of this sweep that applies to a single claim. The sweep adds the two levels that audit could not reach: the system the claim sits inside, and the other agents who will respond to it.A hospital network is deciding whether to deploy an algorithm that flags deteriorating patients for review. The vendor reports 92% sensitivity in its trial. Run the sweep.Zoom. The trial figure comes from a population already suspected of sepsis, where prevalence is high. In the network's ordinary admissions, prevalence is far lower, and the same test at a lower base rate produces mostly false alarms. Meanwhile the compression discarded something specific: the experienced nurse's read of a patient who "looks wrong" despite normal numbers, which appears in no training column. The alert does not augment that judgment; it competes with it, and it will win, because it is a number and the judgment is not.Loop. Alerting changes clinician behaviour; enough low-value alerts produce dismissal habits, which lower the effective sensitivity, which the vendor's next model update addresses by tightening thresholds, which raises alert volume. Separately, the metric that will get managed is response rate to alerts — visible, countable, attributable — not mortality, which is noisy and delayed. The decay loop is already turning before the contract is signed.Position. You are not an outside evaluator. You are a node the alert will act on, and so are the clinicians. More importantly, the relevant unit is a single patient, not a population: a model with strong average performance and a bad tail of missed deteriorations is not acceptable, because patients do not average across their own trajectories. And the costs are asymmetric in opposite directions — a false negative kills someone, a false positive costs a nurse eight minutes, a hundred times a day.Settle. Written down before go-live: stepped rollout over six months; sepsis mortality in alerted wards must fall by at least one percentage point, with no rise in broad-spectrum antibiotic use. If the alert-dismissal rate exceeds 60%, we withdraw and publish why. Note that this names the failure mode in advance, which is what makes the pilot informative rather than decorative.Bridge. Someone must state that a modest mortality gain justifies the clinician time and the antibiotic side effects, and that patients are scored without individual consent. That premise is defensible, and it is not in the data.Four of the five moves produced a question to go and answer rather than an answer. That is the normal output, and it is the point.The same sweep run on "should I take this job" takes about ninety seconds. Zoom: what do people in this class of move typically find after two years? Loop: what does accepting compound, and what does it foreclose? Position: you are one career, not a portfolio of parallel lives, so a small chance of a catastrophic fit is not averaged away by a good expected salary. Settle: what would make you leave within a year, and what will you write down tonight? Bridge: autonomy, money, status, or proximity to family — which one is actually being optimised?Across the whole book, the concepts collapse into a handful of recurring shapes. This is the payoff of treating them as a toolkit: you do not need to remember forty ideas, because most of them are the same failure caught in different weather.The last row deserves emphasis, because it is the failure mode of this act's own material. "There is no alternative" is sometimes a description of a genuine trap and sometimes an alibi, and the difference is checkable: name the competitor, the mechanism, and roughly the magnitude of the loss. If the answer dissolves under questioning, you have a value preference wearing a payoff matrix. Restate the question at a different level. Either find the class, or find what the metric discarded. One minute. Trace one round of consequences and stop. "And then what?" three times surfaces adaptation, rebound, and displacement. Three minutes if you are honest. Locate yourself. Are you inside or outside? One trajectory or a pool? Who pays? One minute. Write the settlement. Claim, threshold, window, and what happens if it fails. Two minutes, and it is the only step that ever gets skipped. Say the bridge premise out loud. Two minutes, occasionally uncomfortable. Check independence. Are the witnesses actually separate? Thirty seconds, and it routinely overturns steps one through five. Proportionality governs the depth. Match the effort to the stakes and to how reversible the decision is — a two-way door deserves a scan, a one-way door deserves the full pass and a written record. And remember that inaction is itself an intervention with its own second-order effects and its own beneficiaries; the sweep is not a licence to defer. Not a formula. It produces questions, thresholds, and premises, not answers. Where it produces an answer, that answer came from the domain knowledge you brought. Not a route to agreement. The Bridge move exists precisely because the sweep often terminates in a genuine disagreement about values, correctly located at last, where it can be conducted rather than buried. Not a substitute for expertise. Position tells you when to defer and to whom; it does not make you the expert. Not a claim that everything is connected. "It's complex" and "everything feeds back" are ways of saying nothing. The useful version names the components, the rules, and the specific pattern being explained. Not free. Every move costs time and occasionally costs you a belief you liked. The proportionality rule is what keeps the price sane. The deepest thing the synthesis turns up is that there is only one procedure here, run at four different scales.A claim, a forecasting model, a regulatory regime, and a person are all healthy to exactly the same degree: the extent to which something outside them can still change them. Drift and echo close that loop at every scale, and every repair — direct observation, independent replication, adversarial collaboration, an honest interlocutor — is the same repair: reconnect to something you do not control.Which leaves one sentence worth carrying out of the book. Name in advance what would change your mind, then arrange for that thing to be observable — and do it at every scale, from a claim you made this morning to an institution you will not live to see replaced. It contains the map, because you must say what the belief is about. It contains the adversary, because you must say what would sink it. It contains the prior, because arranging for observation is where evidence comes from. It contains the social layer, because arranging for observation almost always means involving someone other than you. And it is deliberately silent on what you ought to want, because that is a different argument, on different terrain, with different rules.Toolkit — A portable, ordered, self-checking set of moves for interrogating claims and decisions; defined by its access pattern rather than its contents.Zoom — The move that changes the level of description, either outward from a case to its reference class or inward on what a representation discarded.Loop — The move that traces feedback, delay, and second-order effects, and identifies which loop currently dominates a system.Position — The move that locates the reasoner: inside or outside the system, one trajectory or a member of a pool, and on which side of the costs and benefits.Settle — The move that states, in advance, the observation, threshold, and date at which a claim would be judged wrong.Bridge — The move that names the normative premise required to convert an empirical finding into a recommendation.Standing question (independence check) — The recurring test of whether apparently multiple sources, experts, or memories trace back to a single origin.Access pattern — Which tool is reached for, in what order, and how quickly a wrong reach is detected; what distinguishes a toolkit from a catalogue.Failure atlas — The recurring structural failure shapes into which most of the book's concepts collapse: reification, inside-view planning, drift, echo, loop blindness, metric decay, ensemble illusion, and structural laundering.Proportionality rule — Matching the depth of analysis to the stakes and reversibility of the decision, rather than running the full sweep on everything or nothing.Structural laundering — Presenting a value preference as an unavoidable consequence of the system's structure; the failure mode the Bridge and Settle moves exist to catch.Scale ladder — The observation that the same state–observe–settle–revise loop runs on a claim, a model, an institution, and a person, and that health at every scale means the same thing: having an input you do not control.

strategy-theory-and-applications/1-basic.title: 1-1 Defining Strategy and Its Core Elements
strategy-theory-and-applications/1-basic.description:
Part of 1 Basics of Strategy and FormulationStrategy is one of the most used and least precise words in management. It appears in job titles, quarterly reviews, and political campaigns, often meaning little more than "something important we intend to do." This subsection gives a working definition, separates strategy from the concepts it is routinely confused with, and sets out the core elements a statement must contain before it deserves the name. Later sections build on this foundation: the next one distinguishes levels of strategy and strategic intent, and the one after that turns the elements below into a formulation process.The word descends from the Greek stratēgos, the general who commanded an army, and it retains that martial flavour: strategy is the art of winning under conditions of competition, uncertainty, and limited resources. The classic definition comes from Alfred Chandler, who described strategy as "the determination of the long-run goals and objectives of an enterprise, and the adoption of courses of action and the allocation of resources necessary for carrying out these goals." Kenneth Andrews added that strategy is a pattern of decisions — a consistency that observers can detect across many separate choices, not a single document.Michael Porter sharpened the idea in a way that remains the most useful test: strategy is not about operational effectiveness, which is about doing the same things better than rivals, but about being different — the deliberate choice of a unique and valuable position, rooted in a different set of activities, defended by trade-offs. His formulation forces attention on what a firm declines to do. A firm that tries to be everything to everyone has no position to defend, and its many activities, however well executed, will not add up to an advantage.Henry Mintzberg's "five Ps" are a useful compact summary of how the term is used in practice: strategy as plan (a consciously intended course of action), as ploy (a manoeuvre to outwit a competitor), as pattern (consistency in behaviour, whether intended or not), as position (a place in the environment or market), and as perspective (a shared way of seeing the world). His distinction between intended and emergent strategy is a reminder that realised strategy is often what survives contact with events rather than what was written down.Much confusion dissolves once the adjacent concepts are separated. The table below gives the working distinctions used throughout this book.A goal is a destination; a forecast is a weather report; a plan is a timetable. Strategy is the reasoning that connects the destination to the weather report and tells you which road to take — and, just as importantly, which roads to abandon.
Definitions vary, but when a strategic statement actually guides behaviour, it almost always contains the same six ingredients.1. Objectives. A long-run goal or set of goals that specifies what success looks like and over what horizon. Without an objective there is nothing to be strategic about; the difficulty is making the objective demanding enough to force choices and concrete enough to be judged.2. A diagnosis. An honest, parsimonious account of the situation: what is really going on, what the critical obstacle or opportunity is, and why. Richard Rumelt argues that the diagnosis is the element most often missing and most consequential, because a correct diagnosis of the challenge does half the work of answering it. A diagnosis is a judgement under uncertainty, not a summary of everything known.3. A guiding policy. The chosen overall logic for dealing with the diagnosis — the idea about how the organisation will succeed. Crucially, this includes a claim about the source of advantage: why this approach should produce value that rivals cannot easily match. "Be the best" is not a guiding policy; "be the fastest to serve a dense local market" is.4. Scope. Where the organisation will play — which customers, products, geographies, channels, and stages of the value chain — and, explicitly, where it will not. Scope is the element that makes a strategy finite and therefore actionable. The most diagnostic word in any strategy document is only.5. Coherent actions and resource commitments. A set of moves that reinforce one another and are backed by money, people, and management attention. Porter's notion of fit is the test here: activities should be mutually amplifying, so that the whole is harder to imitate than any single part. A list of unrelated initiatives is a portfolio, not a strategy.6. Trade-offs. The deliberate surrender of otherwise attractive options. Trade-offs are what make a position defensible, because a competitor copying the strategy must also accept the sacrifices it entails. A strategy without trade-offs is a statement of intent that any well-funded rival can match, and it usually collapses into a race to be all things to all customers.
Consider a fictional specialty coffee roaster, Northwind, which sells wholesale beans to independent cafés. Its board paper opens with this: "Our strategy is to be the region's leading, highest-quality coffee roaster, growing revenue 20% a year through excellent customer service, innovation, and our passionate team." Every phrase is pleasant and none is strategic. There is no diagnosis, no scope boundary, no claim about why Northwind specifically should win, no trade-off, and no coherent bundle of actions; a competitor could adopt the identical sentence without changing anything it does. It also, tellingly, cannot be falsified — there is no way to lose.Now the same firm written against the six elements: Objectives: 25% return on capital within three years, with 300 profitable wholesale accounts. Diagnosis: Independent cafés are being squeezed by rising rents and staff costs and cannot afford dedicated barista training, while national roasters sell beans as a commodity and offer no local support. Guiding policy: Win by making each café more profitable per square metre — selling beans bundled with training and menu design rather than beans alone. Advantage comes from dense local logistics and in-house training capability that national roasters cannot serve economically. Scope: Independent cafés with two to ten sites within a four-hour drive. No own-brand retail shops, no national chains, no grocery channel. Coherent actions: Hire two field trainers; run a small-batch roasting schedule with 48-hour turnaround; price as a beans-plus-service retainer; exit the low-margin grocery contract to free roasting capacity. Trade-offs: Forgo grocery volume, and forgo the fast-growing home-subscription segment that would dilute roasting focus. The second version is contestable — a rival might disagree with the diagnosis — and that is a sign of health. It also changes what people do on Monday morning, which is the only reliable evidence that a strategy exists at all.Before a statement is called a strategy, three questions are worth asking. The sacrifice test: what are we giving up? If nothing attractive is being surrendered, this is a wish list. The imitation test: could a competent rival copy this by reading our public materials, and would copying cost them anything? If not, there is no advantage claim. The Monday test: does it change any specific decision about hiring, capital, pricing, or accounts this quarter? If not, it is commentary. These tests connect forward to the rest of the book: the imitation test is developed in the competitive strategy chapters, the Monday test in the chapters on execution and alignment, and the reasons strategists so often fail the sacrifice test are examined in the chapters on the cognitive psychology of strategic choice.

strategy-theory-and-applications/1-basic.title: 1-2 Levels of Strategy and Strategic Intent
strategy-theory-and-applications/1-basic.description:
Part of 1 Basics of Strategy and FormulationStrategy is not a single document produced once at the top of an organisation. It is a layered system: different groups of managers answer different questions, over different time horizons, and the answers must fit together. Standing above that hierarchy is something less tangible but more powerful — strategic intent, the ambition that tells everyone which direction counts as winning. This subsection sets out the levels, shows how they connect, and then examines strategic intent as the animating force that gives the levels a common purpose.Most organisations, whether a multinational, a hospital, or a two-partner consultancy, can be described with three levels of strategy. They are distinguished not by seniority but by the question each level answers.Corporate strategy is the responsibility of the top management team and the board. It concerns the composition and scope of the organisation as a whole: which businesses, markets, and geographies to be in; how capital and talent are allocated between them; whether to acquire, divest, integrate vertically, or form alliances. Its "customer" is ultimately the provider of capital, and its horizon is typically five to ten years or longer.The test of good corporate strategy is not the elegance of the portfolio chart but parenting advantage: does the centre add more value to its businesses than they would enjoy as stand-alone entities, or under a different parent? A corporate centre that merely aggregates financial results and sets budgets is a cost, not a strategy.Below the corporate level sit strategic business units (SBUs) — units with a distinct set of customers, competitors, and economics. Business strategy answers the competitive question: how will we win in this market against these rivals? It is where the choice of value proposition, positioning, and generic strategy (cost leadership, differentiation, or focus) is made, and where trade-offs become concrete. The horizon is usually one to five years.In a single-business firm the corporate and business levels collapse into one, which is why founders of small companies often find the distinction abstract until they open a second product line or a second country.Functional strategy translates the business strategy into the policies and capabilities of each function — marketing, operations, R&D, HR, finance, IT. It answers: what must this function do exceptionally well for the business strategy to succeed, and what resources does that require? Horizons are short for operational plans and longer for capability building such as a manufacturing platform or a data infrastructure.
| Level | Central question | Horizon | Typical decisions | |---|---|---|---| | Corporate | Which businesses, and why under one roof? | 5–10+ years | Acquisitions, divestments, capital allocation, geographic entry | | Business | How do we win against these competitors? | 1–5 years | Value proposition, positioning, pricing logic, segment focus | | Functional | What must each function do to support that? | Months to 3 years | Capacity, skills, systems, supplier and channel policies |Some writers add a fourth, network or ecosystem level — how the organisation positions itself among partners, platforms, and standards-setters, which matters greatly for technology and platform businesses. Others split off operational strategy as the day-to-day scheduling and deployment layer beneath functional strategy. Both are useful extensions rather than contradictions of the three-level scheme.The hierarchy is a constraint system, not a chain of command. Each level narrows the options of the one below it, and each lower level feeds back information about feasibility and cost. Coherence fails in three recognisable ways: The corporate level adds no value. Units are left as a loose portfolio, and "group strategy" is a capital allocation spreadsheet. Levels are copy-pasted. The business unit's strategy document repeats the corporate one with the word "division" inserted, and the functions repeat the business one. Nothing is being decided anywhere. Functions drift. Marketing pursues premium branding while operations is incentivised for low-cost volume — each functional strategy defensible on its own, together incoherent. The remedy in each case is the same discipline introduced earlier: at every level, ask what is being declined, and check that the answers are mutually consistent.Levels describe the architecture of strategy. Strategic intent supplies its ambition. The term was popularised by Gary Hamel and C. K. Prahalad in their 1989 Harvard Business Review article, drawing on firms that had vaulted past far better-resourced rivals: Komatsu's declared aim to "encircle Caterpillar," Canon's ambition to "beat Xerox," Honda's early intent to become a global automotive manufacturer.Their argument was that conventional strategic planning starts from fit — matching ambitions to existing resources — and therefore ratifies the status quo. Strategic intent instead starts from stretch: an aspiration so far beyond current resources that the organisation is forced to invent new ways of competing. The resulting gap between ambition and capability is not a planning error to be corrected but the engine of the whole exercise.
Hamel and Prahalad's five levers of resource leverage explain how the gap is closed: concentrating resources on a few decisive goals; accumulating them through learning and experience; complementing them by blending resource types to create disproportionate value; conserving them by co-opting partners' resources and reusing assets; and recovering investment quickly by shortening the time between spending and payback.A practical way to state intent is the BHAG — a big, hairy, audacious goal, in Collins and Porras's phrase — anchored by a deadline and a measurable outcome, plus a consistent marching rhythm that keeps progress steady rather than episodic.These terms are often used interchangeably and need not be, though organisations vary widely in practice. A workable division of labour: Purpose (mission): why the organisation exists and whom it serves. Vision: a description of the future state if it succeeds. Strategic intent: the winning ambition — what the organisation intends to be best in the world at, expressed with enough stretch to force capability building. Values: constraints on the means used to get there. Goals and objectives: the measurable milestones along the way. Purpose and values are largely stable and non-competitive; strategic intent is inherently comparative and demanding.Strategic intent is powerful and easy to abuse. Stated as pure aspiration, it becomes hubris and demoralises the organisation when milestones are missed. Three safeguards keep it honest: an explicit diagnosis of why the gap can be closed (intent must be paired with a credible logic of resource leverage, not just an adjective like "world-class"); intermediate milestones that make progress visible and falsifiable; and a willingness to change means while keeping the intent stable. When a firm abandons its ambition every time a plan misses, intent was never real; when it refuses to revise any plan that serves the intent, stretch has hardened into dogma.Return to Northwind, the specialty coffee roaster, now expanded so that all three levels are visible. Corporate strategy. Own two businesses — wholesale roasting to independent cafés, and a small equipment-servicing arm — and nothing else. Divest the grocery contract to release roasting capacity; no retail shops, no home subscription. The parenting logic: shared roasting capacity, shared local logistics, and a common customer relationship that neither business could build alone. Business strategy (wholesale). Win by making each café more profitable per square metre, selling beans bundled with training and menu design rather than beans alone. Serve cafés with two to ten sites within a four-hour drive. Functional strategy. Operations runs a small-batch schedule with 48-hour turnaround and holds a deliberately narrow SKU range; HR hires two field trainers and builds an apprenticeship pipeline; finance prices the bundle as a service retainer rather than at cost-plus per kilogram. Each functional choice is what makes the business strategy physically possible. Now add strategic intent: to be the roaster that no independent café in the region can outgrow. Northwind today can serve perhaps forty cafés with its training capacity; the intent demands several hundred. That gap is what justifies the apprenticeship pipeline, the narrow SKU range, and eventually a second roastery — choices that a fit-based plan would have deferred indefinitely. The intent is stable; the plans serving it are revised annually.Levels without intent produce coherent but timid organisations: every unit aligned, nothing attempted. Intent without levels produces slogans: a soaring ambition that no business unit is funded or staffed to pursue. The two work as a pair — the hierarchy converts ambition into specific, funded decisions, while the intent ensures the hierarchy is aiming at something worth the coordination cost. The next subsection turns this structure into a process, examining how strategies at each level are actually formulated, tested, and chosen.

strategy-theory-and-applications/1-basic.title: 1-3 The Strategy Formulation Process
strategy-theory-and-applications/1-basic.description:
Part of 1 Basics of Strategy and FormulationStrategy formulation is the disciplined work of turning an ambiguous competitive situation into a set of commitments specific enough to act on. The previous subsection set out what a strategy must contain — diagnosis, guiding policy, scope, coherent actions, trade-offs — and the one before it distinguished strategy from goals, plans, and forecasts. This subsection is about the process that produces those elements: who does the work, in what order, with what outputs, and where it habitually goes wrong.Two warnings frame everything that follows. First, the process is not a template to be filled in; a filled-in template is exactly what the six elements are meant to help you avoid. Second, the process is not linear. It is presented below as a sequence because sequences are easier to describe than loops, but in practice the stages overlap, feed back on one another, and are cut short or repeated as circumstances demand. The purpose of the sequence is not to be followed literally but to make sure no essential judgement gets skipped under time pressure.A named process buys three things. It imposes discipline — a defence against the natural tendency to start with the answer one already prefers and gather support afterwards. It creates shared language — when a leadership team has agreed what a "diagnosis" or a "strategic option" is, disagreements become substantive rather than semantic. And it allocates attention — it forces time on the questions that are expensive to think about and easy to postpone, particularly the question of what to stop doing.The cost is ritual. Any process repeated annually eventually becomes a document-production exercise, with units rewarded for the polish of their submissions rather than the quality of their thinking. The stages below are worth keeping only if each produces a decision, not a slide.
1. Frame the decision. Before analysis, specify what is actually being decided, by whom, by when, and at what level. "Should we enter the German market in the next eighteen months?" is a frame; "develop a growth strategy" is not. Framing sets the scope of the analytical work and the standard of evidence required, and it is the cheapest place to prevent an expensive exercise from answering the wrong question.2. Diagnose. Establish what is really going on, internally and externally, and reduce it to a handful of critical issues. This is where the familiar analytical toolkits earn their place — industry structure, capability analysis, scenario planning, customer and competitor evidence — but their function is to support a judgement, not to be displayed. The output is one or two paragraphs that a rival could disagree with, not an exhaustive inventory.3. Set the aspiration. Define what success looks like, over what horizon, and measured how. Aspiration and diagnosis are mutually constraining: an ambition that the diagnosis shows to be unreachable is fantasy, and a diagnosis with no ambition attached produces no pressure to change anything.4. Generate options. Produce three to five genuinely different ways of winning, not three variants of the same idea. The most common failure here is what might be called false plurality — one real option surrounded by two deliberately weak ones, included so the chosen course can be said to have been tested. Good option generation is deliberately divergent, even uncomfortable: what would we do if our largest customer disappeared? What would a well-funded entrant do to us?5. Evaluate and choose. Judge the options against explicit criteria — likely value, fit with capabilities, risk, reversibility, feasibility of financing — and then commit. The output is a chosen guiding policy together with the trade-offs it entails. This is the stage that most often fails politically, because genuine choice means some people's proposals lose. The characteristic pathology is averaging: a strategy assembled from the least objectionable parts of every option, which satisfies each sponsor and commits the organisation to nothing.6. Codify and resource. Turn the choice into a short strategy statement in the six-element form, then attach money, people, and management attention to it. Codification is not bureaucracy; writing forces precision, and a document that cannot be summarised in a page has probably not been decided. The resource step is what separates formulation from commentary, and it is the bridge to operational alignment.7. Test and adapt. Specify in advance what evidence would show the strategy is failing, and what events would justify revisiting it. Formulation is not a once-a-year event but a standing commitment to revise beliefs when the world speaks.Running through the sequence is a two-stroke rhythm. Stages 2 and 4 diverge — widening the set of facts considered and options entertained. Stages 3, 5, and 6 converge — reducing many possibilities to one committed course. Groups that diverge without converging produce analysis with no decisions; groups that converge prematurely produce confident strategies built on unexamined assumptions. Naming which stroke the meeting is currently in is often the single most useful intervention a facilitator can make.Formulation is not the sole property of the executive suite, though it is ultimately the executive's accountability. Three modes are common, and most organisations use a blend. Top-down: senior leadership sets the diagnosis and guiding policy, and units align. Fast, coherent, and prone to missing local evidence. Bottom-up: units propose strategies within a corporate frame of financial and portfolio constraints. Rich in evidence, prone to aggregation — a pile of unit plans is not a corporate strategy. Middle-out: corporate sets the ambition and the trade-offs it will enforce; units and functions develop options against them. Slower, but usually produces better diagnosis and higher commitment.
Whoever does the drafting, the choice itself must be traceable to a named decision-maker. Strategies that belong to a committee tend to lack trade-offs, because committees are constructed to avoid them.Most organisations run an annual cycle tied to the budget, sometimes with a mid-year review. The annual rhythm has real virtues — it synchronises resource allocation, and it guarantees that thinking happens at least once a year — but it has a characteristic defect: it tends to treat a continuous question as a periodic one. A competitor's move in March does not wait for September.The practical answer is a hybrid. Keep the calendar cycle for the resource-intensive parts (portfolio, capital, major commitments) and add trigger-based re-formulation for events that invalidate the diagnosis: a structural change in the industry, a technological shift, a shock to the core customer, or performance persistently outside the expected range in either direction. Deciding the triggers when the strategy is agreed is much easier than deciding them during a crisis, when the temptation is always to explain the evidence away.Return to the specialty coffee roaster whose finished strategy statement appeared in the previous subsection. Formulated as a process, it looks like this. Northwind's board frames the decision narrowly — "how do we grow profitably without entering grocery?" — rather than the customary "what is our five-year vision?" Diagnosis follows: cafés are squeezed by rents and staff costs and cannot afford training, while national roasters compete on price and provide no local support. The aspiration is 25% return on capital within three years. Four options are developed, including the two that will lose: private-label grocery supply, and a home-subscription service. Both are genuinely attractive, which is why discarding them counts. In evaluation, the board concludes that grocery volume would consume the small-batch roasting capacity the training bundle depends on, and that subscriptions would fragment a delivery fleet built for dense local routes. The choice — beans bundled with training and menu design, within a four-hour drive — is written in six-element form, and the low-margin grocery contract is cancelled, freeing capacity. The tests are agreed at the same meeting: if average revenue per account does not rise within four quarters, or if field trainers cannot be hired at the modelled cost, the diagnosis is wrong and the board reconvenes.The example matters because the process did not generate the answer; it forced the answer to be explicit, contestable, and paid for. That is all a formulation process can do, and it is a great deal.Two cautions close the section. The first is cognitive: every stage above is a judgement made by people with limited attention, prior commitments, and a documented fondness for confirming what they already believe. How those limits distort diagnosis, option generation, and evaluation is the subject of the next chapter. The second is temporal: a strategy is a hypothesis about the future, and the process that produces it must be connected to a process that learns from its reception — the concern of the later chapters on execution and strategic learning.

strategy-theory-and-applications/2-cogni.title: 2-1 Bounded Rationality and Cognitive Limits
strategy-theory-and-applications/2-cogni.description:
Part of 2 Cognitive Psychology of Strategic ChoiceStrategy is a choice made by people who cannot know everything, cannot consider everything, and cannot hold much in mind at once. That observation sounds like an apology, but it is actually a structural fact about strategy, and it shapes every stage of the formulation process described earlier. This subsection sets out the idea of bounded rationality, the specific cognitive limits that produce it, and — most importantly — what those limits do to the diagnosis, options, and trade-offs a strategist produces.Classical economics models a decision-maker who surveys all alternatives, evaluates them against a consistent utility function, and selects the optimum. Herbert Simon called this figure economic man and argued that no organism, and certainly no manager, could meet the model's requirements. His alternative, administrative man, is a being whose rationality is bounded by three things: the information available, the computational capacity of the mind, and the time in which a decision must be made. Bounded rationality is not a theory of error. It is a theory of what rationality looks like when the decision-maker is finite.Simon's sharpest image for this appears in The Sciences of the Artificial: human rational behaviour is shaped by "a scissors whose two blades are the structure of task environments and the computational capabilities of the actor." Strategy fails when practitioners look only at one blade. The environment — industry structure, competitors, customers — gets most of the analytical attention, but the shape of the choice is equally determined by the mind doing the choosing. A board analysing an industry with great sophistication while operating on four hours of sleep, twelve familiar options, and an unexamined prior is being cut by the second blade.Bounded rationality is often treated as a single vague constraint ("we can't know everything"). It is more useful to break it into distinct limits, because each has a different signature in strategic work and a different remedy.Attention is scarce, not information. Simon's observation that "a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention" has aged into prophecy. Modern strategists are rarely short of data; they are short of the capacity to notice what matters in it. Attention is selective by design — the mind filters aggressively so as not to be overwhelmed — which means the diagnosis a leadership team produces is always a selection from the available evidence, made by people whose attention was already allocated, often by habit or by whoever spoke last.Working memory is small. The classic estimate of "seven plus or minus two" items has since been revised down to roughly four chunks, though chunking — grouping related items into a single unit — massively extends effective capacity. The strategic consequence is that complexity must be compressed to be thought about. Frameworks, mental models, and even crude analogies are compression devices. They make hard problems tractable and, in doing so, discard things.Search is local and sequential. People do not scan option space; they search near the problem and near current practice, one alternative at a time, and stop when something acceptable appears. Cyert and March called the organisational version problemistic search: search is triggered by failure, motivated by a specific problem, and biased toward solutions adjacent to what the firm already does. This is why the option set in a strategy review so often consists of variations on the current business, and why genuinely different options tend to require an outsider or an explicit prompt to appear.Aspiration levels move. Rather than maximising, Simon argued, decision-makers satisfice: they set an aspiration level and accept the first option that clears it. Aspiration levels are not fixed; they adjust to experience, drifting upward after success and downward after failure, and they are powerfully shaped by comparison with peers and with the past. A firm that has just had a good year aspires to more; a firm that has missed twice accepts less. Either way, the aspiration level — not a calculated optimum — is what determines when search stops.
The diagram is deliberately unflattering. The chosen strategy is the first acceptable one found, not the best available — and the aspiration level that defines "acceptable" was itself inherited rather than chosen.Ambiguity, not merely risk. Much strategic information is not merely probabilistic but ambiguous: the same data support several competing interpretations, and no amount of analysis resolves which is right. Ambiguity is expensive to hold in mind, so decision-makers tend to resolve it early by adopting one interpretation and treating it thereafter as fact.Willpower and self-interest are bounded too. Kahneman, extending Simon in his Nobel lecture, added that people are also short of self-control and are neither purely selfish nor purely fair. A leadership team can genuinely intend to exit an underperforming business and, quarter after quarter, fail to do so — not from ignorance but from bounded willpower and attachment.The practical consequences cluster in the places where strategy is hardest.Diagnosis becomes a highlight reel. Because attention is selective and working memory small, a diagnosis reduces a messy situation to a few salient features — usually those that were vivid, recent, or already being tracked. Rumelt's complaint that most strategies lack a real diagnosis is partly a cognitive story: producing a contestable diagnosis requires holding competing explanations side by side, which is exactly what working memory resists.Option sets shrink toward the familiar. Local search plus satisfiing plus a peer-anchored aspiration level is a recipe for incrementalism. This is not always a defect: incremental, adjacent moves are usually better-informed and more executable than bold departures. The failure mode is when the organisation believes it has conducted a broad search when it has merely enumerated its own history.Trade-offs are avoided because comparison is costly. Evaluating options against each other demands simultaneous consideration of incommensurable attributes — a heavy cognitive load. Choosing the option that is best on the dimension currently in focus, and not asking about the others, is cheaper. This is one reason strategies so often lack explicit sacrifices: the sacrifice is only visible if you look at two alternatives at once.Satisficing can be genuinely superior. It would be a mistake to read all this as an argument for more exhaustive analysis. Gigerenzer and colleagues showed that simple, fast, frugal rules often outperform complex models, particularly in uncertain environments where extra information mostly adds overfitting rather than signal. The skill is knowing which decisions deserve expensive deliberation and which are better served by a good-enough rule applied consistently. Bounded rationality is a diagnosis of the condition, not a prescription for paralysis.Simon's most important move was to treat organisations themselves as responses to individual cognitive limits. A firm's structure, routines, standard operating procedures, and division of labour exist largely so that no single person has to hold the whole problem. Hierarchy decomposes decisions; routines store solutions that no longer need to be reasoned out; departments specialise attention.That delegation has a cost that is also cognitive. Organisations learn locally — units optimise what they can see, and the knowledge that matters at the boundary between units tends not to reside anywhere. March's analysis of exploration versus exploitation sharpens the point: learning from experience improves what is already done, which makes the organisation better and better at the current game while progressively less able to notice that the game has changed. The "myopia of learning" is not an absence of intelligence but a consequence of where attention is placed. Slack — deliberately held surplus resource — is one of the few mechanisms that funds search far from current practice, which is why cutting it to zero is often a false economy.The remedies share a logic: they do not ask people to be less bounded, which never works, but move the work out of individual heads and into structures, artefacts, and commitments.Return to Northwind, the specialty coffee roaster, and watch the second blade cut.The board frames the question as "how do we grow profitably?" and, within an hour, is discussing three options: hire more field trainers, add a second roastery, or raise prices. All three are adjacent to current operations — textbook problemistic search. A fourth possibility, licensing the training curriculum to a national distributor rather than delivering it locally, never arises, not because it is a bad idea but because nobody's attention is allocated to it. One director later recalls thinking of it and not raising it, since the conversation had already "moved on."The aspiration level is inherited: 20% revenue growth, because that is what last year's plan said. Nobody asks whether 20% is the right number; it clears the bar, so search stops. When a director proposes the home-subscription segment, the discussion evaluates it on one attribute — brand fit — and drops it, because comparing it properly against the training bundle would require holding two different business models in mind at once.Northwind's strategy is not stupid. It is bounded, in a completely ordinary way. The value of naming the limits is that the remedies become visible: assign one person to search deliberately outside the current business; state the aspiration as a derived requirement rather than a precedent; require each option to be written on a single page with an explicit "what we give up" line; and, as the formulation process suggests, name in advance the evidence that would reopen the question.First, bounded rationality is not a licence for relativism or an excuse for poor analysis. Boundedly rational decision-makers can be careful, evidence-driven, and rigorous; they simply cannot be exhaustive, and the discipline lies in choosing what to compress and being honest about what was compressed. Second, the concept is inseparable from the ones that follow. Satisficing is a heuristic; the aspiration level is a reference point against which framing effects operate; and what a strategist notices is shaped by emotion and mental models. Bounded rationality names the container. The next subsections examine what happens inside it.
